### Section 143 source audit, independently verified

Every citation in this section was read directly from the tree, not taken from the delegated audit, and the delegated audit is still running. Where the two later disagree, the tree wins.

**Header 77 carries no safebox-specific struct; it reuses the header-13 struct.** `server/server/game/packet_info.cpp:157` reads `Set(HEADER_CG_SAFEBOX_ITEM_MOVE, sizeof(TPacketCGItemMove), "SafeboxItemMove");`, the same type registered for header 13 at `packet_info.cpp:121`. The value is 77 at `server/server/game/packet.h:61`, and the client declares the same value independently at `client/Client/UserInterface/Packet.h:58`. A sweep of the whole client tree for the symbol found the only two sends to be `SendSafeBoxItemMovePacket` at `PythonNetworkStreamPhaseGameItem.cpp:68-84` and its Python wrapper at `PythonNetworkStreamModule.cpp:1386-1402`, exposed to scripts as `SendSafeboxItemMovePacket` at `Module.cpp:2626`. The only other reference is a diagnostic name table at `client/Client/EterLib/NetStream.cpp:575`. So this is a single, closed, one-registration record.

**The layout is 9 bytes and is not profile-dependent, even though its builder is.** The server type at `packet.h:633-639` is `BYTE header`, `TItemPos Cell`, `TItemPos CellTo`, `WORD count`. The client type at `client/Client/UserInterface/Packet.h:529-535` is the same four fields under **different names**: `header`, `pos`, `change_pos`, `WORD num`. That divergence matters and is recorded as a caution: the two trees independently declare one layout with different field names, so no Rust field may borrow a name from only one of them as though it were shared. Both `TItemPos` types are the packed three-byte pair, server at `length.h:956-960` inside `#pragma pack(push, 1)` and client at `GameType.h:424-425` inside `#pragma pack (push, 1)` opened at `GameType.h:418` and closed at `:508`. So both sides compute 1 + 3 + 3 + 2 = **9 bytes**, and the client sends exactly that via `Send(sizeof(kItemMove), &kItemMove)` at `PythonNetworkStreamPhaseGameItem.cpp:80`. Neither struct is wrapped in any `__EXTENDED_SAFEBOX__` guard; the macro guards only the builder's parameter types. `protocol/src/cg_inventory.rs` already records this correctly as `cpp_type: "TPacketCGItemMove"`, `base_size: 9`, `Registered`, so this slice needs no inventory change.

**The handler is twelve lines and never reads either window byte.** `CInputMain::SafeboxItemMove` at `input_main.cpp:2462-2473` is the whole of it: reject if `!ch->CanHandleItem()`, reject if `!ch->GetSafebox()`, then `ch->GetSafebox()->MoveItem(pinfo->Cell.cell, pinfo->CellTo.cell, pinfo->count)` at `:2472`. It is dispatched at `input_main.cpp:3810-3812`. Only the two `.cell` halves are read. The two `window_type` bytes are **never read on this path at all**, which is a different fact from being read and validated, and it is why the shared position pair must not be treated as role-bearing here.

**The contrast with header 13 is the whole point of the slice.** `CInputMain::ItemMove` at `input_main.cpp:1060-1066` is three lines and calls `ch->MoveItem(pinfo->Cell, pinfo->CellTo, pinfo->count)`, passing both **whole** `TItemPos` values and the `WORD` count. The signature is `CHARACTER::MoveItem(TItemPos pos, TItemPos change_pos, WORD num)` at `char.h:1209`. So the two headers are byte-identical apart from byte 0 and then diverge completely: header 13 resolves windows through the character, header 77 discards them and addresses a container grid directly.

**A confirmed silent truncation: the wire count is a `WORD` and the container takes a `BYTE`.** `TPacketCGItemMove::count` is a `WORD` at `packet.h:638`, but `CSafebox::MoveItem`'s third parameter is a `BYTE` in **both** profiles, at `safebox.cpp:179` for the active arm and `safebox.cpp:181` for the other. The call at `input_main.cpp:2472` therefore narrows 16 bits to 8 with no cast and no check. This is real and it is consequential, because `safebox.cpp:211-212` treats `count == 0` as "move the whole stack". A client that transmits `count = 256` has that value truncated to 0 and moves the entire stack, and the guard at `safebox.cpp:197` `if (item->GetCount() < count) return false;` is applied to the already-truncated value, so the range check it performs is not the one the wire requested. No such truncation exists on the header-13 path, because `char.h:1209` takes a `WORD`. The normal client cannot trigger it, because its builder's parameter is already a `BYTE` at `PythonNetworkStreamPhaseGameItem.cpp:68`, so `num` at `:78` can never exceed 255. The defect is therefore latent in normal play and reachable only from a client that does not go through this builder. It is recorded, not reproduced: the codec preserves the `WORD` and never truncates.

**The container API is itself profile-dependent, under the same macro as Section 142.** `safebox.h:20` and `:22` give `MoveItem` as `(DWORD, DWORD, BYTE)` or `(BYTE, BYTE, BYTE)` across an `#if` at `safebox.h:19`-`:23`, and `safebox.cpp:164-168` does the same for `GetItem`, with `safebox.cpp:178-182` doing it again for the `MoveItem` definition. The active arm is the `DWORD` one, which is what makes the container a flat 32-bit cell index rather than a page number, and it corroborates Section 142's profile finding from a second, independent site. The dead arm would narrow any index above 255, which is consistent with its 5-column, 135-cell geometry.

**What `MoveItem` actually validates, in order.** `safebox.cpp:186` computes `max_position = 5 * m_iSize`, so the range is a flat index into a five-column grid, matching Section 142. `:188-189` rejects `bCell` or `bDestCell` at or above that bound; the comparison is `>=`, so it never clamps or wraps. `:191-192` resolves the source with `GetItem`, which itself bounds-checks at `safebox.cpp:170`. `:194-195` rejects an exchanging item. `:197-198` rejects when the stack is smaller than the count. Only then does the stack-merge branch at `:203-223` run, and its own guards are that destination and source differ, the destination is stackable, it lacks `ITEM_ANTIFLAG_STACK`, and the vnums match, followed by a socket-by-socket equality loop at `:207-209` that can still reject the merge outright.

**Three further defects in the move path.** At `:211-212` a zero count is promoted to the whole source stack, which is what makes the `WORD`-to-`BYTE` truncation dangerous. At `:214` the merge count is clamped by `MIN(g_bItemCountLimit - item2->GetCount(), count)`, so the wire count is silently reduced rather than rejected. And in the non-merge path the item is detached and re-homed at `:244-245` with **both `Remove` and `Add` return values discarded**, the same defect class already recorded for Section 142's check-in at `input_main.cpp:2358-2361`; `m_pkGrid->Get` at `:229` is likewise unchecked, and `Add` can still fail on its own `IsValidPosition` test at `safebox.cpp:58` after the item has already been removed. **This was first written here as an `IsValidPosition` *or* `IsExchanging* test citing `safebox.cpp:56-62` and `:194-195`, and that was wrong:** `CSafebox::Add` at `safebox.cpp:56-91` has no exchange check at all, and the only `IsExchanging` in the file is at `safebox.cpp:194`, which is inside `CSafebox::MoveItem`, a different method. The correction is recorded rather than smoothed over.

**One useful positive fact about equality.** The merge branch is explicitly excluded when source and destination are the same object at `safebox.cpp:203`, so a same-cell move cannot silently merge an item into itself. It then falls to `:226-227`, where `IsEmpty(bDestCell, ...)` is false for the occupied cell and the move is rejected. So header 77 **does** have an effective source-equals-destination guard, reached indirectly, which is the opposite of header 13, where Section 138 established that no equality guard exists.

**The client builder is well-behaved where Section 142's were not.** `SendSafeBoxItemMovePacket` at `PythonNetworkStreamPhaseGameItem.cpp:72-84` assigns all four fields before sending, sets the window of **both** positions to `INVENTORY` at `:77` and `:79`, sends exactly `sizeof(kItemMove)`, checks the `Send` result at `:80-81`, and returns the `SendSequence()` result. It does call `__PlaySafeBoxItemDropSound(bySourcePos)` at `:73` before the send, and it does not call `__CanActMainInstance()`. The window bytes are therefore hardcoded to `INVENTORY` on the wire by the client and ignored by the server, which is the precise statement of their opacity for this record. The Python wrapper at `Module.cpp:1388-1401` reads exactly three positional integers with no arity switch and **no `default:` label**, returning `Py_BuildException()` on a short tuple, so there is no fallthrough path that can send an uninitialised value. This is a genuine improvement on the check-in and check-out wrappers of Section 142, which had either no `default` at all or `default: break` and could both transmit indeterminate bytes. The wrapper's order is `(source, target, count)` at `:1389`, `:1392`, `:1395`, which matches the server's `MoveItem(Cell.cell, CellTo.cell, count)` exactly, so **there is no transposition here**, unlike Section 142. The one inherited defect is that the wrapper **discards the builder's `bool` return** at `Module.cpp:1399`, so a send failure is invisible to the script.


### Section 143 delegated audit, reconciled against the tree

The independent read-only audit ran in the reduced scope agreed after my own verification had already covered the rest. Every claim below was then re-checked directly against the source before being recorded, and one of my own errors was found and corrected in the process.

**It found a real error in my work, and I have kept the correction visible.** I had written that `CSafebox::Add` could still fail on its own `IsValidPosition` or `IsExchanging` test, citing `safebox.cpp:56-62` and `:194-195`. Reading `CSafebox::Add` at `safebox.cpp:56-91` in full shows it has **no** exchange check: its only guard is `IsValidPosition(dwPos)` at `:58`, after which it proceeds to `SetWindow`, `SetCell`, `Save`, an unchecked `m_pkGrid->Put` at `:69`, and `m_pkItems[dwPos] = pkItem` at `:70`. The only `IsExchanging` in the whole file is at `safebox.cpp:194`, inside `CSafebox::MoveItem`. Both the ledger and the Section 142 module text were corrected, and the Section 142 text was tightened to name the method rather than say only "inside the same container", which was true but ambiguous.

**The `CGrid` asymmetry is real, directional, and has no out-of-bounds read.** `CGrid::Put` at `libgame/grid.cpp:50-66` is fully protected, but **transitively**: it calls `IsEmpty` at `:52`, and `IsEmpty` performs the row check at `:92-93` and the column check at `:95-96`. `CGrid::Get` at `:68-82` bounds-checks **only** `iPos`, at `:70`; it never checks `iStart` at `:75` nor `iStart + x` at `:80`, and it only ever writes `false` into `m_pGrid`, so it cannot read out of bounds. The asymmetry is therefore one-directional: `Put` validates a whole range, `Get` validates a single index. This refines the Section 142 note, which recorded the same class of hazard without establishing which direction was safe.

**The rollback in the move path is sound, and its failure branch is dead code.** `safebox.cpp:226` calls `IsEmpty(bDestCell, 1, item->GetSize())` and `:231` then calls `Put` with the identical arguments. The only mutation between them is `Get(bCell, 1, size)` at `:229`, which can only clear cells, never occupy them. So `Put` cannot fail once `IsEmpty` has succeeded, and the failure branch at `:232-235`, which restores the source, is unreachable. That is a genuine, and slightly surprising, result: the rollback looks load-bearing and is not.

**One out-of-bounds write is possible but is not normal-client reachable.** `Get(bCell, 1, size)` at `safebox.cpp:229` escapes the allocation only when `size > 1` and `bCell` lies in the last grid row, which for a 54-row container means `bCell >= 265`. The check-in path cannot create that state, because `input_main.cpp:2310` calls `IsEmpty` first and `grid.cpp:92-93` rejects a row overflow. Only a DB-driven `CSafebox::Add` can create it, because `safebox.cpp:69` discards the `Put` result and `:70` records the item regardless. The same unguarded `Get` is also reached from `Remove` at `safebox.cpp:111`. There is no out-of-bounds read anywhere on this path.

**A more serious defect than any of the above: the safebox stack merge orphans the source item.** At `safebox.cpp:216-217` the merge calls `Remove(bCell)`, and the guard `if (item->GetCount() >= count)` is already guaranteed by the earlier check at `:197-198`, so `Remove` **always** runs. `CSafebox::Remove` at `:105-115` calls `pkItem->RemoveFromCharacter()` at `:113` and sets `m_pkItems[dwPos] = NULL` at `:115`. The following `:219` then decrements the count of an item that is no longer held by the container **or** by the character. A partial merge therefore leaves the remainder owned by nobody, unreachable, and never re-added, and a full merge leaves a zero-count orphan still referenced by nothing. This is a different and worse failure than the discarded-return-value class, because it loses a pointer rather than a status, and it is specific to this handler: `CHARACTER::MoveItem` performs the equivalent merge at `char_item.cpp:7800-7804` with **no** `Remove` at all, so the item stays owned while its count is reduced.

**The non-merge path never reads `count` at all.** After the merge branch, `:226-245` moves the whole item and the count is not consulted again, in contrast to `char_item.cpp:7825-7846` which does split. So for a non-stackable item, a requested count of one still moves the entire stack, and this is a different behaviour from header 13 rather than a defect in the codec.

**Header 77 is the only reuse of the struct, and the mall has no move verb at all.** In `packet_info.cpp`, only `:121` and `:157` name `TPacketCGItemMove`, out of 92 client-to-game rows, and no second size is registered for it. On the client, the token appears three times, and `:76` is the only assignment of header 77 anywhere in the tree. For the mall, header 77 always and only touches `ch->GetSafebox()` at `input_main.cpp:2472` with no `bMall` flag, unlike `SafeboxCheckout` at `:2368` and `:2377-2380`. `MoveItem` is a non-virtual `CSafebox` member and so does exist on the mall object, but no inbound header reaches it: the only mall header is 69, which dispatches to `SafeboxCheckout(..., true)`, a withdrawal. **The mall container therefore has no move operation on the wire in this tree at all**, which is a cleaner statement than "header 77 is not routed to the mall".

**The cross-direction collision is now closed, and it needs two sizes for one value.** `header 77` is a **9-byte** outbound client-to-game record and a **5-byte** inbound game-to-client record: the client registers `HEADER_GC_PARTY_INVITE` as `sizeof(TPacketGCPartyInvite)` at `PythonNetworkStream.cpp:108`, the struct is 5 packed bytes at `client/Client/UserInterface/Packet.h:2221-2225` inside the packed region at `:300-301` to `:3928`, and dispatch is at `PythonNetworkStreamPhaseGame.cpp:472-474` into `RecvPartyInvite` at `:3520-3537` with the fixed read at `:3523`. The server side is at `packet.h:2029-2033`, sent from `char.cpp:5943-5946`, and `client/Client/EterLib/NetStream.cpp:674` confirms the same value in the client's own game-to-client string table, next to `:575` for the client-to-game name. This is the strongest form of the collision argument in the whole series: a header-value-keyed table would need two different sizes for one number, so the directions must never share a table.

**Two further client-side facts worth keeping.** The builder omits `__CanActMainInstance()`, which the sibling `SendItemMovePacket` does call at `PythonNetworkStreamPhaseGameItem.cpp:734-735`, and the audible feedback helper `__PlaySafeBoxItemDropSound` at `:710-719` only `TraceError`s a bad index in `PythonSafeBox.cpp:57-61` and the builder then continues to `Send` anyway at `:80`. So a detected error changes the sound, not the transmission. Both are caller-layer and are not reproduced.

**One thing that remains genuinely unknown, and is recorded as unknown rather than guessed.** There is no client-side Python caller in this tree, so the `SendSafeboxItemMovePacket` script call site and the argument arity in real use cannot be cited. The wrapper itself is safe, having no arity switch and no `default:` label, but what scripts actually pass to it is not determinable from this checkout, exactly as for Section 142.


### Section 143 implementation: `protocol/src/cg_safebox_move.rs`

**The slice is a design decision, not a layout.** Section 138 receipted `CgItemMove` on the explicit contract that it stores **no** header field and always encodes 13, because header 13 was the only encodable value. Header 77 needs the same nine bytes with a different byte 0. The decision recorded here is to add a **separate record type** in a **new module** and to leave `cg_item_move.rs` byte-for-byte untouched, for three reasons that the audit established rather than assumed.

First, the two records are not one record with two spellings. Header 13's handler passes both whole `TItemPos` values so the server resolves the destination window; header 77's handler passes only the two `.cell` halves and never reads a window byte on any path. Folding them would force one meaning onto the window bytes where the source has two incompatible ones. Second, `CgItemMove` is already receipted with a public contract, and changing it would invalidate that receipt and its tests for no gain. Third, the two trees do not even agree on the field names, so a shared type would have to invent a neutral naming that matches neither.

**The stored-header rule, applied consistently.** `protocol/src/cg_safebox.rs` stores a closed three-value `SafeBoxKind` enum because headers 69, 70, and 71 are three legal values for one record. Header 77 is a **single** encodable value, so this record stores **no** header field and `header()` is an associated function, exactly as `CgItemMove` does. The rule is therefore the same in both modules: store a header only when more than one value must round-trip, and make the stored form a closed enum so no unencodable state can exist.

**Surface.** `CgSafeboxItemMove { from: CgItemPos, to: CgItemPos, count: u16 }` with `new`, `header`, `encode`, `encode_into`, `to_frame`, `decode`, and `decode_frame`; error type `CgSafeboxMoveError` with `Truncated`, `LengthMismatch`, and `InvalidHeader`; constants `CG_SAFEBOX_MOVE_WIRE_SIZE = 9` and `CG_SAFEBOX_MOVE_PAYLOAD_SIZE = 8`, plus a re-export of the shared `CG_ITEM_POS_SIZE`. The shared `CgItemPos` is reused, so this is the **sixth** Rust codec to share one packed position layout. `count` is a `u16` and is never truncated, which is the codec-level counterpart of the caller defect recorded above.

**Nothing else changed.** `cg_wire.rs` and `cg_inventory.rs` are untouched, because the live inventory already carried header 77 as `base_size: 9`. There is no second framer, no `#[repr(C)]` compatibility struct, no `unsafe`, and no gameplay policy. The only edit outside the new file is the single `pub mod cg_safebox_move;` line in `lib.rs`.

**Tests: 15 added, taking the protocol crate from 318 to 333 unit tests.** Coverage is the exact golden bytes a stock client produces, the layout at every offset, agreement with the live inventory for both header 13 and header 77, full-width `WORD` round-trips including 255, 256, 257, 511, 512, and `u16::MAX`, all **256** values of **both** window bytes through both decoders, position boundaries including the legacy `0xffff` sentinel, exhaustive rejection of all 255 wrong headers at the exact length in both the raw and the framed path, a mutual-rejection test proving the two records are not interchangeable, raw and framed length-before-header precedence, framed header validation at the exact payload length, accessor-versus-encoder agreement including the appending `encode_into` path, fragmented streaming at every split point, a strict byte-at-a-time prefix that must retain a partial tail, two records streaming back to back, and `Display` stability through a `dyn Error`.

**Mutation testing: 13 mutations applied, 13 caught**, with the source restored after each. Removing raw header validation, removing framed header validation, relaxing the exact length to a minimum, removing the framed length check, encoding `count` big-endian, **truncating `count` to `u8`**, swapping the source and destination positions, reading the framed `count` at the wrong offset, moving the raw header check to after the field reads, making `header()` return 13, adding a `window_type` allowlist to the decoder, clamping `count` to 255, and changing the wire-size constant to 10. The `u8` truncation mutation matters most: it is the legacy defect reproduced in the codec, and the full-width round-trip test is what catches it, so the guarantee that `count` survives at sixteen bits is tested rather than asserted.

**Gates.** `cargo build`, `cargo fmt --all -- --check`, `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets --locked --offline -- -D warnings`, `RUSTDOCFLAGS="-D warnings" cargo doc --workspace --no-deps`, `cargo test --workspace --all-targets`, and `cargo test --workspace --doc` are all clean. **1013 tests across 27 test binaries, 0 failed, plus 6 doc-tests, so 1019 in total.** Three consecutive all-targets runs were made to confirm stability after one early run reported a spurious `exit 101` with a partial count; the three clean runs agree exactly at 1013, and the partial run's own output showed no test failure, so it is recorded as a build-lock artifact of running the gates back to back rather than a real failure, and is noted here rather than quietly dropped.


### Section 144 selected: header 21, the item-destroy record

**Header 21 is the same 4-byte layout as the already-implemented `CgItemUse`, and asks for the same design answer Section 143 just settled.** `server/server/game/packet.h` sets `HEADER_CG_ITEM_DESTROY = 21` and declares `command_item_destroy` / `TPacketCGItemDestroy` at `packet.h:627-631` as `BYTE header` plus one packed `TItemPos Cell`, so 1 + 3 = **4 bytes** and a 3-byte framed payload. That is byte-for-byte the shape of `TPacketCGItemUse` at `packet.h:599-603`, which is header 11 and which Section 139 already receipted in `protocol/src/cg_item_use.rs`. So this is a second legal header value attaching to a layout that already has a receipted codec storing no header, and Section 143's answer should carry over: a separate record type in a new module, leaving the receipted codec untouched. The auditor is explicitly asked to argue against that if the 4-byte case differs.

**The handler is three lines and passes the whole position, not just the cell.** `CInputMain::ItemDestroy` at `input_main.cpp:1053-1058` is a null check on `ch` and then `ch->DestroyItem(pinfo->Cell)`, dispatched at `input_main.cpp:3703`. The contrast with the Section 143 safebox handler is the point: that one extracted `pinfo->Cell.cell` and discarded the window, this one hands the entire `TItemPos` to the character. So for this record the window byte is genuinely **read and used**, not merely carried, and the audit must determine how exactly. That is the opposite of the Section 143 situation and it is why the two records cannot share one type.

**Two neighbours make the guard surface worth auditing rather than assuming.** `ItemDrop` ends at `input_main.cpp:1050` with `ch->DropItem(pinfo->Cell, pinfo->count)`, and `ItemMove` follows at `:1060-1066` with `ch->MoveItem(pinfo->Cell, pinfo->CellTo, pinfo->count)`. All three sit within eight lines of each other and none of them is more than a null check, so the set of checks the character method performs is the entire security surface for all three. Whether the destroy path is protected is therefore a question about `CHARACTER::DestroyItem` and not about the handler, and that is what the audit is being asked to establish.

**The live inventory already has this record**, as `pub const HEADER_CG_ITEM_DESTROY: CgHeader = CgHeader(0x15)`, so the expected change set is again one new module plus one `pub mod` line, with no inventory or framer edit. That expectation is stated as a hypothesis for the auditor to check, not as a fact.

**The remaining `TItemPos` family is being enumerated programmatically** so the order of the rest of the slices is exact rather than remembered. Twelve `TPacketCG*` records embed a packed `TItemPos`; five are already done as item-move, item-use, item-use-to-item, item-give, and the two safebox transfer headers. The rest are item-drop, item-drop2, item-destroy, item-sell, exchange, and the private-shop check-in. One of those, `TPacketCGItemSell` at `packet.h:649-655`, sits inside `#ifdef ENABLE_SELL_ITEM` and a first search found **no** `#define` for that macro anywhere in either tree, which would make header 22 a compiled-out record rather than an unimplemented one. That is exactly the kind of claim that has been wrong before, so the audit is required to produce the define sites and `#if` sites the way Section 142 did for `__EXTENDED_SAFEBOX__`, and to say explicitly whether the header is registered.


### Section 143 independent review: MINOR, with one real test gap

Reviewer `sec143-review` (`sub-dbf7f491`), report `/tmp/agent-reports/cg_safebox_move_review.md`, worked read-only in `/tmp/rev143` and confirmed nothing under `/workspace` changed. Verdict **MINOR**: the codec is correct, all fifteen module tests pass, and the layout, widths, error precedence, and both handler bodies verify against the oracle.

**The most valuable finding was about my own reasoning, not the code.** The module had justified being a separate record type by claiming that merging would have to pick one meaning for the window bytes. That is false: the window bytes are opaque at this boundary, and a merged type would have kept both `TItemPos` values whole and never interpreted them, so there was no meaning to arbitrate. The reviewer also noted the mechanism I had declined already exists and is receipted, at `cg_client_version.rs:61` and `cg_handshake.rs:51`. The conclusion was right; the argument was wrong. The doc now **withdraws the reasoning explicitly** rather than quietly restating it, and gives the real reason: two types make handing a header-77 record to a header-13 call site a **compile error**, while a single `kind` field lets the same mistake compile and fail on the wire. The honest cost, roughly duplicated layout code and a two-place `TItemPos` change, is now stated rather than elided.

**One real surviving mutation.** Changing `CG_SAFEBOX_MOVE_PAYLOAD_SIZE` from 8 to 7 left the whole workspace green, because the constant was only a `Vec::with_capacity` hint and a loop bound. A public constant that documents the payload size must be pinned against real output, and there are now two tests that do it: one asserts the declared sizes equal the bytes actually produced, and one asserts the re-exported `CG_ITEM_POS_SIZE` is 3 and agrees with the `cg_item_move` original. Both mutations are now caught.

**Three citation imprecisions, all corrected.** `TItemPos` was cited as `length.h:956-960`, which is the pack directive plus the field declarations; the typedef closes at `:1057`, so the house form `956-1057` is used instead. The client builder was cited only at `PythonNetworkStreamPhaseGameItem.cpp:68`; the non-extended arm at `:70` is now cited too. And `safebox.cpp:203` was described as a rejection when it is the self-merge guard `item != item2`; the rejection is the `IsEmpty` test at `:226-227`.

**Two omissions closed.** The module did not document the cross-direction collision, even though the sibling safebox and item-give modules both do: header 77 is `HEADER_GC_PARTY_INVITE` at `packet.h:164` and client `Packet.h:161`, a five-byte inbound party invite, while header 13 is `HEADER_GC_STUN` at `packet.h:113`. And the inactive non-extended profile is now recorded accurately: `safebox.cpp:181` narrows **both** `cell` words as well as the count, which is worse than the count alone, even though `__EXTENDED_SAFEBOX__` at `prodomodefines.h:61` makes that arm unreachable.

**One consistency change and two benign survivors.** `InvalidHeader` is now the struct form `InvalidHeader { actual: u8 }` used by twelve of the fourteen sibling CG modules, instead of a tuple variant, so the cross-rejection test no longer has to spell two shapes in one expression. The reviewer's own `saturating_add` to `+1` and a "reject count 0" mutation both survive and are observationally identical or semantically wrong, and are recorded as such rather than papered over.

**A methodology error of my own, caught and fixed.** My first mutation harness piped cargo output through `grep ... | head -4` and then tested the truncated string for `FAILED`. Because the workspace suite runs twenty-seven binaries, a failure in a later binary was invisible, and two of my "caught" verdicts were not supported by the evidence. The harness was rewritten to capture complete output and use the real exit code plus a summed failure count, then **proven** against a deliberate break before being trusted. Every Section 143 mutation was then re-run from scratch. Three of the original thirteen were not real mutations at all: two added a dead read instead of removing the header check, and one was ambiguous against three occurrences. Corrected and re-run properly, **all fifteen mutations are caught**, including the reviewer's survivor.

### Section 144 audit: header 21, the item-destroy record

**My premise for question B3 was wrong, and the correction matters.** I asked whether `IsSecured()`, `IsExchanging()`, and `GetCount() <= 0` were absent, the way they genuinely are on the safebox path. All three are **present** in `CHARACTER::DestroyItem` at `char_item.cpp:7407-7442`: `IsExchanging()` at `:7420`, `GetCount() <= 0` at `:7426`, and `IsSecured()` at `:7430` guarded by `__ENABLE_INVENTORY_PROTECTED_SYSTEM__`, which **is** defined at `prodomodefines.h:169` and included at `char_item.cpp:48`. The destroy path is at least as well guarded as its siblings. I had carried the safebox finding across to a record it does not describe.

**A confirmed use-after-free fires on every successful destroy.** `char_item.cpp:7438` calls `ITEM_MANAGER::instance().RemoveItem(item)`, whose tail at `item_manager.cpp:594` is `M2_DESTROY_ITEM(item)`, reaching the plain `M2_DELETE(item)` at `item_manager.cpp:649`. The pooling and debug-allocator alternatives are commented out at `server/server/game/stdafx.h:6` and `:8`, so the plain `delete` path is the live one. The very next line, `char_item.cpp:7439`, passes `item->GetName()` into `ChatPacket`, and `item.h:66` dereferences `m_pProto` from the freed object. This is not latent and not script-dependent: it runs on every destroy that passes the guards. It is a legacy C++ robustness follow-up and is **not** reproduced or normalised in the transport-free codec.

**The window byte is read and validated here, the opposite of Section 143.** `CHARACTER::DestroyItem` takes the whole `TItemPos` and calls `IsValidItemPosition` at `char_item.cpp:10015`, which range-checks per window. But the check is nearly a no-op for the two windows that matter: `GetItem` at `char_item.cpp:260` returns `m_pointsInstant.pItems[wCell]` for both `INVENTORY` and `EQUIPMENT` from the **same array** at `:262-269` with the **same bound** at `:10020-10022`, while `GetWear` at `:655` indexes `pItems[INVENTORY_MAX_NUM + bCell]`, so the two window values alias. `SAFEBOX` and `MALL` pass `IsValidItemPosition` but then fall into `GetItem`'s `default: return NULL` at `:301`, so container items are simply not destroyable through this header. The window byte is therefore read and range-checked, but it does not confine the request, and no `IsEquipped` check exists; the path is nonetheless sound because the unequip happens as a documented side effect at `item.cpp:369-377` with the wear slot cleared at `:1562`.

**The client wrapper is the safe kind, but for a reason worth recording.** `netSendItemDestroyPacket` at `PythonNetworkStreamModule.cpp:826-835` takes **exactly one** argument, reads it into `Cell.cell` at `:830`, and returns `Py_BuildException()` on failure at `:831`. There is no arity switch, no `default:`, and no fall-through, so it is not in the uninitialised-value family. The real defect is subtler: `TItemPos Cell;` at `:828` is default-constructed, and the client `SItemPos()` constructor at `GameType.h:426-430` sets `window_type = INVENTORY` and `cell = WORD_MAX`. Because only `cell` is ever assigned, **the window byte is fully initialised but permanently 1**, so it would pass any "every byte is defined" check while no other window is reachable. The sibling `netSendItemDropPacketNew` at `:837` does it the other way, with a real `switch (PyTuple_Size(poArgs))`, so this codebase contains both wrapper styles. The builder at `PythonNetworkStreamPhaseGameItem.cpp:641-654` is clean: `__CanActMainInstance()` at `:643`, every byte assigned, `Send` checked at `:648`, and the registered script name is `SendItemDestroyPacket` at `:2572`. Exactly one send path exists.

**A cross-direction collision that is not merely a size mismatch, but a naming trap.** Header 21 is `HEADER_CG_ITEM_DESTROY` at `packet.h:30` and client `Packet.h:30`, but in the opposite direction the server calls 21 `HEADER_GC_ITEM_SET` at `packet.h:122` while the **client calls the same record `HEADER_GC_ITEM_SET2`** at client `Packet.h:117`, with the client's own `HEADER_GC_ITEM_SET` at 20. So a tooling step that pairs game-to-client records by name across the two trees would match the wrong records, which is a sharper hazard than the two-sizes-for-one-value problem alone. Header 21 was genuinely absent from the recorded collision set and is now added.

**A correction to the family census, in the auditor's favour and against my own first pass.** There are **thirteen** `TPacketCG*` records embedding a packed `TItemPos`, not the twelve I had recorded: `TPacketCGDragonSoulRefine` at `packet.h:2771` was missing, and it is variable-length, holding a `TItemPos` **array**, so it can never be a fixed-size codec. The census was re-derived with a brace-matching parser that finds every `typedef struct ... { ... } TPacketxxx;` and inspects the body, giving 266 parsed packet typedefs, 18 containing a `TItemPos`, and 13 of those being client-to-game. A looser regex I tried first reported fourteen by falsely matching `TPacketCGPrivateShop`, which is `BYTE bHeader; BYTE bSubHeader;` and contains no position at all; the parser result is the one recorded.

**`TPacketCGItemSell` is compiled out, so header 22 is unreachable rather than unimplemented.** `ENABLE_SELL_ITEM` has exactly two sites in both trees, `packet.h:31` and `packet.h:649`, and **zero** `#define` sites, so the guarded struct never exists, header 22 is never registered in `packet_info.cpp`, and the client has neither the constant nor a builder. This is the same evidence pattern Section 142 established for `__EXTENDED_SAFEBOX__`, and it is why header 22 must never be given a codec despite appearing in the client's header enum.

**Remaining fixed-width work, in the exact order the census gives:** header 12 `TPacketCGItemDrop` at `packet.h:612`, 8 bytes; header 20 `TPacketCGItemDrop2` at `:619`, 10 bytes; header 27 `TPacketCGExchange` at `:724`, 14 bytes active and profile-dependent through `ENABLE_REMOVE_LIMIT_GOLD`, which widens `arg1` to an eight-byte `unsigned long long`; and the private-shop check-in at `packet.h:1380`. Header 205 is variable-length. Header 22 is permanently out.


### Section 144 implementation: `protocol/src/cg_item_destroy.rs`

**The record.** Header 21 `HEADER_CG_ITEM_DESTROY`, declared at `packet.h:627-631` as a `BYTE header` plus one packed `TItemPos Cell`. `TItemPos` is three packed bytes at `length.h:956-1057`, so the record is exactly **4 bytes** and its framed payload **3**. Nothing in the declaration is conditional, so unlike the safebox transfer this width is not profile-dependent. `protocol/src/cg_inventory.rs` already carried `base_size: 4`, so again the only edit outside the new file is one `pub mod cg_item_destroy;` line; `cg_wire.rs` and `cg_inventory.rs` are untouched, and there is no second framer, no `#[repr(C)]` compatibility struct, no `unsafe`, and no gameplay policy.

**A separate type even though the layout is identical to an existing codec.** `TPacketCGItemUse` at `packet.h:599-603` is the same 4-byte shape and is already receipted as `cg_item_use.rs`. The Section 143 reasoning applies unchanged and is now stated as an API-level guarantee rather than a wire-level one: two types make passing a header-21 record to a header-11 call site a compile error, whereas one type with a `kind` field would let it compile and fail on the wire. A test asserts the two records really do agree on every byte after byte 0, so the duplication is visible rather than assumed. The operation differs outright, too: the safebox move handler discards both window bytes, while `DestroyItem` receives the whole `TItemPos` and range-checks the window.

**Surface.** `CgItemDestroy { cell: CgItemPos }` with `new`, `header`, `encode`, `encode_into`, `to_frame`, `decode`, and `decode_frame`; `CgItemDestroyError` with `Truncated`, `LengthMismatch`, and `InvalidHeader { actual: u8 }` in the struct form used by the sibling modules; constants `CG_ITEM_DESTROY_WIRE_SIZE = 4` and `CG_ITEM_DESTROY_PAYLOAD_SIZE = 3`, plus the re-exported `CG_ITEM_POS_SIZE`. This is the **seventh** Rust codec to share the one packed three-byte position, and the field is named `cell` to match `cg_item_use` while the module documents that the two trees disagree (`Cell` on the server, `pos` on the client).

**Tests: 18 added, taking the protocol crate from 335 to 353 unit tests.** Coverage includes the golden bytes at exact source offsets, the exact byte sequence a stock client sends, all **256** window values through both decode paths, cell boundaries including the client's own `0xffff` default, exhaustive rejection of all 255 wrong headers **at the exact length** in both the raw and the framed path, mutual rejection against header 11, the shared-layout assertion above, length-before-header precedence on both paths, header-before-field ordering, accessor-versus-encoder agreement including the appending `encode_into` path, every raw and framed length from 0 to 12 outside the exact size, fragmented streaming at every split point, a byte-at-a-time prefix that must retain partial tails, two records streaming back to back, the declared-size pins, and `Display` stability through a `dyn Error`.

**Mutation testing: 12 mutations applied, 12 caught**, using the corrected harness. Removing raw header validation, removing framed header validation, relaxing the exact length to a minimum, removing the framed length check, changing the emitted header to 11, normalising the window byte to 1, encoding the cell big-endian, reading the position one byte early, moving the raw header check after the field reads, drifting the wire-size constant to 5, drifting the payload-size constant to 2, and shifting the framed position offset. Mutations 6 and 10-11 are the ones that matter most here: normalising the window to the single value the stock client can send would silently destroy the 255 other legal values, and the two constant mutations are the exact class of gap the Section 143 review found surviving.

**Defects recorded and deliberately not reproduced.** The use-after-free at `char_item.cpp:7439`, which fires on every successful destroy; the permanently-1 client window byte; the server's `GetItem` aliasing `INVENTORY` and `EQUIPMENT` onto the same array; the container windows that pass `IsValidItemPosition` but then hit `GetItem`'s `default: return NULL`; the absent `IsEquipped` check; the discarded return value at `input_main.cpp:1057`; and the `HEADER_GC_ITEM_SET` versus `HEADER_GC_ITEM_SET2` naming drift across the two trees.

**Gates.** Build, `cargo fmt --all -- --check`, strict workspace Clippy with `-D warnings`, strict rustdoc, all-target tests, and doc tests are all clean. **1033 tests across 27 test binaries, 0 failed, plus 6 doc-tests, so 1039 total.** Measured after formatting: `protocol/src/cg_item_destroy.rs` is 26,861 bytes / 677 lines / sha256 `3b19b9993d4ef15cd3c4ba801243294198ffc9a3792ed448bc36a09b080dc302`, and `protocol/src/lib.rs` is 20,788 bytes / 687 lines / sha256 `8dc74bbbd6d612a3957383fbd809820f9c37dda4128418f4dfc10f7ca954c9d9`. The tree is 137 Rust files and 95,111 lines.

### A note on the census correction, recorded because both numbers were wrong

I had carried "twelve `TPacketCG*` records embed a packed `TItemPos`"; the auditor found **thirteen**, the extra being the variable-length `TPacketCGDragonSoulRefine` at `packet.h:2771`, which holds a `TItemPos` **array** and so can never be a fixed-size codec. My own first attempt to confirm that number used a non-greedy regex and reported **fourteen**, falsely matching `TPacketCGPrivateShop`, which is `BYTE bHeader; BYTE bSubHeader;` and contains no position at all. Replacing it with a brace-matching parser that finds each `typedef struct ... { ... } TPacketxxx;` and inspects the real body gives the agreed figure: 266 packet typedefs parsed, **26** struct definitions anywhere in the file whose body mentions a `TItemPos`, 19 of them named `TPacket*`, and **13** of those client-to-game. The 7 non-packet helpers are `SPrivateShopItem`, `packet_item_use`, `packet_item_move`, `packet_exchange`, `SSubPacketGCAuraSetItem`, `SSubPacketGCAuraRefineCheckIn`, and `SSubPacketGCAuraRefineCheckOut`. The lesson is the one already learned for header searches: a pattern that has not been checked against a known negative can invent a record, and here the invented record was the harmless-looking kind.


### Section 145 pre-audit: header 12, the item-drop record

Recorded from a direct read while the delegated audit runs, so the evidence is not lost and the auditor can be checked against it rather than the other way round. Line numbers are mine and are re-verifiable.

**My own earlier claim about this handler was wrong, and the correction matters.** I had written that `CInputMain::ItemDrop` ends at `input_main.cpp:1050` with `ch->DropItem(pinfo->Cell, pinfo->count)`. That is the **`ItemDrop2`** handler. The truth is that the two headers are genuinely different operations and not two spellings of one:

* `CInputMain::ItemDrop` at `input_main.cpp:1027-1040` handles header 12, casts `TPacketCGItemDrop`, null-checks `ch` at `:1032`, then branches on `pinfo->gold > 0` at `:1036` into `ch->DropGold(pinfo->gold)`, and otherwise calls `ch->DropItem(pinfo->Cell)` at `:1039` with **one** argument.
* `CInputMain::ItemDrop2` at `input_main.cpp:1042-1051` handles header 20, casts the 10-byte `TPacketCGItemDrop2`, repeats the same gold branch at `:1047`, and otherwise calls `ch->DropItem(pinfo->Cell, pinfo->count)` at `:1050` with **two** arguments.

So header 12 reads no count field, because its struct has none, and the out-of-struct read I had worried about does not exist. The correction was sent to the auditor immediately.

**The `DWORD gold` field is read, and it selects the operation.** `input_main.cpp:1036` makes `gold > 0` the sole discriminator between dropping currency and dropping an item. A client that sets `gold` never reaches the item path at all, which means the window byte in the same record is simply ignored on the gold path. The codec must therefore preserve `gold` at full 32-bit width and must not validate it against anything, because the only server-side bound is a comparison against the character's own balance.

**Header 12 cannot drop a partial stack, and the reason is a default argument.** The declaration at `char.h:1190` is `bool DropItem(TItemPos Cell, WORD bCount=0);`, so the one-argument call at `:1039` passes zero. Inside the method, `char_item.cpp:7498-7499` is `if (bCount == 0 || bCount > item->GetCount()) bCount = item->GetCount();`, which turns zero into "the whole stack" rather than into one. The partial-drop machinery at `:7510-7530` is real and does split a stack, creating a fresh item at `:7522`, but header 12 can never reach it. Only header 20, which carries an explicit `WORD count`, can.

**A second dead branch, the same shape as the safebox rollback.** Because `:7498-7499` has already replaced any zero with `item->GetCount()`, the `if (bCount == 0)` guard at `char_item.cpp:7512-7517` can never be true, so its `return false` and its test-server log line are unreachable. This is the third instance of that pattern in this audit series, after the safebox move rollback at `safebox.cpp:231-235` and the merge guard at `:216`. A recurring shape across three separate files is worth naming as a class rather than as three unrelated slips.

**A signedness narrowing on the gold path changes behaviour.** `CHARACTER::DropGold` is declared `bool DropGold(int gold)` at `char_item.cpp:7554` and `char.h:1265`, taking a **signed** `int`, while the wire field is an unsigned `DWORD` passed straight through at `input_main.cpp:1037`. Any value at or above `0x80000000` therefore arrives negative and is rejected by the first test at `:7556`, so the top half of the wire range is unreachable for gold. The bound that does apply is `gold > GetGold()` at the same line, which is the only real validation on this path.

**The gold path is guarded less thoroughly than the item path, in two specific ways.** `DropGold` checks its amount at `:7556`, `CanHandleItem()` at `:7559`, and a time limit at `:7562-7569`. It has **no `IsDead()` test**, although `DropItem` has one at `char_item.cpp:7467`, so a dead character can drop currency while being unable to drop items. It also has **no `IsSecured()` test**, although `DropItem` has one at `:7489-7495` under `__ENABLE_INVENTORY_PROTECTED_SYSTEM__`, so a protected inventory still permits gold to be dropped. The item-level checks that are absent here, `IsExchanging`, `isLocked`, and the quest-running test, are arguably not applicable, because this path creates a synthetic ground item rather than removing one from a container; the two missing checks above are character-level and so are genuine asymmetries.

**`abs()` on an unsigned value at `char_item.cpp:7446` is dead.** The line is `bCount = abs(bCount);` where `bCount` is a `WORD`. A `WORD` promotes to `int` across the usual arithmetic conversions, so the value is always in `0..=65535` and `abs` is the identity function. The line is a no-op, which suggests it was written for a signed count and the type was later changed. The auditor is asked to confirm and to say whether any caller can pass a value for which the intent would have mattered.


### Section 145 audit: header 12, the item-drop record, reconciled

The delegated audit was checked line by line against the tree rather than accepted. It confirmed claims 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 7, 8, 9, 10 and 13 of the brief, confirmed my mid-audit correction to the `ItemDrop`/`ItemDrop2` mix-up exactly, and found two further real errors of mine plus a small number of line-number imprecisions. Those are recorded below instead of being quietly fixed, because the point of the ledger is that a future reader can see what was wrong.

**My error one: header 12 is not free.** The brief asserted it was "genuinely free" of cross-direction collision. It is not. `packet.h:112` declares `HEADER_GC_ATTACK = 12`. The collision is, however, **dead**, and that distinction matters:

* No `TPacketGCAttack` exists in the server tree, and `grep -RniI 'GC_ATTACK' server/server/` returns exactly one line, the declaration itself. There is no send site.
* The client has no `HEADER_GC_ATTACK` constant anywhere. Its GC enum skips 12 entirely, going from 11 at `Packet.h:108` to 13 at `:109`, its receive map has no entry between `PythonNetworkStream.cpp:62` and `:63`, and its own second string list skips index 12, going from `stringList[11]` to `stringList[13]`.
* An inbound 12 would therefore be rejected by `CheckPacket` at `PythonNetworkStream.cpp:536-543`, which clears the receive buffer and posts a quit message.
* The client *does* carry an unused ten-byte `TPacketGCAttack` at `Packet.h:2102-2108`, but nothing registers or dispatches it.

So header 12 belongs in a **third** category, weaker than both of the existing ones: *nominally colliding, server-enum-only, no two sizes required*. It is categorically weaker than 21 and 77, which are live two-sizes collisions. If a live GC 12 were ever implemented, the client's unused ten-byte struct is exactly what would force two sizes.

**My error two: the collision-set list itself.** The brief listed 52 and 60 as colliding. Line 4102 of this ledger records them as **free**. The brief was wrong and the ledger was right; I had conflated "colliding" with "free" when composing the question.

**Two line-number imprecisions of mine, now corrected.** `CInputMain::ItemDrop` begins at `input_main.cpp:1024`, not `:1027`: `:1024` is the signature and `:1026` is the `command_item_drop` cast, and `:1027` is blank. And `char.h:1265`, which declares `bool DropGold(INT gold);`, sits **inside** `#ifdef ENABLE_REMOVE_LIMIT_GOLD` at `char.h:1262`. That macro is defined, at `prodomodefines.h:157`, so the signed `int` signature is the active one and my narrowing finding stands. But `GetGold()` in that same guard returns `unsigned long long` at `char.h:1263`, so the second half of the test at `char_item.cpp:7556`, `gold > GetGold()`, is evaluated in unsigned 64-bit arithmetic, and only the first half, `gold <= 0`, is signed. The codec doc now says this precisely.

**Registration is unambiguous.** `packet.h:612-617` declares `command_item_drop`, registered exactly once, at `packet_info.cpp:118`, under the name `"ItemDrop"`. The auditor swept all 129 `Set()` rows, 93 in `CPacketInfoCG` at `:96-195` and 36 in `CPacketInfoGG` at `:201-243`, and found the only other 12 in the tree at `packet_info.cpp:214`, where it is `HEADER_GG_FIND_POSITION` in a different table with a different processor at `input_p2p.cpp:32`. That is a shared value, not a duplicate registration. One latent hazard is worth naming: `packet_info.cpp:20-21` makes `Set` silently first-wins, so a genuine duplicate would be invisible.

**The layout, confirmed.** `packet.h:274` opens `#pragma pack(1)` for the packet declarations and does not close it until `:3540`. Inside that, `command_item_drop` is `BYTE header` at offset 0, packed `TItemPos Cell` at `:1..4` using the three-byte `SItemPos` from `length.h:956-1057`, and `DWORD gold` at `:4..8`. One plus three plus four is **eight bytes**, and the framed payload is **seven**. Nothing in the declaration is conditional, so the width is not profile-dependent.

**Confirmed, and the reason the record is not inert: `gold` selects the operation.** `input_main.cpp:1036` is `if (pinfo->gold > 0)`, the **sole** discriminator between dropping currency and dropping an item. A client that sets `gold` never reaches the item path, and the window byte in the same record is ignored on that path. The only bound the server applies to the amount is a comparison against the character's own balance, which is character state, so the codec preserves `gold` as an opaque 32-bit word and applies none of its own.

**Confirmed: header 12 cannot drop a partial stack.** `char.h:1190` declares `bool DropItem(TItemPos Cell, WORD bCount=0);`, so the one-argument call at `:1039` passes zero, and `char_item.cpp:7498-7499` turns any zero into `item->GetCount()`. The split machinery at `:7510-7530` is real and does create a fresh item at `:7522`, but `DropItem` has only two call sites server-wide, `:1039` and `:1050`, so only header 20 can reach it. Header 20 is therefore a strict **superset** of header 12, not an equivalent spelling: it shares the gold discriminator and adds the only partial-drop capability the protocol has.

**Confirmed dead code, the third instance of one recurring shape.** Because `:7498-7499` has already replaced every zero, the `if (bCount == 0)` guard at `char_item.cpp:7512-7517` can never be true, so its `return false` and its test-server log line are unreachable. The same shape appears in the safebox move rollback at `safebox.cpp:231-235` and in that method's merge guard at `:216`. Three separate files showing one pattern is a class, not three slips, and the ledger now names it as such. Separately, `abs()` at `char_item.cpp:7446` is a no-op, because a `WORD` promotes to `int`, the value is always in `0..=65535`, and `abs` is the identity there. The same no-op appears at `:7604` in `MoveItem`; the only meaningful `abs` in the file is at `:6648`. The original intent is **not** determinable: the `bCount` name on a `WORD` parameter is a style hint, not evidence.

**Confirmed, and the two guard asymmetries are real.** `DropGold` checks its amount at `:7556`, `CanHandleItem()` at `:7559`, and a time limit at `:7562-7569`. It has **no `IsDead()` test**, although `DropItem` has one at `:7467`, so a dead character can drop currency but not items. It has **no `IsSecured()` test**, although `DropItem` has one at `:7489-7495` under `__ENABLE_INVENTORY_PROTECTED_SYSTEM__`, itself defined at `prodomodefines.h:169`, so a protected inventory still permits currency to be dropped. Both are character-level checks, which is what makes them genuine asymmetries rather than not-applicable cases. The `IsExchanging`, `isLocked`, quest-running and anti-flag checks that are absent from `DropGold` **are** not applicable, because that path creates a synthetic ground item instead of removing a container item, and the auditor agrees on that split.

**Two further findings the audit added, both of which I had missed.**

* *Neither path is rate limited as shipped.* `g_ItemDropTimeLimitValue` and `g_GoldDropTimeLimitValue` are both initialised to `0` at `questmanager.cpp:35` and `:33`, and both guards are written `if (0 != g_...)`, so a default server drops with no delay whatsoever. The limits are only ever set from configuration, at `:1605` and `:1600`.
* *`DropGold` can report success on a failed placement.* `Save()` at `:7595` and `return true` at `:7596` sit **outside** the `AddToGround` block, while the actual currency deduction `PointChange` at `:7582` sits **inside** it. A drop whose ground placement fails still returns true and still persists the character. The severity is nil only because the handler discards the return value at `input_main.cpp:1037`; a caller that checked it would see a false success.

**The client's own wrapper is one of the safe ones, and it is safer than a naive read suggests.** `netSendItemDropPacket` at `PythonNetworkStreamModule.cpp:802-824` switches on the arity at `:805`, with `case 1` at `:807` reading only `Cell.cell` and `case 2` at `:811` reading both fields, and its `default:` arm at `:817-818` **returns** `Py_BuildException()` rather than breaking, so no arity falls through to a send. It then calls `SendItemDropPacket(Cell, 0)` at `:822`, hardcoding the currency word to zero, so the stock client can never reach the gold path through this wrapper at all. In `case 1` the window byte is never assigned, but it is also **not** indeterminate: `TItemPos Cell;` at `:804` is default-constructed through `SItemPos()` at `GameType.h:426-430` to `(INVENTORY, WORD_MAX)`, so the transmitted window byte is deterministically `1`. Calling that uninitialised would be wrong, and the codec doc now distinguishes the two cases explicitly. `netSendElkDropPacket` at `:866-875` and `netSendGoldDropPacketNew` at `:877-886` are bare-read wrappers with no arity switch at all.

**A corrected client-census, and it is a class of three, not one.** I had recorded the header-83 `default: break;` fall-through as a one-off. Parsing the whole module properly, by matching each `switch (PyTuple_Size(...))` to **its own** closing brace, gives thirteen arity switches:

| wrapper | switch | `default:` | class |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `netSendAuraRefineCheckIn` | `:46` | `:69` | safe, returns |
| `netSendAuraRefineCheckOut` | `:82` | `:99` | safe, returns |
| `netSendItemUsePacket` | `:747` | `:759` | safe, returns |
| `netSendItemUseToItemPacket` | `:772` | `:794` | safe, returns |
| `netSendItemDropPacket` | `:805` | `:817` | safe, returns |
| `netSendItemDropPacketNew` | `:841` | `:859` | safe, returns |
| `netSendItemMovePacket` | `:894` | `:918` | safe, returns |
| `netSendGiveItemPacket` | `:943` | `:963` | **unsafe**, `break` then sends |
| `netSendSafeboxCheckinPacket` | `:1329` | none | **unsafe**, no `default:` arm at all |
| `netSendSafeboxCheckoutPacket` | `:1360` | `:1376` | **unsafe**, `break` then sends |
| `netSendMallCheckoutPacket` | `:1409` | `:1425` | safe, returns |
| `netSendDailyGift` | `:2002` | `:2014` | safe, returns |
| `netSendItemCheckoutPrivateShopPacket` | `:2232` | `:2258` | safe, returns |

Twelve have a `default:` arm and ten of those return from it, so ten are safe. The three that are not:

* `netSendGiveItemPacket` declares `int iTargetVID;` at `:940` and `int iItemCount;` at `:942`, both genuinely uninitialised. Its `default: break;` at `:963-964` falls through to `:968`, sending both. This is the header-83 finding already recorded in the `cg_item_give.rs` doc; the new part is that it is one of three.
* `netSendSafeboxCheckoutPacket` declares `int iSafeBoxPos;` at `:1357`, uninitialised. Its `default: break;` at `:1376-1377` falls through to `:1381` and sends it.
* `netSendSafeboxCheckinPacket` is the **worst** of the three, because its switch at `:1329-1347` has **no `default:` arm at all**. It declares `int iSafeBoxPos;` at `:1327`, uninitialised, and any arity other than 2 or 3 falls straight through to `:1350` and sends it. A missing `default:` is worse than a `break`ing one, because nothing in the code even suggests the arity was meant to be rejected.

My first attempt at this census was itself wrong twice, and both errors are worth recording as method notes. A naive scan that asks only "does a `default:` label appear within sixty lines of this switch" **double-counted** line `:1376` against both safebox switches and so reported two fall-throughs where there is one plus one missing arm. And a scan that classifies a wrapper as safe merely because the token `return Py_BuildException` occurs anywhere between the `switch` and the `default` misclassifies every one of them, because the `case` arms all return. The `default` arm has to be extracted and inspected on its own, and the switch has to be closed by brace matching rather than by a line window. The count of three is the one that survives that.

**A corrected packet census, and both of my numbers were wrong.** A non-greedy `TPacket\w+` followed by a non-greedy brace pair is wrong in **both** directions and cannot be repaired by tuning. The audit's brace-matching parser, with comments and string literals blanked and line numbers preserved, finds **102** `TPacket` typedefs against the non-greedy parser's 96, because six of them contain nested constructor braces and the non-greedy match stops inside the body: `TPacketCGAura`, `TPacketCGBiologist`, `TPacketCGCubeRenewalSend`, `TPacketCGDragonSoulRefine`, `TPacketCGInventoryProtected`, and `TPacketCGPremiumPlayers`. Had the non-greedy parser been used here it would have reported 12 client records, not the 14 I originally recorded and not the 13 the correct parser gives. Of those 13, `TPacketCGDragonSoulRefine` is the missing variable-length client record. Two further corrections: `TPacketCGItemSell` is confirmed compiled out, behind `ENABLE_SELL_ITEM` at `packet.h:31` and `:649`, with **zero** `#define` for that macro anywhere; and `TPacketCGPrivateShopItemCheckin` at `packet.h:1380-1386` has **no header field** and is a variable-length sub-record under `HEADER_CG_PRIVATE_SHOP = 236`, dispatched through `input_main.cpp:3954` to `:4021-4025` with `iExtraLen` at `:4641`. It is relabelled as variable-length here rather than filed as a fixed record, which is how I had it.

**Two further items, confirmed and relevant to how the cast is reached.** The inbound cast cannot be reached with a short frame: `input.cpp:83` looks up the registered length and `:92-93` returns early on `m_iBufferLeft < iPacketLen` before any advance at `:112-113`. And the window-byte aliasing is identical here to the destroy record: `GetItem` at `char_item.cpp:254-305` returns `INVENTORY` and `EQUIPMENT` from the same `pItems` array with the same bound at `:269`, and `GetWear` at `:655` offsets the same array by `INVENTORY_MAX_NUM`, so an `EQUIPMENT` window byte naming an inventory cell drops an inventory item.

**What remains genuinely undetermined.** Script reachability. This worktree contains exactly one `.py` file, `client/Client/UserInterface/Version.py`, so which scripts call these four Python entry points, and with what arity, cannot be known from this tree. Any claim about reachable arity would be invention. The client can build both 12 and 20, through two builders and four Python entry points, and nothing else in the tree calls them.


### Section 144 independent review: MINOR, with one real method defect

The reviewer worked read-only in a fresh copy at `/tmp/sec144`, never in `/workspace/target`, and confirmed the `cg_item_destroy.rs` SHA-256 was unchanged on return. Verdict MINOR: no blocker, no major, and **no change to the codec's behaviour is required**. What follows is what was checked, and the one finding that was a genuine defect in my own process.

**The method defect, which is the most important item in this block.** The review brief specified `cargo test --workspace --all-targets --locked` as the mutation gate. That is **unsafe as a gate**, because without `--no-fail-fast` Cargo stops at the first failing test binary. It reached only 14 of the 27 workspace binaries and never ran the protocol integration tests at all, so a mutation that broke only a later binary would have been reported as a survivor. This is the same masking hazard as the `head -4` pipe defect in Section 143, arrived at from a different direction, and it is now the reason every mutation harness in this series carries `--no-fail-fast` and reports how many binaries actually reported a result. Re-running the Section 145 mutation set under the corrected harness showed 27 of 27 binaries reporting, and the one survivor was unchanged, so no Section 145 conclusion moved. **This is a correction to a stated verification method, not a correction to a recorded outcome.** The reviewer also proved the harness itself twice before trusting it: a control mutation emitting header 12 was caught eight times over, and a control that appended a deliberately failing `#[test]` to the *last* binary in the workspace was caught, which is exactly the class the old gate would have missed.

**Layout re-derived independently and confirmed.** `SItemPos` at `length.h:956-1057` is a `BYTE` plus a packed `WORD`, three bytes; `packet.h:627-631` adds the `BYTE header`, giving four bytes and a three-byte framed payload. Corroborated four separate ways: `packet_info.cpp:120`, the client at `Packet.h:30` and `:523-527`, the client's own packing at `GameType.h:418`, and `cg_inventory`'s `base_size: 4`. Not profile-dependent, verified by checking that neither struct contains an `#ifdef`.

**All 33 `file:line` citations in the doc block were opened individually. Zero were wrong.** The reviewer also caught a distinction that changes a claim, and in the codec's favour: the doc cites `char_item.cpp:10015` for `CHARACTER::IsValidItemPosition`, **not** `SItemPos::IsValidItemPosition` at `length.h:973`. That distinction decides the container claim, and the codec got it right. Had it cited the `length.h` overload, the claim would have been false, because that one returns `false` for `SAFEBOX` and `MALL` at `:985-987`.

**The three legacy claims were each confirmed on the real code path, and none is overstated.**

* The use-after-free is real and fires on every successful destroy: `char_item.cpp:7438` calls `ITEM_MANAGER::instance().RemoveItem(item)`, whose tail at `item_manager.cpp:594` reaches `item_manager.h:519` and then `item_manager.cpp:649`, a plain `delete` in `debug_allocator.h:157` with the custom operators commented out at `stdafx.h:6` and `:8`. `:7439` then dereferences the freed object through `item.h:66`.
* The `GetItem` aliasing is real: `char_item.cpp:254-305` returns `INVENTORY` and `EQUIPMENT` from the same `pItems` array under the same bound at `:269`, with the bound itself at `:10020-10022`, and `GetWear` at `:655` offsets the same array by `INVENTORY_MAX_NUM`.
* The container claim is real for the reason given above: `DestroyItem` calls the `CHARACTER` overload at `char_item.cpp:7418`, which does admit `SAFEBOX` and `MALL` at `:10027-10037`, while `GetItem` has no such case and so hits `default: return NULL` at `:301-302`.

The reviewer noted the guard list in the doc is incomplete, since `CanHandleItem` at `:7410`, `IsDead` at `:7416`, `isLocked` at `:7422` and the quest test at `:7424` are also present. That is correct and harmless, because the doc never claims to be exhaustive and all of those are above the boundary the doc draws.

**Collision and naming drift confirmed on both trees.** The server calls 21 `HEADER_GC_ITEM_SET` at `packet.h:122` with `packet_item_set` at `:1427`; the client calls 20 `HEADER_GC_ITEM_SET` at `Packet.h:116` and 21 `HEADER_GC_ITEM_SET2` at `:117`, with `packet_set_item2` at `:1776-1793` matching field for field and registered at `PythonNetworkStream.cpp:71-72`. `grep -rn ItemSet2 server` returns nothing, so the naming difference is real drift rather than a client-only rename.

**Scope and purity confirmed by search, not by reading.** No `unsafe`, no `#[repr(...)]`, no `transmute`, no `size_of`, and no packed-struct sizing. Crate-wide there is exactly one `resolve_client_frame_size`, at `cg_wire.rs:300`, and exactly one `ClientFrameDecoder`, at `:559`; `check_header` and `check_exact` are private per module. No gameplay policy leaked: all 256 window bytes and all 65 536 cells round-trip.

**Mutations: 23 run, 20 caught, 2 survivors, 1 compile error then caught on retry, and no real gap.** The three survivors are each reported here rather than papered over, because two are *observationally equivalent* and one is a style point only:

* Removing the header check's position, so fields are read first and the header second, **survives**. It is equivalent, not a defect: `check_exact` has already proved four bytes are present, so the earlier read cannot panic, and the same `InvalidHeader` is returned. The ordering is real in the source but unobservable from the public API, and no test can make it observable.
* Moving the header byte into the frame payload **was caught**, four times over. A `&bytes[1..]` slice change **survives**, again as an equivalent re-spelling of the same decode.
* Rebuilding the error tuple as a struct-variant **survives**, which is a style observation only.

One mutation is worth recording as a *closed* gap: changing `CG_ITEM_DROP`-style `PAYLOAD_SIZE` is caught by the test that asserts the declared constants against the bytes actually produced, which is the test that closed the same surviving mutation in `cg_safebox_move` back in Section 143. And one mutation produced a **compile error** rather than a test failure, because the `CgHeader` tuple constructor is private; the reviewer correctly treated that as "not yet answered", re-expressed the mutation as `header()` returning the wrong public constant, and got a proper catch.

**A second reviewer observation about the ledger itself, recorded because it is a real navigation hazard.** A scan for `##` headings stops at Section 142, because the Section 143 material is filed under `###` subheadings at lines 4105 and 4211-4279, *after* the Section 144 selection block at 4280. Section 143 is real and complete; the ledger is simply not in numeric order, and a reader who trusts heading depth alone will conclude that the last completed section is 142. That is worth fixing, but it is a structural edit to a 4 400-line document and it is not a compatibility question, so it is recorded here as a known hazard rather than performed silently.

**Three corrections applied to the codec as a result, none of them behavioural.**

* The test named `raw_header_is_checked_before_any_field_is_read` promised an ordering it cannot observe, which is the same equivocation as the surviving mutation. It is renamed to `a_wrong_header_yields_a_header_error_even_when_the_position_is_valid` and now says in a comment that the ordering is unobservable precisely because `check_exact` has already proved the read is in bounds.
* The doc claimed "unlike three other wrappers in this client" this one has no arity switch, which both undercounted and was unstable. It is replaced with the verified census in the Section 145 block below: thirteen arity switches, ten safe `default` arms, three unsafe. The count is no longer asserted as "three others" anywhere.
* Two citation nits: the doc cited `GetItem`'s `default: return NULL` at `:301` when `:301` is the label and the `return NULL` is at `:302`, and it described a clause that did not parse. Both are corrected. A third nit is also folded in: the doc now states the **second, independent** reason the record is four bytes, namely that `packet.h:274` opens `#pragma pack(1)` and does not close it until `:3540`, which is a different fact from `TItemPos` being three bytes within its own `#pragma pack(push, 1)`.


### Section 145 implementation: `protocol/src/cg_item_drop.rs`

**Scope.** One new transport-free protocol module, `protocol/src/cg_item_drop.rs`, plus exactly one `pub mod cg_item_drop;` line in `protocol/src/lib.rs`. No other source file changed. `cg_inventory` already carried header 12 with `base_size: 8` and `cpp_type: Some("TPacketCGItemDrop")`, so the existing inventory needed no edit, and no second framer, packed compatibility struct, `unsafe`, or gameplay policy was introduced.

**The record.** `CgItemDrop` encodes header 12 followed by one shared packed `CgItemPos` and one opaque `DWORD`. The layout is `[0x0c][window_type][cell:u16 LE][gold:u32 LE]`, which is exactly **eight** wire bytes: one header byte, a three-byte packed position, and a four-byte currency word. The framed payload is therefore **seven** bytes. The type reuses the already source-verified `CgItemPos` from `cg_item_move`, the ninth Rust codec to share that one three-byte layout.

`header` is deliberately **not** stored. The codec accepts only header 12 and always writes it, so a stored copy could only ever hold a value the encoder rejects. `gold` is documented as an opaque 32-bit word and is never bounded, because the only server-side bound is a comparison against the character's own balance, which is character state and not this record's business.

**Errors.** Three variants, `Truncated`, `LengthMismatch`, and `InvalidHeader`, each carrying the exact expected and actual values. Both decoders check the **exact** length before validating the header, and both validate the header before reading any field, so a short buffer reports `Truncated` rather than a misleading `InvalidHeader`, and a long buffer is rejected rather than silently truncated.

**Eighteen tests**, covering: agreement with the existing `cg_inventory` and `cg_wire` size resolvers; a golden record with explicit source offsets in both raw and framed form; a `Display` and `Box<dyn Error>` check; round-trips for the whole `u32` currency range including `0x8000_0000` and `u32::MAX`, chosen because those are exactly the values the legacy signed narrowing makes unreachable, so the test pins that the codec does **not** inherit that narrowing; all 256 window bytes; cell boundaries including `0xffff`, which `SItemPos()` itself produces; every wrong header byte at the exact length; the non-interchangeability of headers 12 and 20; length-before-header precedence in both directions; every length outside the exact size; every split point of a four-record stream; byte-at-a-time streaming that asserts the 1-to-7-byte tail is retained; two records back to back; and the declared constants asserted against the bytes actually produced.

**Mutations: 15 run under the corrected `--no-fail-fast` harness, 14 caught, 1 survivor, and the survivor is provably equivalent.**

| # | mutation | result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| a | raw header validation removed | caught |
| b | framed header validation removed | caught |
| c | raw exact-length relaxed to a minimum | caught |
| d | framed length check removed | caught |
| e | emitted header changed 12 to 11 | caught |
| f | window byte normalised to 1 | caught |
| g | currency word encoded big-endian | caught |
| h | currency word narrowed through a signed `int` | **survives, equivalent** |
| i | currency word read one byte early | caught |
| j | framed currency offset shifted | caught |
| k | wire-size constant 8 to 9 | caught |
| l | payload-size constant 7 to 6 | caught |
| m | a `count` field invented | caught |
| h2 | currency word truncated to `u8` | caught |
| h3 | currency word negated | caught |

Mutation h survives for a reason worth stating precisely, because it is the second time this has come up. `i32::from_le_bytes(..) as u32` is a **bit-preserving reinterpretation**, not a value change: `0x8000_0000` becomes a negative `i32` and casting back yields `0x8000_0000` again. So the mutation cannot be observed through any API this codec offers, because the codec's guarantee is bit preservation and the mutation preserves bits. The legacy narrowing is a defect in what the *server* does with the value, at `char_item.cpp:7556`, and reproducing or detecting it is deliberately outside this record's boundary. Two follow-up mutations were added specifically to show the harness is not simply blind here: truncating the word to `u8` and negating it are both caught, so the guarantee that *is* being tested is genuinely enforced. Recording this as an equivalent survivor, rather than deleting mutation h or contriving a test, is the honest outcome.

**Final locked/offline receipt.** `cargo build --workspace --locked` clean. `cargo test --workspace --all-targets --no-fail-fast --locked --offline` is **1 051 tests across 27 test binaries**, all passing, with all 27 binaries reporting. `cargo test --workspace --doc --locked --offline` is **6 doc-tests** across 8 targets, all passing. `cargo fmt --all -- --check` clean. `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets --locked -- -D warnings` clean. `RUSTDOCFLAGS="-D warnings" cargo doc --workspace --no-deps --locked` clean. The suite total is 1 057.

**Measurements at the Section 145 receipt.** `protocol/src/cg_item_drop.rs` is **27 714 bytes / 685 lines**, SHA-256 `d0767075bde0d09042905a1701bae4cc34bd785c5e88c167bedb640f762d33e2`. `protocol/src/lib.rs` is **20 810 bytes / 688 lines**, SHA-256 `ab641c97a41c5201dcc1c5bc1cafe2ba785a295c7f8cd6432b314a668e5a2f5d`. The workspace holds **138 Rust files** and **95 960 scanned lines** excluding `target`, `.overlord`, and vendored `extern`.

**Section 144's figures are superseded, and the earlier receipt is kept.** Applying the Section 144 review's corrections changed `cg_item_destroy.rs` from 26 861 bytes / 677 lines / SHA-256 `3b19b9993d4ef15cd3c4ba801243294198ffc9a3792ed448bc36a09b080dc302` to **28 562 bytes / 702 lines**, SHA-256 `295d6f688909d390d74df27e4d2801248f21b7a4baed92e581bf9d87c6774a84`. The change is documentation and one test rename only: no production line, no error variant, and no encoded byte differs. The earlier figures are recorded rather than overwritten so that the Section 144 receipt stays auditable against the SHA a reader would have seen at the time.

**Not done, and not claimed.** This is a transport-free record codec. It does not open a socket, frame a live descriptor, install keys, perform TEA, authenticate a session, resolve a character, place an item on the ground, move currency, apply a drop rate limit, enforce a partial-drop policy, or reproduce any of the dead code, narrowing, missing guard, or fall-through defects recorded above. In particular, the codec does not model the fact that header 12 can only ever drop a whole stack, nor that a zero `gold` selects the item path. Those are server and gameplay policies, and they belong to a future adapter, not to a wire boundary.

**The broader rewrite remains open.** One more fixed record codec is not a completed server. The persistent goal must stay active, and `goal.complete()` must not be called until the entire rewrite and its cleanup have been audited against the objective.

### Section 145 final receipt, document hashes, and hygiene

**Document hashes at the Section 145 receipt.** `docs/REWRITE_LEDGER.md` was 877 288 bytes / 4 535 lines at the Section 145 receipt; Section 146 appends the `cg.rs` cleanup and its receipt. `AGENTS.md` is **41 805 bytes / 115 lines**, SHA-256 `33e8e3a9873fe86a71238409b07c957a...`. `README.md` is **28 025 bytes / 92 lines**, SHA-256 `64321aa0c0d1d3c8791e860bbb299cce...`. This ledger deliberately records **no digest of itself**, because writing the digest into the file changes the digest, so any quoted value is stale the moment it is written. Size and line count are recorded instead, and the two shorter documents carry the digests that a reader can actually check. `AGENTS.md` and `README.md` each gained the compatibility rules for headers 12 and 21, the three-bucket header-collision taxonomy, the client-wrapper census, and the `--no-fail-fast` gate requirement.
