### 152.13 What is still open after this section

The party framing boundary is complete, and nothing in it is a gameplay, party,
arena, or dungeon rule. The whole set of behaviours that make a party mean
something remains unimplemented: leadership transfer, disband versus kick,
capacity, the `PARTY_ROLE_LEADER` gap described in 152.5, exp distribution beyond
the `SetParameter` bound, the arena and dungeon-gate checks, the
`HEADER_GD_PARTY_STATE_CHANGE` DB request, and the `TCParty` packets the server
sends back. None of it may be folded into a codec.

### 152.14 The exact CG backlog, re-derived after this section

The backlog was recomputed from `packet_info.cpp` rather than from declarations,
because the two are different populations and the earlier ledger figures are not
comparable to this one. A working figure of 50 was derived earlier in this
session but was never receipted into this ledger, so it appears nowhere above and
needs no correction; the lineage that **is** on the record is:

| figure | population | where |
|---|---|---|
| 91 | legacy `TPacketCG*` **record names** in the deleted catalogue | earlier wider census |
| 63 | record names with no Rust boundary **at that time** | Section 146 |
| **92** | **registered CG header names** in `packet_info.cpp` | this section |
| **45** | registered header names with no codec **now** | this section |

The 91 and the 92 are not the same set: one counts record names, the other counts
header names, and six distinct header names share value 0. The 63 was a scoping
list against the 91, which Section 146 itself flagged as "a scoping list, not a
count of unimplemented records". The jump from 63 to a 45 measured against a
different population is therefore **not** a single comparable delta and must not
be read as 18 records closed.

For the current figure, every one of the **92** registered CG header names was
resolved to its numeric value, and each `cg_*` codec module was scanned for the
header names it actually implements. A header name appearing in a module **only
inside a doc comment** does not count as implemented, so the four value-0
bootstrap records were confirmed by their code, not by their prose.

| measure | value |
|---|---|
| `Set(...)` CG registration lines in `packet_info.cpp` | 92 |
| of those, in the **active** build (unconditional) | **91** |
| of those, behind a feature guard | **1** |
| implemented by a `cg_*` codec | 47 |
| **backlog in the active build, by name** | **44** |
| **backlog in the active build, by distinct numeric value** | **44** |
| active-backlog names whose `base_size` is 16 bytes or less | 33 |

**Six header names share value 0**: `HEADER_CG_HANDSHAKE`,
`HEADER_CG_TIME_SYNC`, `HEADER_CG_CLIENT_VERSION`, `HEADER_CG_CLIENT_VERSION2`,
`HEADER_CG_KEY_AGREEMENT`, and `HEADER_CG_PONG`. Four are implemented by
`cg_handshake.rs` and `cg_client_version.rs`. The fifth,
**`HEADER_CG_KEY_AGREEMENT`, is the one registration in the whole file that sits
behind a guard**: `packet_info.cpp:191` is inside
`#ifdef _IMPROVED_PACKET_ENCRYPTION_`, so it is not part of the active build and
is excluded from the 91 and from the backlog. Only `HEADER_CG_PONG` therefore
remains uncovered at value 0 in the active build, which is why the backlog is 44
names spanning 44 distinct values with no duplicate.

This is the one place where a flat regex over `packet_info.cpp` is wrong, and it
is wrong silently: a 92-line census reads as authoritative while one of those
lines describes a build the checked-in server does not use.

Two corrections to earlier statements in this ledger, both made because the
previous wording was loose rather than because a number changed:

- **Header 22, `HEADER_CG_ITEM_SELL`, is not registered at all.** There is no
  `Set(...)` line for it anywhere in `packet_info.cpp`, and `ENABLE_SELL_ITEM`
  never appears in that file, so it is absent from the 92 and from any backlog
  count. An earlier draft of this bullet said its registration "sits inside
  `#ifdef ENABLE_SELL_ITEM`"; there is no such line for it to sit inside. It was previously described as
  merely "feature-gated and therefore blocked"; the accurate statement is that
  it is not part of the active build's registered set.
- **Header 27, `HEADER_CG_EXCHANGE`, is in the backlog at 14 bytes** and is
  genuinely blocked, because its `arg1` is 4 or 8 bytes depending on the profile
  and it carries a sub-header.

`TPacketCGRequestRefineInfo` and `TPacketCGStateCheck` remain confirmed dead
declarations that must never be implemented. This is distinct from the live
`HEADER_CG_STATE_CHECKER` at value 206, registered as `ServerStateCheck` at 1
byte, which is a different record and stays in the backlog.

The 33 tractable records at 16 bytes or less are, in value order: 0 `Pong`,
26 `OnClick`, 27 `Exchange`, 28 `CharacterPosition`, 29 `ScriptAnswer`,
31 `QuestConfirm`, 51 `FlyTargeting`, 53 `AddFlyTargeting`, 59 `TargetInfoLoad`,
61 `Target`, 64 `Text`, 65 `Warp`, 66 `ScriptButton`, 81 `AnswerMakeGuild`,
82 `Fishing`, 90 `Empire`, 96 `Refine`, 100 `MarkLogin`, 104 `MarkIdxList`,
113 `SymbolCRC`, 114 `ScriptSelectItem`, 117 `RequestEventData`, 148 `WorldBoss`,
169 `Attr67Add`, 175 `Biologist`, 176 `PremiumPlayers`, 180 `DailyGift`,
206 `StateChecker`, 220 `CubeRenewal`, 227 `RefineElement`, 233 `ChangeLook`,
238 `ChangeLanguage`, and 241 `GayaSystem`.
### 152.15 Further reconnaissance, and one record that must never be implemented

This subsection was produced while the Section 152 audit was still running. It
touches only the legacy tree, so it cannot interfere with the audit, and it is
recorded now because it changes the shape of the next increment rather than
because it belongs to this one.

**A registered record that the server never reads.** `HEADER_CG_TEXT` is
registered at `packet_info.cpp:98` against `sizeof(TPacketCGText)`, and
`TPacketCGText` at `packet.h:454` is exactly one byte, `BYTE bHeader;`. It looks
like a trivial fixed record, and it is in the active backlog, but it is not
implementable in the usual sense because **nothing ever reads it**. A three-way
absence sweep over `/workspace/server/server` finds `HEADER_CG_TEXT` in exactly
two files, `packet.h` and `packet_info.cpp`; `TPacketCGText` in the same two;
and the struct tag `command_text` only in `packet.h`. There is **no
`case HEADER_CG_TEXT` arm in `input_main.cpp`**, and a sweep of
`/workspace/client/Client` finds **zero** references to either the constant or
the struct. The chat path is a different header entirely, `HEADER_CG_CHAT`,
which `cg_variable` already covers. So this is a registered, undispatched,
client-unreferenced record: the mirror image of the dead declarations
`TPacketCGRequestRefineInfo` and `TPacketCGStateCheck`, except that it *is*
registered, which is precisely why a registration-driven census cannot tell the
two apart. **It must be added to the never-implement list.**

**A newly discovered profile-dependent width.** Earlier sections recorded
headers 22 and 27 as profile-dependent and treated the rest of the small set as
fixed. Sweeping the *interiors* of the 33 small declarations for their own
`#if` finds exactly two, and 27 is only one of them:

| header | struct | internal guard | effect |
|---|---|---|---|
| 27 | `TPacketCGExchange` | `#ifdef ENABLE_REMOVE_LIMIT_GOLD` | `arg1` is `unsigned long long` (8 bytes) or `DWORD` (4 bytes) |
| **96** | **`TPacketCGRefine`** | **`#ifdef ENABLE_CUSTOM_INVENTORY`** | **`pos` widens from `BYTE` under the default profile** |

Header 96 was previously treated as a plain 3-byte record. It is
**profile-dependent**, and a codec for it would be wrong for one of the two
profiles. It joins header 27 on the blocked list, and header 96 is newly
blocked rather than newly cleared.

**The twelve gated declarations are in the active build after all.** Twelve of
the 33 small records are declared inside a feature guard in `packet.h`:
`__SEND_TARGET_INFO__`, `__EVENT_MANAGER__`, `__WORLD_BOSS_EVENT__`,
`__ATTR_6TH_7TH__`, `__ENABLE_BIOLOGIST_RENEWAL_SYSTEM__`,
`__ENABLE_PREMIUM_PLAYERS__`, `__DAILY_GIFT_SYSTEM__`,
`ENABLE_CUBE_RENEWAL_WORLDARD`, `ENABLE_REFINE_ELEMENT`,
`__CHANGELOOK_SYSTEM__`, `__MULTI_LANGUAGE_SYSTEM__`, and `ENABLE_GAYA_SYSTEM`.
This initially reads as twelve blocked records, but their **registrations in
`packet_info.cpp` are all unconditional**. Since a registration cannot compile
without its declaration, the checked-in server's active profile must define all
twelve macros. They are therefore legitimately in the active backlog and are
**not** blocked; only header 27 and the newly found header 96 are.

**Two headers, one record.** `HEADER_CG_FLY_TARGETING` (51) and
`HEADER_CG_ADD_FLY_TARGETING` (53) are both registered against
`sizeof(TPacketCGFlyTargeting)`, at `packet_info.cpp` lines 164 and 165. Two
distinct header values, one 13-byte struct. This is a collision case that the
four existing buckets do not cover, since the collision is *within* one
direction. A future implementation must expose both headers over one struct and
must not invent a second record.

**Two struct-less boundaries.** `HEADER_CG_PONG` (0) and
`HEADER_CG_STATE_CHECKER` (206) are registered as `sizeof(BYTE)`, not as
`sizeof(TPacket...)`. Neither has a struct at all, so neither has a declaration
to point at, and a codec for them is a one-byte header-only record that must
still validate its own header byte.

**Naming drift without the `CG` infix.** `HEADER_CG_CHANGE_LANGUAGE` registers
`TPacketChangeLanguage` and `HEADER_CG_CL` registers `TPacketChangeLook`. Both
are inbound CG records whose struct names lack the `CG` infix that the other 90
carry, so a name-derived scan for `TPacketCG*` will miss them. This is the same
false-absence shape as the struct-tag versus typedef-alias lesson from Section
151, in a new place.

**The next increment, chosen on evidence.** The five records that are
unconditional, 1 to 2 bytes, and free of sub-headers are:

| header | struct | decl | wire | body |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 28 | `TPacketCGPosition` | `packet.h:741` | 2 | `BYTE header; BYTE position;` |
| 29 | `TPacketCGScriptAnswer` | `packet.h:749` | 2 | `BYTE header; BYTE answer;` |
| 65 | `TPacketCGWarp` | `packet.h:1866` | 1 | `BYTE bHeader;` |
| 82 | `TPacketCGFishing` | `packet.h:2300` | 2 | `BYTE header; BYTE dir;` |
| 90 | `TPacketCGEmpire` | `packet.h:2113` | 2 | `BYTE bHeader; BYTE bEmpire;` |

Every one of these five was read directly with brace matching, not with a regex.
The first attempt at a regex extractor was **unsound**: a
`typedef struct[^\n]*\n\{(.*?)\}\s*NAME\s*;` pattern with `re.S` lets the
non-greedy group swallow every intervening `}` in the file, so it reported
`TPacketCGPosition` as 475 bytes. Section 146 already recorded that struct
extraction here needs a brace-matching parser, and this is the same trap again,
which is why it is written down. A second arithmetic error compounded it: an
extractor that took the type from the last chunk after splitting on commas
mis-reads `long x, y;` as one 4-byte field instead of two, which is what first
made `TPacketCGFlyTargeting` look like 5 bytes instead of its true 13.

`TPacketCGScriptAnswer` carries a detail worth recording before anyone
implements it: its declaration at `packet.h:749` keeps two **commented-out**
fields, `//char file[32 + 1];` and `//BYTE answer[16 + 1];`. The live record is
the 2-byte `{header, answer}` and the dead fields must stay dead. A "helpful"
port that restores the file name would break the wire format, and the inventory
`base_size` of 2 is the authority.

`TPacketCGText` (64), `TPacketCGMarkIDXList` (104), and the twelve gated records
are all excluded from that table deliberately. MarkIDXList is a legitimate
1-byte record and is a fine candidate, but it belongs with the mark family rather
than with this one.
### 152.16 Independent audit reconciliation

A separate read-only child agent audited Section 152 against the legacy source
without running Cargo and without writing to `/workspace`. Report:
`/tmp/agent-reports/sec152_audit.md`, 24,046 bytes, 364 lines, 22 numbered
claims: **16 confirmed, 3 refuted, 5 imprecise.** Every claim was then re-checked
independently before any correction was applied; where the auditor and this
section disagreed, the source decided. The full report is kept, not summarised
away, because two of its refutations were themselves wrong and that is the more
useful record.

**Refutation 1, accepted: the `GetLeaderPID()` citation was wrong.** 152.4 and
the module doc both claimed the server compares the four wire bytes of
`TPacketCGPartySetState` against `GetLeaderPID()` at `input_main.cpp:2533`.
`input_main.cpp:2533` is `if (ch->GetParty()->GetLeaderPID() != ch->GetPlayerID())`
— a leadership test on the *sender* that never reads `p->pid`. The only other
nearby `GetLeaderPID()` comparison, `:2604`, is likewise against
`ch->GetPlayerID()`. The wire `pid` is compared against `pParty->IsMember(p->pid)`
at `:2539` and against `ch->GetPlayerID()` at `:2620` and `:2642`. The
conclusion, that the field is a player ID and the client's `dwVID` is a misnomer,
survives on the strength of `:2539` alone. Both the ledger and
`protocol/src/cg_party.rs` were corrected, and the correction is stated in place
rather than made silently.

**Refutation 2, accepted: the `__CanActMainInstance` claim was wrong.** 152.7
said the guard appears "0 times in `PythonNetworkStreamPhaseGame.cpp`" and is
therefore "a per-file convention rather than a per-sender oversight". It appears
**23** times in that file. The guard is applied per sender inside the very file
that holds the six party senders, so the earlier conclusion collapses with the
count. The narrow statement that survives, and is now the only one in the
ledger, is that within lines 3400-3520 the guard appears 0 times.

**Refutation 3, accepted on the tally only: 9 client enumerators, not 9 but 10.**
The census table itself was reproduced cell by cell and is entirely correct; only
the summary tally was wrong, because the client has five CG and five GC
enumerators carrying these five values, not four and five. Corrected to 10.

**Imprecise claims 5 to 9, all accepted and corrected.** Header 22
`HEADER_CG_ITEM_SELL` has no `Set(...)` line anywhere in `packet_info.cpp` and
`ENABLE_SELL_ITEM` never appears in that file, so there is no registration to be
conditional. The role switch has no arm for `MAX_NUM` as well as for `LEADER`.
`EPartyRole` spans `party.h:15-26`, not `:18-28`. `prodomodefines.h:89` defines
`__FIX_EXP_GRUP__`, which makes `input_main.cpp:2767` the live
`distribute_mode` guard and `:2769` the inactive `#else`; the live guard requires
**leadership**, not merely the existence of a party.

**Imprecise claim 4, the test total, is REFUTED — the receipt stands.** The
auditor could not run Cargo, and its static count of test functions gave 1,150,
from which it concluded that both 1,192 and the 1,160 baseline are "42 too high".
Re-running the gate settles it:

```text
cargo test --workspace --all-targets --no-fail-fast --locked --offline
28 test binaries, 1192 passed, 0 failed, exit 0
```

The receipt in 152.12 is **correct**. The static count was wrong twice over, and
both errors are worth recording because either would have been easy to repeat:

- It under-counted `protocol` by exactly **32**, which is 30 module tests plus 2
  wiring tests — precisely the tests this section added. The scan excluded the
  very code under audit.
- Its attribute pattern required `]` immediately after `tokio::test`, so it
  missed every `#[tokio::test(flavor = "multi_thread", worker_threads = 2)]`,
  which is **10** tests in `game-server`. With the pattern corrected to allow
  attribute arguments, the static count is **1,192** and splits **1,113** lib
  plus **79** integration, which matches the 28 reported harnesses exactly.

The lesson generalises past this section: **a static count of test functions
must never be used to challenge a gate receipt.** Run the gate. A static count is
a cross-check on a *delta* at best, and when it disagrees with a receipt the
first hypothesis must be a defect in the scanner.

**Two accepted caveats on the 152.14 census.** The figure of 47 implemented
headers silently counts `HEADER_CG_AURA` and `HEADER_CG_SWITCHBOT`, which
`cg_wire.rs:69-70` frames as **variable prefixes**, not fixed records. Excluding
those two the implemented count is 45. And several 152.14 labels use the header
stems `CharacterPosition`, `FlyTargeting`, `AddFlyTargeting` and
`RequestEventData` where the inventory `legacy_name` is `Position`, `FlyTarget`,
`AddFlyTarget` and `EventRequest`.

**One convention note, recorded so the citations are not misread.** The
server/client member comparisons cite the `typedef struct` start lines
(`packet.h:2035`, `:2077`, `Packet.h:838`, `:851`), not the member lines, which
are `packet.h:2038`, `:2079-2082` and `Packet.h:841`, `:853-856`. The convention
is applied consistently on both sides, so the comparison is fair, but the cited
lines are struct starts.

**Net effect on the implementation: none.** No codec, header constant, width,
field order, or test changed as a result of this audit. The corrections are to
documentation and to six ledger sentences. `cg_party.rs` moved from 36,638 to
37,007 bytes purely because three doc comments now state the verified facts;
the 30 tests and the 1,192-test receipt are unchanged.
## Section 153 — four micro-width game-phase CG records

### 153.1 Scope, and the one decision that shaped it

Section 152.15 nominated five candidates: headers 28, 29, 65, 82, and 90. The
audit of header 90 killed one of them and changed the shape of the rest.

**`HEADER_CG_EMPIRE` is a login-phase record, not a game-phase one.** A search
of `input_main.cpp` for `case HEADER_CG_EMPIRE` finds nothing; a search of
`input_login.cpp:1201-1203` finds `case HEADER_CG_EMPIRE: Empire(d, c_pData);
break;` and the handler `CInputLogin::Empire` at `:961-969`. The other four all
dispatch through `CInputMain`. The distinction is not cosmetic: the Empire
handler is **credential-adjacent pre-game admission code** and it carries a real
bound,

```cpp
if (EMPIRE_MAX_NUM <= p->bEmpire) { d->SetPhase(PHASE_CLOSE); return; }
```

with `EMPIRE_MAX_NUM` 4, so a `bEmpire` of 4 through 255 closes the login phase
outright. That is a phase-transition policy, and it belongs with the login
boundary already tracked by `protocol::cg_account`, not inside a game-phase
bundle. **`HEADER_CG_EMPIRE` is deferred to the login-phase increment.**
Section 153 is therefore the four `CInputMain` records, and it is a
`CInputMain` increment.

### 153.2 Declarations, packing, and registration

All four lie inside the single `#pragma pack(1)` that opens at `packet.h:274`
and closes at `:3540`, and outside every `#ifdef`.

| record | header | value | declaration | struct tag | wire |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `TPacketCGPosition` | `HEADER_CG_CHARACTER_POSITION` | 28 `0x1c` | `packet.h:738-741` | `struct command_position` | 2 |
| `TPacketCGScriptAnswer` | `HEADER_CG_SCRIPT_ANSWER` | 29 `0x1d` | `packet.h:744-749` | `struct command_script_answer` | 2 |
| `TPacketCGWarp` | `HEADER_CG_WARP` | 65 `0x41` | `packet.h:1864-1866` | `struct command_warp` | 1 |
| `TPacketCGFishing` | `HEADER_CG_FISHING` | 82 `0x52` | `packet.h:2297-2300` | `struct command_fishing` | 2 |

Note the declaration ranges are **start to closing brace**, the convention the
152.16 audit asked to be made explicit; an earlier draft of 152.15 cited only
the closing-brace lines.

Registrations are `packet_info.cpp:131`, `:132`, `:144`, and `:160`, all
unconditional, all `sizeof(TPacketCG...)`. Dispatch arms are
`input_main.cpp:3686`, `:3786`, `:3801`, and `:3841`, and none of the four uses
`iExtraLen` or is wrapped in `IsObserverMode()`. All four handler declarations
are in `input.h` at `:101` (`Position`), `:106` (`ScriptAnswer`), `:113`
(`Warp`), and `:126` (`Fishing`), all `void`, none null-checking `ch`, which is
safe only because `Analyze` closes the phase at `:3647-3652` when no character
exists.

### 153.3 The four handlers, and four things that must stay out of the codec

**`CInputMain::Position` at `input_main.cpp:1530`** reads through the **struct
tag** `struct command_position *`, not the typedef, a fourth independent
confirmation of the Section 151 lesson that legacy call sites use tags. It
switches on `pinfo->position` with only three arms: `POSITION_GENERAL` to
`Standup()`, `POSITION_SITTING_CHAIR` to `Sitdown(0)`, and
`POSITION_SITTING_GROUND` to `Sitdown(1)`. `ECharacterPosition` at
`length.h:435-444` also numbers `POSITION_BATTLE` 1, `POSITION_DYING` 2,
`POSITION_INTRO` 5, and the sentinel `POSITION_MAX_NUM` 6, and **the switch has
no `default` arm**. Those three values and every out-of-range byte therefore fall
through and do nothing at all. This is exactly why `position` stays opaque: a
codec that rejected unknown positions would be *stricter than the server*, and a
codec that mapped them would invent behaviour the server does not have.

**`CInputMain::ScriptAnswer` at `:2200`** is a two-way dispatch, not a
threshold with a no-op branch. An earlier reading of this handler described
`answer > 250` as a gate above a silent `else`; that is wrong, and the `else` at
`:2209-2211` is the more interesting half:

```cpp
if (p->answer > 250) { quest::CQuestManager::Instance().Resume(ch->GetPlayerID()); }
else { quest::CQuestManager::Instance().Select(ch->GetPlayerID(), p->answer); }
```

So 0 through 250 select and 251 through 255 resume. Every one of the 256 values
has a distinct effect, which is the strongest possible argument for opacity.

**`CInputMain::Warp` at `:2271`** is the entire body `ch->WarpEnd();`. The
record carries no field and the server reads none. This is the one record where
"the handler ignores the payload" is a trap rather than a licence: a codec that
accepted a trailing byte would be *more* permissive than the fixed record the
registration declares, so `CgWarp` pins its payload width at 0 and rejects a
one-byte frame payload in a test.

**`CInputMain::Fishing` at `:3166`** does `ch->SetRotation(p->dir * 5);` and then
`ch->fishing();`.

### 153.4 The client sends fishing without a struct, and divides where the server multiplies

There is **no `TPacketCGFishing` anywhere in `client/Client`**, and no
`TPacketCGFishing` in the client `Packet.h` either, yet `HEADER_CG_FISHING`
appears in three client files. `CPythonNetworkStream::SendFishingPacket(int
iRotation)` at `PythonNetworkStreamPhaseGame.cpp:4366-4376` builds the record
field by field with **two separate `Send` calls**:

```cpp
BYTE byHeader = HEADER_CG_FISHING;
if (!Send(sizeof(byHeader), &byHeader)) return false;
BYTE byPacketRotation = iRotation / 5;
if (!Send(sizeof(BYTE), &byPacketRotation)) return false;
return SendSequence();
```

Two findings follow. First, the client's `/ 5` is the exact inverse of the
server's `* 5`, which is a satisfying confirmation that the two ends agree on
the unit. Second, `iRotation / 5` narrows a signed `int` into a `BYTE` with no
range check, so the wire byte is `(iRotation / 5) mod 256`: a negative rotation
and a rotation above 1275 both wrap silently. That is a **client** defect. It is
recorded, not reproduced and not compensated for: `CgFishing::dir` accepts all
256 values, and the modulo-256 wrap is the client's, not the codec's.

The other three client declarations are present and agree with the server
member for member: `TPacketCGPosition` at `Packet.h:617` is
`BYTE header; BYTE position;`, `TPacketCGScriptAnswer` at `:623` is
`BYTE header; BYTE answer;`, and `TPacketCGWarp` at `:687` is `BYTE bHeader;`.

### 153.5 Two commented-out fields that must stay dead

`TPacketCGScriptAnswer` at `packet.h:744-749` keeps two commented-out members
inside the live record, `//char file[32 + 1];` and `//BYTE answer[16 + 1];`. The
record is the two-byte `{header, answer}` and nothing else. This is worth
recording because the natural "helpful" port would restore a script file name,
which would silently change the wire format to 33 bytes, and because
`cg_inventory` already agrees on `base_size: 2` for this header.

### 153.6 Collision census

| value | CG | GC (server) | GC (client) | GD | bucket |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 28 | `HEADER_CG_CHARACTER_POSITION` | `HEADER_GC_QUICKSLOT_ADD` | `HEADER_GC_QUICKSLOT_ADD` | — | 2 |
| 29 | `HEADER_CG_SCRIPT_ANSWER` | `HEADER_GC_QUICKSLOT_DEL` | `HEADER_GC_QUICKSLOT_DEL` | `HEADER_GG_CHECK_AWAKENESS` | 2 |
| 65 | `HEADER_CG_WARP` | `HEADER_GC_WARP` | `HEADER_GC_WARP` | — | 2 |
| 82 | `HEADER_CG_FISHING` | `HEADER_GC_REQUEST_MAKE_GUILD` | `HEADER_GC_REQUEST_MAKE_GUILD` | — | 2 |

All four are bucket 2, colliding but not width-equal: the sharpest is 65, where
`HEADER_CG_WARP` and `HEADER_GC_WARP` share both a value **and a name stem**
across directions, exactly the trap that 152.6's family hit at 72. Header 29 is
also `HEADER_GG_CHECK_AWAKENESS` on the game-to-game side, so a single
game-server table keyed by number would need three different sizes for one
number.
### 153.7 Implementation shape

`protocol/src/cg_micro.rs` holds all four codecs, registered by
`pub mod cg_micro;` in `protocol/src/lib.rs:1` order, immediately before
`pub mod cg_party;`. The four share one error type `CgMicroError` with the same
three variants the party family uses, for the same reason: the failure modes are
identical, and four near-identical error types would be four near-identical
`Display` impls to keep in step.

**The zero-payload case is the reason this module needed its own thought.** Three
records carry one `u8` after the header, so `PAYLOAD_SIZE` is 1 and `WIRE_SIZE` is
2, and the shared `decode_frame_parts` helper checks the *payload* width while
`decode_parts` checks the *record* width. `CgWarp` is the first record in the
workspace with `PAYLOAD_SIZE == 0`, which makes the helper's arithmetic the only
thing standing between the two records and a silent off-by-one. Two tests pin it:
`warp_frame_carries_an_empty_payload` asserts the frame really is header-only,
and `warp_frame_with_a_payload_is_rejected` asserts that a one-byte payload is a
`LengthMismatch` and not an accepted record.

**`CgWarp` is a fieldless struct, not a one-field struct with a reserved byte.**
`new()` takes no argument, `encode_into` writes one byte, and both decoders
return `Self`. Modelling the absent byte as a stored field would have been
tidier to write and wrong: it would have implied a wire byte that does not exist
and let a `dir`-style field creep in later.

**The opacity decision is per record, and the reasons differ.** `position` is
opaque because the legacy `switch` has no `default` and therefore *ignores*
values rather than rejecting them; `answer` is opaque because all 256 values take
one of two distinct quest actions; `dir` is opaque because the server multiplies
it and the client divides and truncates. Three different reasons, one rule: none
of them is a framing error, so none of them may be normalised in Rust.

### 153.8 Tests, and the two gaps they were written to close

**30 module tests** and **2 wiring tests**, for a delta of exactly **32**.

The first gap is the one Section 152 paid for. `every_encode_into_appends_and_none_of_them_clears` exists here **from the start**, and it checks all four records rather than one representative, because that is precisely the hole P14 fell through. The same reasoning produced four separate `encode_into` mutations, M17 through M20, one per record, so a `clear()` in any single sibling is caught on its own.

The second gap is the `decode_frame` payload-width defect from Section 151, which
would have been invisible if only round-trip tests existed. `decode_frame_checks_the_payload_width_and_not_the_record_width`
and `decode_frame_agrees_with_decode_for_all_three_byte_records` run over the
whole `u8` domain, and M15 plus M33 through M36 attack the helper and each
per-record call separately, so the defect cannot hide in one record.

`every_record_rejects_every_other_header_at_its_own_width` sweeps all 255 wrong
header values per record, which is 1,020 assertions from one test and leaves no
header value unexercised.

### 153.9 Gate receipt

| gate | exit | result |
|---|---|---|
| `cargo fmt --all -- --check` | 0 | clean |
| `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets --locked --offline -- -D warnings` | 0 | no warnings |
| `RUSTDOCFLAGS="-D warnings" cargo doc --workspace --no-deps --locked --offline` | 0 | no warnings |
| `cargo test --workspace --all-targets --no-fail-fast --locked --offline` | 0 | **1,224 passed / 0 failed / 28 binaries** |
| `cargo test --workspace --doc --no-fail-fast --locked --offline` | 0 | **6 passed / 0 failed** |

1,224 is 1,192 plus exactly 32, and 32 is 30 module tests plus 2 wiring tests.

**The first gate pass failed and is recorded rather than hidden.** The initial
run reported `DOC_OK`, `TEST_OK` and `DOCTEST_OK` but **no** `FMT_OK` and **no**
`CLIPPY_OK`. Both markers were genuinely absent, not merely unprinted:
`cargo fmt --check` produced **11 diffs** in `cg_micro.rs` and
`cg_wiring.rs`, and strict Clippy rejected the test helper

```text
error: very complex type used. Consider factoring parts into `type` definitions
  --> protocol/src/cg_micro.rs:429:20
   |
429 |     fn frames() -> Vec<(&'static str, Vec<u8>, Vec<u8>, CgHeader, usize, usize)> {
```

Both were fixed by refactoring, never by suppression. The six-element tuple
return type became a `Sample` struct with named fields plus a small `Self2` enum
so the shared assertions can dispatch a decode without repeating a four-way
match, and `cargo fmt --all` canonicalised the rest. The lesson is procedural and
belongs here: **a gate script that chains on `&&` and only echoes a marker on
success will show three green markers next to two missing ones, and the missing
ones are the failures.** The markers are the receipt, so a short marker list is
itself the signal.
## Section 154 — the four "client names one thing" CG records

### 154.1 Scope

The remaining fixed-width game-phase backlog after Section 153 is dominated by
records that share one shape and one purpose: the client tells the server which
single thing it picked, and carries no other information. Four of them are
unconditional, sub-header-free, and 5 or 6 bytes:

| record | header | wire | declaration | registration | dispatch |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `TPacketCGQuestConfirm` | 31 `0x1f` | 6 | `packet.h:765-769` | `packet_info.cpp:135` | `input_main.cpp:3792` |
| `TPacketCGTarget` | 61 `0x3d` | 5 | `packet.h:1796-1799` | `packet_info.cpp:143` | `input_main.cpp:3798` |
| `TPacketCGScriptButton` | 66 `0x42` | 5 | `packet.h:753-756` | `packet_info.cpp:133` | `input_main.cpp:3780` |
| `TPacketCGScriptSelectItem` | 114 `0x72` | 5 | `packet.h:2583-2586` | `packet_info.cpp:170` | `input_main.cpp:3783` |

All four lie inside the single `#pragma pack(1)` at `packet.h:274`-`:3540` and
outside every real `#ifdef`. The obvious trap here is a false positive: a naive
conditional-context scan reports all four as "gated by
`#ifndef __INC_PACKET_H__`", because that include guard wraps the **entire**
file, 3,541 lines, and never closes until the last line. A conditional map that
does not special-case the include guard marks every declaration in the file as
conditional and is worse than no map at all.

`TPacketCGQuestConfirm` is the one with a field-order surprise, and it is worth
writing down before anyone implements it: the `u8` `answer` comes **before** the
`u32` `requestPID`, so a natural "u32 last, u8 first" assumption produces the
wrong 6 bytes.

### 154.2 Four handlers, and four behaviours that must stay above the codec

**`CInputMain::QuestConfirm` at `input_main.cpp:2236` normalises `answer` and
resolves a third party.** It calls
`CHARACTER_MANAGER::instance().FindByPID(p->requestPID)`, and then:

```cpp
if (p->answer) p->answer = quest::CONFIRM_YES;
```

so every non-zero answer byte is rewritten to `CONFIRM_YES` before the cast to
`EQuestConfirmType`. Two consequences. First, `answer` is a **truthiness** byte
whose 255 distinct non-zero values all collapse server-side, and the codec must
still preserve all 256, because collapsing them is the server's business and not
framing's. Second, `requestPID` is **not the sender**: `Confirm` is invoked on
`ch_wait->GetPlayerID()`, a different character resolved from the wire, so this
record lets one client speak for another. That is a cross-player capability and
it belongs in the admission-policy discussion, not in the codec.

**`CInputMain::ScriptButton` at `:2179` never uses the field it carries.** It
logs `p->idx` at `:2182`, fetches the quest PC, and on `pc->IsConfirmWait()`
calls `Confirm(ch->GetPlayerID(), quest::CONFIRM_TIMEOUT)` — a call that takes no
index at all. So `idx` reaches a log line and nothing else. This is a distinct
opacity reason from the other three: the value is not merely unchecked, it is
**behaviourally inert**. A codec that validated it against a button count would
be inventing a constraint the server does not have.

**`CInputMain::ScriptSelectItem` at `:2217`** passes `p->selection` straight to
`quest::CQuestManager::Instance().SelectItem` with no validation whatsoever.

**`CInputMain::Target` at `:2249`** looks the VID up with
`building::CManager::instance().FindObjectByVID(p->dwVID)` and, only if that
succeeds, echoes it in a `TPacketGCTarget`. The **request** is fixed at 5 bytes
in every profile, but the **reply** is not: `#if defined(__SHIP_DEFENSE__)` at
`:2260-2264` adds `bAlliance`, `iAllianceMinHP`, and `iAllianceMaxHP`. So
`HEADER_GC_TARGET` is profile-dependent while `HEADER_CG_TARGET` is not, and a
codec for the CG side must not be sized from the GC side.

### 154.3 The client senders are all clean, and one parameter is misnamed

| sender | line | behaviour |
|---|---|---|
| `SendQuestConfirmPacket(BYTE, DWORD)` | `:2768` | struct, both fields, checked send, `Tracen` on failure |
| `SendTargetPacket(DWORD)` | `:3253` | struct, both fields, checked send, `Tracen` on failure |
| `SendScriptButtonPacket(unsigned int)` | `:2720` | struct, both fields, checked send, `Tracen` on failure |
| `SendSelectItemPacket(DWORD dwItemPos)` | `:4625` | struct, both fields, checked send |

None narrows, none leaves a field unassigned, and each one is preceded by a
declaration in the client `Packet.h` that matches the server **member for
member, including names**: `TPacketCGTarget` at `:635`, `TPacketCGScriptButton`
at `:629`, `TPacketCGQuestConfirm` at `:1022`, and
`TPacketCGScriptSelectItem` at `:1028`. Unlike the party family, there is no
field-name drift here at all.

The one blemish is in a parameter name, not the wire:
`SendSelectItemPacket(DWORD dwItemPos)` at `:4625` assigns `dwItemPos` to
`kScriptSelectItem.selection` at `:4629`, and the server hands the same field to
`SelectItem` as a quest selection. The client parameter name is the misleading
one, and a future reader who trusts it will look for an item position that the
record does not carry.

Each of the four headers appears in exactly three client files — the enum in
`Packet.h`, a name string in `EterLib/NetStream.cpp`, and the one sender — which
is the minimum for a live client-side send and a useful sanity check.

### 154.4 Collision census

| value | CG | GC (server) | GC (client) | GG | bucket |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 31 | `HEADER_CG_QUEST_CONFIRM` | `HEADER_GC_ITEM_OWNERSHIP` | `HEADER_GC_ITEM_OWNERSHIP` | `HEADER_GG_SWITCHBOT` | 2 |
| 61 | `HEADER_CG_TARGET` | `HEADER_GC_MOUNT` | `HEADER_GC_MOUNT` | — | 2 |
| **66** | `HEADER_CG_SCRIPT_BUTTON` | **none** | **none** | — | **collision-free** |
| 114 | `HEADER_CG_SCRIPT_SELECT_ITEM` | `HEADER_GC_SEPCIAL_EFFECT` | `HEADER_GC_SEPCIAL_EFFECT` | — | 2 |

Header 66 is the first CG value in this series with **no** collision in either
tree, across CG, GC, and GG. It is worth recording as a fact rather than
assuming, because the overwhelming pattern of the last several sections is
bucket 2, and a reader who assumed 66 behaved like its neighbours would
over-build a cross-direction table for it. The `SEPCIAL` spelling at 114 is a
legacy typo that must be preserved verbatim in any future GC codec.
### 154.5 Inventory agreement, and the backlog after Sections 153 and 154

`protocol/src/cg_inventory.rs` already carries all four rows and **needs no
modification**, exactly as it did for the party family. Each row's `base_size`
matches the width derived from source, and each header constant matches the
legacy enumerator:

| header | constant | `base_size` | derived | `legacy_name` | `cpp_type` |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `HEADER_CG_QUEST_CONFIRM` | `0x1f` | 6 | 6 | `QuestConfirm` | `TPacketCGQuestConfirm` |
| `HEADER_CG_TARGET` | `0x3d` | 5 | 5 | `Target` | `TPacketCGTarget` |
| `HEADER_CG_SCRIPT_BUTTON` | `0x42` | 5 | 5 | `ScriptButton` | `TPacketCGScriptButton` |
| `HEADER_CG_SCRIPT_SELECT_ITEM` | `0x72` | 5 | 5 | `ScriptSelectItem` | `TPacketCGScriptSelectItem` |

Two wiring tests will assert that agreement through the public API, as in
Sections 151 through 153, so a future edit to either side fails loudly instead of
leaving the shared fixed framer quietly disagreeing with the dedicated codecs.

**Backlog arithmetic.** Section 152.14 recorded the active-build position as 91
unconditional registrations, 47 implemented, and a backlog of 44 names over 44
distinct values, of which 33 have `base_size` at most 16. Section 153 implements
4 of those 33 and Section 154 will implement 4 more, which projects the position
to **51 implemented** and a backlog of **36 names over 36 distinct values**, with
25 remaining at `base_size` 16 or less. Three of those 36 are permanently
unimplementable rather than merely pending, and the distinction matters for
planning:

- `HEADER_CG_TEXT` (64) is registered but never dispatched and the client never
  references it. **Never implement.**
- `HEADER_CG_STATE_CHECKER` (206) is registered, the client sends it, and the
  server's only dispatch is commented out. **Never implement as a live path.** See
  Sections 155.2 and 155.4.
  > **CORRECTED in 157.10 — this is wrong.** The record *is* live: `input.cpp:227`
  > handles it in `CInputHandshake::Analyze` through an `else if` chain, which a
  > `case`-shaped search cannot see. It is implementable. The reasoning above is
  > kept for the record; the conclusion is reversed.
- `HEADER_CG_KEY_AGREEMENT` (**251**, `0xfb`) sits behind
  `#ifdef _IMPROVED_PACKET_ENCRYPTION_` in `packet_info.cpp:191` and is not in the
  active build. It is the only one of the 92 `Set()` calls that is conditional, and
  it is already excluded from the 91. (The value 251 was mis-recorded as `0` before
  the hex-parsing defect in Section 155.1 was found; the `0xfb` tail is exactly the
  region the old parser dropped.)
- Header 22 `HEADER_CG_ITEM_SELL` has no registration at all.

Two more are blocked on an explicit profile rather than on work: header 27
`TPacketCGExchange` and header 96 `TPacketCGRefine`, whose widths depend on
`ENABLE_REMOVE_LIMIT_GOLD` and `ENABLE_CUSTOM_INVENTORY` respectively.

And one is deferred by phase rather than by difficulty: header 90
`HEADER_CG_EMPIRE` is a `CInputLogin` record that closes the login phase on an
out-of-range empire byte, so it belongs with the login boundary.
## Section 155 — an audit of my own census tool, and the phase placement of the three 1-byte records

This section exists because auditing Section 154 turned up a defect in the
instrumentation I had been using since Section 136, and because a naive text
search produced a claim that was false. Both are recorded rather than quietly
fixed, because both classes of error are silent and both would have propagated.

### 155.1 The enum parser was decimal-only, and it silently dropped 24 headers

The collision and backlog censuses were built by `enum_vals`, whose enumerator
pattern was:

```python
r'\b(HEADER_(?:CG|GC|GD|GG)_[A-Z0-9_]+)\s*(?:=\s*(\d+))?\s*(?:,|$)'
```

`\d+` matches decimal only. The legacy enums end in a **hexadecimal** block, so
for `HEADER_CG_PONG = 0xfe,` the name group matched, the optional value group
failed, the pattern then demanded `,` or end-of-body but found `=`, and the
**whole match failed**. The enumerator was not recorded as `None`; it was
recorded *nowhere*. A later diagnostic that tested `sv.get(name) is None`
therefore reported twelve missing headers as "None-valued" and understated the
problem, which is exactly how a missing value hides inside a plausible-looking
count.

Recovered with a corrected pattern that accepts `(0x[0-9a-fA-F]+|\d+)` and
parses with `int(x, 0)`:

| tree | old | fixed | recovered |
|---|---|---|---|
| server `packet.h` | 261 | **273** | 12 |
| client tree | 235 | **247** | 12 |

The twelve server headers are exactly the hex tail, and they are the only hex
enumerators in the file: `0xf1`/`241`, `0xfa`/`250`, `0xfb`/`251` (twice),
`0xfc`/`252` (twice), `0xfd`/`253` (twice), `0xfe`/`254` (twice), and
`0xff`/`255` (twice).

**The recorded censuses survive.** I re-ran the collision set for every value
touched by Sections 151 through 154 — 1, 2, 3, 4, 28, 29, 31, 44 through 53, 61,
65, 66, 82, 104, and 114 — against the corrected maps. The server-side name set
changed for **none** of them, because the recovered values are 241 and
250 through 255 and no implemented or candidate record lives in that range. So
the bug was real, long-lived, and harmless to the conclusions already on the
record. That is worth stating plainly, because the default reaction to finding a
long-standing tool defect is to assume everything downstream is suspect, and
re-deriving is the only way to know.

**What did change is one recorded value.** `HEADER_CG_PONG` is **`0xfe` (254)**,
and it had been carried as a phantom `0` — a header that does not exist, sitting
in the 1-byte backlog table. The backlog *counts* still reconcile
(44 before Section 153, minus 4, gives 40 measured), so the arithmetic in
Sections 152.14 and 154.5 stands; only the value attached to one name was wrong.

The durable rule: **a census parser must be validated against a known hex case
before its output is used for collision work.** One deliberately mixed-radix
enumerator at the end of the file was enough to lose a dozen entries, and no
count-based sanity check would ever have shown it.

### 155.2 A `case` inside a comment is not a dispatch, and grep cannot tell

Searching the server for `case HEADER_CG_STATE_CHECKER` returns
`input_udp.cpp:111`. That line is **dead code**, inside a `/* ... */` block
running from `:106` to `:114`:

```cpp
	/*
	case HEADER_CG_HANDSHAKE:
	   Handshake(pDesc, c_pData);
	   break;

	case HEADER_CG_STATE_CHECKER:
		StateChecker(c_pData);
		break;
	*/
```

and the enclosing `CInputUDP::Process` at `:124` opens another `/*` at `:125`.
So the checked-in server has **no live UDP dispatch at all**, and the state
checker is unreachable. I then wrote a small liveness filter that tracks `/* */`
depth line by line and confirmed the classification against five other arms:
`input_udp.cpp:111` is DEAD, while `input_login.cpp:1218`, `input_auth.cpp:211`,
`input_login.cpp:1169`, `input_main.cpp:3661` and `input_main.cpp:4102` are all
LIVE. The liveness filter is a fixture from this point on, and the rule is now
part of the source-audit skill: **never claim a legacy record is dispatched, or
that it is not dispatched, from a raw text search.** Both directions of that
claim were wrong here — "registered but never dispatched" was nearly right for
the wrong reason, and the dispatch site that appeared to prove otherwise was
inside a comment.

### 155.3 Phase placement of the three 1-byte records, corrected

`HEADER_CG_PONG` is not a game-phase record. It is live in **four** places
across three phase analysers:

| phase | site | note |
|---|---|---|
| Auth | `input_auth.cpp:211` | `Pong(d)` |
| Login | `input_login.cpp:1169` | `Pong(d)` |
| Game | `input_main.cpp:3661` | inside `CInputMain::Analyze`, which spans `:3643`-`:4086` |
| Dead | `input_main.cpp:4102` | inside `CInputDead::Analyze`, which starts at `:4088` |

The two `input_main.cpp` sites are **different functions**, not a duplicate arm
— the second is the dead-character phase, which has its own `Analyze`. A codec
for `0xfe` therefore cannot be filed under the game-phase bundle, and this is
the same class of correction as header 90 `HEADER_CG_EMPIRE` in Section 152.

`HEADER_CG_MARK_IDXLIST` (104, `TPacketCGMarkIDXList` at `packet.h:2246`, a
single `BYTE header`, so one byte) is dispatched **LIVE from
`input_login.cpp:1218`** and is therefore a **login-phase** record of the guild
mark family, not a game-phase one. Its size made it look like a free win; its
phase makes it a boundary question.

`HEADER_CG_STATE_CHECKER` (206) is registered unconditionally at
`packet_info.cpp:173` with `sizeof(BYTE)`, the client sends it from
`ServerStateChecker.cpp:59`, and the server's only dispatch is dead. Its
`CInputUDP::Process` has `default:` at `:116` logging `"unknown UDP header %u"`,
but that path is itself inside the commented region. **It must never be
implemented as a live path.**

### 155.4 A latent macro shadowing that would silently change a header value

`input_udp.cpp:13` contains

```cpp
#define HEADER_CG_STATE_CHECKER	1
```

which **redefines the enumerator's 206 as the literal 1** for the whole
translation unit. It is harmless today only because the single use is inside the
comment. Anyone who uncomments the UDP dispatch, or adds a new reference in that
file, silently gets a header value of 1 — which is `HEADER_CG_LOGIN` — and the
resulting confusion would point at the login path, not at this line. It is
recorded as a C++ follow-up alongside the other legacy robustness items, and as a
reason never to derive a UDP header value from a file that redefines the enum.

### 155.5 What an unhandled header actually does, in `CInputMain`

`CInputMain::Analyze` spans `input_main.cpp:3643`-`:4086`. Its top-level
`switch (bHeader)` at `:3659` contains **exactly one** `default:` — at `:4078`,
at brace depth 3, belonging to a nested "unknown private shop subheader" switch.
There is **no top-level default**. A depth-tracking scan of `:3659`-`:4086`
returns no depth-1 `default:` at all.

So a registered header with no `case` in this function — `HEADER_CG_TEXT` (64)
and `HEADER_CG_STATE_CHECKER` (206) are the two registered instances — falls
through the switch with `iExtraLen` still `0`, returns `0`, and is **consumed
and silently ignored**. It is not logged and it does not close the descriptor.
That is the precise legacy behaviour to reproduce for this boundary, and it is
the opposite of the rewrite's stated rule that retained unknown client headers
must close rather than retry. The two must be recorded separately: the legacy
fact, and the hardening rule that deliberately diverges from it.
### 155.6 Section 153 mutation receipt

All **37 of 37** mutations were caught. **Survivors: none.**

| group | mutations | target | all caught |
|---|---|---|---|
| header constants | M01-M04 | the four `header()` bodies | yes |
| size constants | M05-M10 | the six `WIRE_SIZE` / `PAYLOAD_SIZE` constants | yes |
| shared guards | M11-M16 | `check_exact` boundaries, `check_header` inversion, both decode helpers | yes |
| `encode_into` | M17-M21 | one per record, plus a field-order swap | yes |
| decode indices | M22-M27 | all six single-byte field reads | yes |
| frame projection | M28-M29 | `to_frame` for position and warp | yes |
| decode width | M30-M36 | record-vs-payload size at all seven call sites | yes |
| error variant | M37 | `InvalidHeader { expected, actual }` | yes |

Representative evidence: M01 reported `exit 101` with 10 failing tests across
`-p protocol --lib` and `-p protocol --test cg_wiring`, i.e. the dedicated
codec tests and the shared-framer wiring tests both reacted, not just one.

**Restoration was proven by hash, not by absence of strings.** The restored
`cg_micro.rs` is 34,200 bytes at `sha256 4abb97d8df7aabb4…`, identical to the
pre-sweep recording, with no `.mutbak`, `.orig`, `.rej` or `.bak` residue, and
all 37 anchor strings again resolve exactly once.

A check I ran alongside it was **wrong and I am recording that too**. I verified
that none of the 37 *replacement* strings still appears in the file, and it
reported five hits: M01, M02, M03, M04 and M28. That is not residue. M01 through
M04 swap one real header constant for another inside the four `header()` bodies,
so each replacement is itself legitimate original text, and M28's replacement
`[0_u8; 0]` is the genuine body of `CgWarp::to_frame`. An absence check built on
"the mutated text is absent" is only meaningful when the replacement cannot
coincide with valid source. The hash comparison has no such weakness, and the
lesson is the same one the source-audit skill already carries: **a negative
check needs a positive control.** Here the control is the hash.
## Section 156 — the login-phase guild mark family

### 156.1 The family is contiguous, and it is all login-phase

`input_login.cpp` carries a run of six consecutive cases, and unlike most
families in this rewrite they are physically adjacent, which makes the grouping
unambiguous from the source rather than a judgement call:

| header | value | case | handler | record | wire |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `HEADER_CG_MARK_LOGIN` | 100 | `:1207` | `GuildMarkLogin` | `TPacketCGMarkLogin` | 9 |
| `HEADER_CG_MARK_CRCLIST` | 101 | `:1214` | `GuildMarkCRCList` | `TPacketCGMarkCRCList` | 322 |
| `HEADER_CG_MARK_IDXLIST` | 104 | `:1218` | `GuildMarkIDXList` | `TPacketCGMarkIDXList` | 1 |
| `HEADER_CG_MARK_UPLOAD` | 102 | `:1222` | `GuildMarkUpload` | `TPacketCGMarkUpload` | 773 |
| `HEADER_CG_GUILD_SYMBOL_UPLOAD` | — | `:1229` | `GuildSymbolUpload` | variable | variable |
| `HEADER_CG_SYMBOL_CRC` | 113 | `:1234` | `GuildSymbolCRC` | `TPacketCGSymbolCRC` | 13 |

All six `case` labels are LIVE under the comment-depth filter. Every one of them
sits in `CInputLogin`, so this is a **login-phase** family, which is the single
most important fact about it and the reason it was nearly filed in the wrong
bundle: header 104 has a one-byte record and reads like a free win.

`HEADER_CG_GUILD_SYMBOL_UPLOAD` is the family's only variable-length member. It
is also the only case in the run that checks for failure and propagates it:

```cpp
case HEADER_CG_GUILD_SYMBOL_UPLOAD:
	if ((iExtraLen = GuildSymbolUpload(d, c_pData, m_iBufferLeft)) < 0)
		return -1;
	break;
```

so it consumes the remainder of the buffer, unlike every fixed sibling. That is
a different shape class and it is deliberately out of scope for a fixed-record
section.

**A seventh case follows the family and is worth one line.** At `:1239`,
`HEADER_CG_HACK` is registered with `sizeof(TPacketCGHack)` — 257 bytes — and its
handler is `case HEADER_CG_HACK: break;`. The server accepts a 257-byte record,
reads the header, and discards it without inspecting a single byte of the
payload. It is a live no-op, not dead code, and it must never be treated as an
implemented or dispatched feature.

### 156.2 Field-name drift: identical in two records, total in the third

The two trees agree on `MarkIDXList` and `MarkLogin` **exactly**, member for
member including names, which is worth stating because it is not the usual
outcome in this repository:

| record | server `packet.h` | client `Packet.h` | agreement |
|---|---|---|---|
| `TPacketCGMarkIDXList` | `:2246` `BYTE header;` | `:322` `BYTE header;` | exact |
| `TPacketCGMarkLogin` | `:2234` `BYTE header; DWORD handle; DWORD random_key;` | `:310` `BYTE header; DWORD handle; DWORD random_key;` | exact |
| `TPacketCGSymbolCRC` | `:2285` `guild_id`, `crc`, `size` | `:374` `dwGuildID`, `dwCRC`, `dwSize` | **none** |

`TPacketCGSymbolCRC` has **zero** name overlap between the two trees. The widths
and order still agree, so the wire bytes are identical and a codec is safe, but
any reader matching server code against client code by field name will fail on
this record. This is the party-family drift pattern recurring in a new family,
which is why the ledger keeps restating the rule: **derive the layout from both
trees and match on width and order, never on names.**

`TPacketCGMarkLogin` deserves a second note because of what it carries:
`DWORD handle` and `DWORD random_key` are the same two words that terminate the
357-byte `GcLoginSuccess` record described in Section 133. The mark login
request re-presents the account's login handle and random key so the DB can
attribute the mark to a session. Both stay opaque little-endian `u32`s here; the
codec does not validate, correlate, or compare them.
### 156.3 A cross-tree enumerator-name divergence, and a client-asserted digest

Searching the client for `HEADER_CG_SYMBOL_CRC` returns **nothing**. The record
is not missing and the client does send it; the *enumerator is named
differently in the two trees*:

| tree | enumerator for value 113 |
|---|---|
| server `packet.h` | `HEADER_CG_SYMBOL_CRC` |
| client `Packet.h:77` | `HEADER_CG_GUILD_SYMBOL_CRC` |

The client sender is `CGuildMarkDownloader::__SendSymbolCRCList` at
`GuildMarkDownloader.cpp:478-497`, and line `:483` assigns
`kSymbolCRCPacket.header = HEADER_CG_GUILD_SYMBOL_CRC;` into a
`TPacketCGSymbolCRC` — the same struct name the server uses. So the wire value,
the struct, and the 13-byte layout all agree; only the constant's name differs,
and the earlier search for the server's name found no client hit at all.

This is a **third** distinct class of cross-tree divergence in this repository,
and it is worth listing them together because each one invalidates a different
habit:

1. **Field-name drift** — `TPacketCGSymbolCRC`, and the whole party family.
   Caught by matching widths and order, not names.
2. **Struct absent from one tree** — `TPacketCGFishing` has no client struct at
   all; the client writes two `Send` calls instead.
3. **Enumerator-name divergence** — here. Caught only by searching for the
   *value* on both sides after a name search came back empty.

Rule 3 generalises into the standing practice: **when a name search returns zero
hits in the other tree, re-search by the numeric value before concluding
absence.** A zero-hit name search is a claim about a name, not about a record.

**The payload is a client-asserted file digest, and the server trusts it.**
`__SendSymbolCRCList` computes all three values locally, in a loop over
`m_kVec_dwGuildID`, from a file on the client's disk:

```cpp
kSymbolCRCPacket.dwGuildID = m_kVec_dwGuildID[i];
std::string strFileName = GetGuildSymbolFileName(m_kVec_dwGuildID[i]);
kSymbolCRCPacket.dwCRC  = GetFileCRC32(strFileName.c_str());
kSymbolCRPCacket.dwSize = GetFileSize(strFileName.c_str());
```

The server's `GuildSymbolCRC` receives a CRC, a size, and a guild id, all
supplied by the client, with no proof that the client holds the symbol image the
guild actually owns. The three fields therefore stay opaque little-endian `u32`s
at the codec boundary, and any trust decision belongs to the guild-symbol
service, not to framing. The same loop also shows the record is sent **once per
guild id**, which is why it is a fixed 13-byte record and not a batch: batching
is the server's job on the way back.
### 156.4 Receipt update, and one number that did not reconcile

`AGENTS.md` and `README.md` both carried `1,192`, which is correct for the state
before Section 153. The post-mutation and post-gate receipt is:

| quantity | value |
|---|---|
| all-targets tests | **1,224 passed / 0 failed** |
| workspace doc-tests | **6 passed / 0 failed** |
| total | **1,230** |
| test binaries | 28 |
| format, strict Clippy, rustdoc | clean, no warnings, no suppressions |
| mutations on the new module | **37 / 37 caught, 0 survivors** |
| Rust files | 145 |
| scanned lines | 101,155 |

`1,224` is `1,192 + 32`, and 32 is the 30 module tests plus 2 wiring tests.

**The file count reconciles exactly and the line count does not, and I am
recording that rather than choosing the convenient number.** The pre-Section-153
claim was 143 files and 99,308 lines. Section 153 added exactly two Rust files,
`cg_micro.rs` at 956 `wc -l` lines and `cg_wiring.rs` at 524, so the file count
predicts 145 and the line count predicts 100,788. The measured line count is
**101,155**, leaving a **+367** residual. The file total is therefore right and
the old line total was already stale before this section added anything, so
99,308 was never a valid baseline to diff against.

Both new numbers were recomputed from the rule the ledger states rather than
inherited: every `*.rs` under `/workspace` excluding `target`, `.overlord`, and
vendored `extern`, counted with `wc -l` semantics. That set includes the one file
under `tools/`, which is correct because `AGENTS.md` describes `tools/` as
auxiliary tooling outside the locked test run, and a file count is a file count
whether or not its tests are gated. The two numbers are now measured, rule-based,
and reproducible, which the previous pair was not.
### 156.5 Implementation

`protocol/src/cg_mark.rs` holds the three fixed login-phase mark records,
registered by `pub mod cg_mark;` in `protocol/src/lib.rs` immediately before
`cg_micro`. It follows the established shape from `cg_party` and `cg_micro`: one
`CgMarkError` with the same three variants, explicit `read_u32_le` /
`write_u32_le`, `check_exact` before `check_header`, and six constants naming
each record's record width and frame payload width separately.

**27 module tests and 2 wiring tests**, for a delta of 29.

`CgMarkIdxList` is the second header-only record in the workspace after
`CgWarp`, and it is a different kind of header-only: `CgWarp`'s handler calls
`ch->WarpEnd()` and reads nothing, whereas `GuildMarkIDXList` resolves a whole
index list from the session. Both produce an empty frame payload, and both
tests pin that a non-empty payload is a `LengthMismatch` rather than an
accepted record. Reusing the pattern across two independent records is the
point: a shape that appears twice is no longer a curiosity, it is a category.

**The three widths are 1, 9 and 13, all distinct, and that has a consequence
worth stating.** Because the length check runs before the header check, and
because no two of these records share a width, no cross-decoding among the three
can ever produce `InvalidHeader` — the width always decides first. I discovered
this because my first version of the cross-decode test asserted the opposite and
failed. The test now pins the real behaviour and asserts explicitly that
`InvalidHeader` never appears, and a companion test pads a foreign record to the
right width to show the header error surfacing when width stops being the
discriminator.

### 156.6 Four test bugs of my own, recorded because three of them were instructive

The first run of the new tests gave **22 passed, 4 failed**. All four failures
were bugs in the tests, not in the codecs, and the module needed no change. That
is the right outcome and it is still worth writing down, because each failure
was a different wrong assumption:

- **`encode_into_into_an_empty_buffer_equals_encode`** compared
  `CgMarkLogin::new(1, 2)` against a sample built from `new(0, 0)`. A fixture
  mismatch, not a codec difference.
- **`length_is_checked_before_the_header`** asserted `LengthMismatch` for a
  two-byte slice given to a nine-byte record. It is `Truncated`, because two is
  *short*, not long. The corrected test now shows the **same slice** yielding
  `Truncated` for the 9-byte login and 13-byte symbol CRC but
  `LengthMismatch` for the 1-byte index list, which is the width deciding the
  variant.
- **`a_complete_width_with_a_foreign_header_…`** expected
  `CgMarkLogin::new(0, 1)` from `[0x64, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 1]`. The trailing
  byte is the **most** significant byte of the second word, so the value is
  `0x0100_0000`. I had assumed the last byte of a little-endian field was the
  least significant, which is exactly backwards, in the one test whose whole job
  was to pin the byte order.
- **`the_three_records_reject_each_others_headers`** is the one described above.

The general lesson: **a new codec module's first test run is evidence about the
tests, not about the codec.** Four of twenty-six failed, and in every case the
codec was right and the expectation was wrong. Writing the expectation from the
declared layout rather than from intuition is what makes the difference.

### 156.7 The gate failed on first run, in both formatting and Clippy

The first full gate for this section printed **`DOC_OK` and nothing else** — no
`FMT_OK`, no `CLIPPY_OK`, no `TEST_OK`, no `DOCTEST_OK`. This is the second time
this exact signature has appeared, and it is worth restating the rule it taught:
**a short marker list is itself the failure signal.** A reader scanning for green
markers sees a passing documentation build and may stop there.

The failures were seven rustfmt line-width diffs in `cg_mark.rs` and **three
real Clippy errors in the new tests**:

| lint | line | problem |
|---|---|---|
| `clippy::needless_range_loop` | `:879` | `col` used to index `encoded` |
| `clippy::default_constructed_unit_structs` | `:945` | `CgMarkIdxList::default()` on a unit struct |
| `clippy::useless_vec` | `:976` | `vec![0u8; N]` used only for slicing |

All three were fixed by refactoring the test code, and none was suppressed. I
also renamed a variable that a copy-paste had carried over from the warp test:
`warp_like` in a guild-mark test became `idx_frame`. A name inherited from a
different record's test is a small thing, but it is the kind that misleads the
next reader, and Clippy's silence about it is exactly why it had to be caught by
hand.

One consequence for the mutation plan: `cargo fmt` rewrote
`Self { guild_id, crc, size }` into the multi-line form, which destroyed the
anchor for the M19 mutation. The list was re-derived against the formatted file
and re-verified — **all 41 anchors resolve exactly once** — rather than trusting
anchors captured before a formatter ran.
### 156.8 The "implemented" metric needed a definition, and two plausible ones were wrong

While closing this section I tried to restate how many CG records are
implemented, and got three different answers from three defensible-looking
definitions. The number is reported often enough that the definition belongs in
the ledger rather than in someone's head.

| definition | result | why it is wrong |
|---|---|---|
| any mention of the constant in a `cg_*.rs` file | 58 | counts doc comments; `HEADER_CG_HACK` appears **only** in a `//` comment |
| a `pub const fn header()` body returning it | 14 | measures *style*: `cg_attack.rs` predates that accessor and writes `HEADER_CG_ATTACK.value()` inline |
| code references, comments stripped, `cg_inventory.rs` excluded | **54** | correct |

The correct rule: a CG header is implemented when some `protocol/src/cg_*.rs`
other than `cg_inventory.rs` **references its constant in code**, with `//` and
`/* */` comments removed first. The comment-stripping is the load-bearing part.
`cg_mark.rs` names `HEADER_CG_HACK`, `HEADER_CG_KEY_AGREEMENT` and
`HEADER_CG_GUILD_SYMBOL_CRC` in its module documentation, on purpose, to explain
why those three are *not* implemented here — and a mention-based count reads that
documentation as three completed records.

`cg_wire.rs` and `cg_variable.rs` **do** count. They own the variable-prefix
headers (`HEADER_CG_CHAT`, `HEADER_CG_MESSENGER`, `HEADER_CG_MYSHOP`,
`HEADER_CG_PRIVATE_SHOP`, `HEADER_CG_SHOP`, `HEADER_CG_GUILD`,
`HEADER_CG_WHISPER`, `HEADER_CG_SYNC_POSITION`, `HEADER_CG_FISH_EVENT_SEND`,
`HEADER_CG_AURA`, `HEADER_CG_SWITCHBOT`, and others), so excluding them would
have understated the total by ten and invented a backlog that does not exist.

**The corrected arithmetic reconciles with every figure already on the record:**

| point | implemented | backlog (names / distinct values) |
|---|---|---|
| after Section 152, as recorded in 152.14 | 47 | 44 / 44 |
| after Section 153 (4 records) | 51 | **40 / 40** |
| after Section 156 (3 records) | **54** | **37 / 37** |

So the backlog figure of 40 that Section 154.5 used was right, and the
projection of 36 after Section 154 lands stands. Only the *implemented* count was
drifting, by one, because a doc comment was being counted as a codec. The
lesson is the same one that produced the hex-enumerator defect in Section 155.1:
**a metric whose definition is not written down will be re-derived slightly
differently by each person, and the drift is invisible because every individual
count is plausible.**

| gate | exit | result |
|---|---|---|
| `cargo fmt --all -- --check` | 0 | clean |
| `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets --locked --offline -- -D warnings` | 0 | no warnings, no suppressions |
| `RUSTDOCFLAGS="-D warnings" cargo doc --workspace --no-deps --locked --offline` | 0 | no warnings |
| `cargo test --workspace --all-targets --no-fail-fast --locked --offline` | 0 | **1,253 passed / 0 failed / 28 binaries** |
| `cargo test --workspace --doc --no-fail-fast --locked --offline` | 0 | **6 passed / 0 failed** |

1,253 is 1,224 plus exactly 29, and 29 is the 27 module tests plus 2 wiring
tests. `AGENTS.md` and `README.md` are updated to 1,253 + 6 = 1,259, and the
workspace now holds 146 Rust files and 102,280 scanned lines, counted with the rule
stated in Section 156.4.
### 156.10 A documentation gap in `AGENTS.md`, and two numbers I guessed

The `AGENTS.md` bullet that describes `protocol/` named the older modules but
**omitted four that now exist**: `cg_party` (Section 152), `cg_quickslot_add`,
`cg_quickslot_del` and `cg_quickslot_swap` (Section 151), `cg_micro` (Section
153), and `cg_mark` (Section 156). The quickslot modules were mentioned only at
line 91, in a compatibility rule, never in the module list — so a reader
consulting `AGENTS.md` to learn what the `protocol/` crate contains was being
shown an incomplete picture of the crate. The sentence now describes all four
groups.

**Two of the header ranges in that new sentence were wrong when I first wrote
them, because I guessed instead of deriving.** I wrote the party family as
"headers 70-78" and the quickslot family as "headers 123, 124, and 125". The
inventory constants give the real values:

| module | asserted | actual |
|---|---|---|
| `cg_party` | 70-78 | **72, 73, 74, 75, 78** |
| `cg_quickslot_*` | 123, 124, 125 | **16, 17, 18** |
| `cg_micro` | 28, 29, 65, 82 | 28, 29, 65, 82 (correct) |
| `cg_mark` | 100, 104, 113 | 100, 104, 113 (correct) |

The quickslot values were wrong by more than a hundred, and a plausible-looking
range is exactly the failure mode: "70-78" reads as a deliberate span and is
indistinguishable from a correct one at a glance. Both are corrected, and every
header number now asserted in that sentence is checked against
`cg_inventory.rs`. The standing rule applies to documentation with the same
force as to code: **derive the number from the source constant, never from
memory, and never from a pattern that looks like the neighbouring family.**
### 156.11 Section 156 mutation receipt

All **41 of 41** mutations were caught. **Survivors: none.**

| group | mutations | target | all caught |
|---|---|---|---|
| header constants | M01-M03 | the three `header()` bodies | yes |
| size constants | M04-M09 | the three `WIRE_SIZE` and three `PAYLOAD_SIZE` constants | yes |
| shared guards | M10-M12 | both `check_exact` boundaries and the header comparison | yes |
| `encode_into` | M13-M15 | one per record, each clearing the buffer | yes |
| word order and endianness | M16-M18 | login pair, symbol-CRC triple, and `read_u32_le` itself | yes |
| constructor | M19 | `CgSymbolCrc::new` ignoring its `size` argument | yes |
| decode offsets | M20-M29 | all ten field reads, slice and frame | yes |
| record-vs-payload width | M30-M35 | all six decode call sites | yes |
| shared helper defeats | M36-M37 | both helpers skipping the header check | yes |
| frame projection | M38, M40, M41 | index list gaining a payload, login dropping a word, symbol CRC dropping a word | yes |
| error variant | M39 | `InvalidHeader { expected, actual }` swapped | yes |

Two details worth recording. M18 mutates `read_u32_le` itself to
`from_be_bytes`, so a single swapped helper would break every word in the module
at once; it was caught, which confirms the tests are sensitive to the byte order
rather than merely to the width. And every mutation that was caught reported
failing **both** `-p protocol --lib` and `-p protocol --test cg_wiring`, so the
dedicated module tests and the public-surface wiring tests each contributed
detection rather than one carrying the other.

**Restoration was verified three ways**: the file is back to 38,989 bytes with no
`.mutbak` residue, all 41 anchor strings resolve exactly once, and the tool
reported `restore protocol/src/cg_mark.rs OK`.

The plan itself needed a repair. The mutation list was first built against the
**unformatted** file, and `cargo fmt` then rewrote
`Self { guild_id, crc, size }` into the multi-line form, destroying the M19
anchor. Rather than let a dead mutation sit in the list looking like coverage,
M19 was re-derived against the formatted text and the whole list re-verified
before the sweep started. A mutation list built before a formatter has run is
not yet a plan.

The mutation sweep restores `cg_mark.rs` to 38,989 bytes with SHA-256 beginning

### 156.14 A note on the worktree "debris" scan

A whole-worktree scan for `.bak`, `.orig`, `.rej`, `.tmp` and `.mutbak` returns

```
.overlord/prime-agent-data/models.json.bak

```

The first is live runtime state under `.overlord/`, which `AGENTS.md` forbids

is demonstrated. A hygiene check that reported "5 files found" without this
