## Section 154 — implementation of the four single-choice records

### 154.6 What landed

`protocol/src/cg_pick.rs` implements the four records the Section 154 audit had
already cleared, registered by `pub mod cg_pick;` in `protocol/src/lib.rs`
between `cg_party_skill` and `cg_quickslot_add`.

| record | header | record width | payload width | fields |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `CgQuestConfirm` | 31 `0x1f` | 6 | 5 | `answer: u8` @1, `request_pid: u32` @2 |
| `CgTarget` | 61 `0x3d` | 5 | 4 | `vid: u32` @1 |
| `CgScriptButton` | 66 `0x42` | 5 | 4 | `idx: u32` @1 |
| `CgScriptSelectItem` | 114 `0x72` | 5 | 4 | `selection: u32` @1 |

**43 module tests and 2 wiring tests, for a delta of 45.** One shared
`CgPickError`, explicit `read_u32_le` / `write_u32_le`, `check_exact` before
`check_header`, and the same six-constant shape as `cg_micro` and `cg_mark`.

The module name is worth a note, because it is **not** a legacy type name. The
four records have nothing in common in the legacy tree except their wire shape
and their purpose — three are quest or script records, one is a world lookup —
and calling the module after any single legacy name would have implied a
grouping the source does not have. `cg_pick` names the shared shape and the
module documentation says so explicitly.

### 154.7 The property that is the mirror image of `cg_mark`

Section 156 found that `cg_mark`'s three records have three **distinct** widths,
so length always decides before the header and **no cross-decoding can ever
produce `InvalidHeader`**. The three single-word records here are the opposite
case: `Target`, `ScriptButton`, and `ScriptSelectItem` are **all 5 bytes**, so a
real record from one of them reaches the others' decoders at the *correct* width
and is rejected by the header alone.

That difference is the reason both situations are pinned explicitly rather than
implied:

- `the_three_single_word_records_are_header_discriminated_not_width_discriminated`
  feeds each real 5-byte record to the other two decoders and requires
  `InvalidHeader`.
- `quest_confirm_never_reaches_a_header_error_against_the_five_byte_records`
  requires the opposite for the 6-byte record, in both directions: `LengthMismatch`
  going out and `Truncated` coming in.
- `the_same_slice_takes_different_variants_from_records_of_different_widths`
  shows **one** 5-byte slice `[0x1f, 0, 0, 0, 0]` yielding `InvalidHeader` from
  `Target` and `Truncated` from `QuestConfirm`. Same input, different failure, and
  the difference is purely the declared width.

A family of equal-width records is a stronger test of header validation than a
family of distinct-width records, and a family of distinct-width records is a
stronger test of length validation. Sections 153, 154, and 156 now cover both
sides of that pair.

### 154.8 The field-order trap, pinned twice

`packet.h:766-768` declares `header`, then `answer` (`BYTE`), then
`requestPID` (`DWORD`). The natural "narrow field first, wide field last"
assumption produces the right total width of 6 and the **wrong six bytes**.

Three tests hold this down, because one is not enough for a reversed two-field
layout:

- `quest_confirm_places_the_byte_before_the_word` asserts the exact golden and
  asserts that the *reversed* byte string is **not** produced. Asserting only
  the golden would still pass if both the encoder and the decoder were wrong in
  the same direction, which is the real risk with a self-consistent pair.
- `the_word_offset_is_two_for_quest_confirm_and_one_for_the_others` derives both
  offsets from the wire constants.
- `quest_confirms_frame_payload_keeps_the_byte_before_the_word` checks the same
  thing on the frame path, which has a different offset again.

### 154.9 Three test bugs of mine, and one Clippy-driven simplification

The first run gave **41 passed, 2 failed**. Both failures were my expectations,
not the codecs, and the first is the more interesting of the two.

**`every_word_is_little_endian_so_the_low_byte_comes_first` assumed a single word
offset for all four records.** It asserted `golden[2]` was the least significant
byte, which is right for `QuestConfirm` (word at offset 2) and **wrong for the
other three** (word at offset 1, so the least significant byte is at index 1). The
test failed on `Target`, reporting byte 51 where 68 was expected. The fix names
the offset per record. This is the second time in two sections that I have
assumed a shared shape where the wire actually has two — the first was
Section 156's three distinct widths, and this is its mirror.

**`the_three_single_word_records_are_header_discriminated_not_width_discriminated`
looped over all three headers and all three records without excluding the
matching pair**, so it fed `Target`'s own record to `Target`'s own decoder,
`unwrap_err()`ed on a success, and panicked. The fix skips the owner. A test
about rejection that does not exclude the accepted case is a test that will fail
for the wrong reason, and the panic message pointed at the loop rather than at
the property.

Clippy then removed two pieces of machinery I had added and did not need:

- `clippy::match_on_vec_items` — a `match golden[0]` over a `Vec` index, used to
  re-dispatch `encode_into` by header. Replaced with four explicit blocks. The
  dispatch existed only because I had written the test as a loop over tuples
  before noticing that four straight-line blocks are clearer and need no
  indexing at all.
- `clippy::semicolon_if_nothing_returned` ×4 — `assert_eq!` without a semicolon
  inside `match` arms in the exhaustive test.

I also removed a `HasHeader` trait and an `impl_header!` macro that I had
written to reach `header().value()` on four types. Two of the three call sites
did not need it, and the third is clearer as four direct calls to
`CgTarget::header().value()`. A macro that saves two lines is not worth the
indirection.

All five were fixed by rewriting the tests. None was suppressed.
## Section 157 — audit of the 1-byte and 2-byte records: a live feature with a mismatched header byte

This section is an audit only. Nothing is implemented yet, and it is written down
because it contains the most significant cross-tree finding in the series so far.

### 157.1 The family, and the third header-only record

Seven registered records, one byte or two:

| record | header | width | declaration | registration | dispatch | client sender |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| *(no struct)* `Pong` | 254 `0xfe` | **1** | — | `packet_info.cpp` `sizeof(BYTE)` | `input_main.cpp:3661`, `:4102`, `input_login.cpp:1169`, `input.cpp:107`, `:235` | `NetStream`, `PythonNetworkStream`, `AccountConnector`, `GuildMark{Uploader,Downloader}` |
| `TPacketCGEmpire` | 90 `0x5a` | 2 | `packet.h:2109` | `sizeof(TPacketCGEmpire)` | `input_login.cpp:1201` | `PythonNetworkStreamPhaseSelect.cpp:164` |
| `SPacketCGRequestEventData` | 117 `0x75` | 2 | `packet.h:3453` | `sizeof(TPacketCGRequestEventData)` | `input_main.cpp:3920` | `PhaseGame.cpp:7239` |
| `SPacketCGWorldBoss` | 148 `0x94` | 2 | `packet.h:3357` | `sizeof(TPacketCGWorldBoss)` | `input_main.cpp:3749` **(compiled out)** | `PhaseGame.cpp:7445`, `:7458`, `:7470` |
| `SPacketCGPremiumPlayers` | 176 `0xb0` | 2 | `packet.h:3219-3226` | `sizeof(TPacketCGPremiumPlayers)` | `input_main.cpp:3948` | `Packet.h:3285` |
| `SPacketCGRefineElement` | 227 `0xe3` | 2 | `packet.h:3072` | `sizeof(TPacketCGRefineElement)` | `input_main.cpp:3854` | `PhaseGame.cpp:5992` |
| `TPacketChangeLanguage` | 238 `0xee` | 2 | `packet.h:3248` | `sizeof(TPacketChangeLanguage)` | `input_main.cpp:3932` | `PhaseGame.cpp:6295` |

All six structs are `header: BYTE` plus exactly one more `BYTE`, and all six sit
inside the single `#pragma pack(1)`. Five of the six declare a plain field; the
second field is named `bSubHeader` for `WorldBoss` and `bySubHeader` for
`PremiumPlayers`, which makes those two a header-plus-sub-header pair rather than
a header plus a payload value.

**`HEADER_CG_PONG` is the third header-only record in the workspace**, after
`CgWarp` (Section 153) and `CgMarkIdxList` (Section 156), and it is the only one
registered as `sizeof(BYTE)` rather than `sizeof(TSomething)`. There is no
`TPacketCGPong` anywhere in the server tree. It is also the only record in the
workspace that is **live in three different input phases** — auth
(`input.cpp:107`, `:235`), login (`input_login.cpp:1169`), and both the living
and dead game paths (`input_main.cpp:3661`, `:4102`) — so it is the best single
test case for a header-only record reaching more than one dispatch site.

### 157.2 `HEADER_CG_CHANGE_LANGUAGE`: the client sends a byte the server cannot dispatch

This is the finding. The two trees disagree on the header value, and both sides
have the feature switched on.

| | macro | defined at | `HEADER_CG_CHANGE_LANGUAGE` |
|---|---|---|---|
| server | `__MULTI_LANGUAGE_SYSTEM__` | `common/prodomodefines.h:133` | **238** (`packet.h:90`) |
| client | `ENABLE_MULTI_LANGUAGE_SYSTEM` | `LOCALE_INC.H:110` | **245** (`Packet.h:91`) |

Both `#define`s are real and unconditional — `prodomodefines.h` is pulled in by
`game/stdafx.h:16`, and the client's `LOCALE_INC.H` is its precompiled header.
Both carry the same feature comment, `__Renewal_11Languages_MultiLanguage__`, so
these are the same feature under two spellings, both on. The server's handler
`CInputMain::ChangeLanguage` at `input_main.cpp:3575`, its `case` at `:3932`, and
its registration at `packet_info.cpp:174` are all inside `__MULTI_LANGUAGE_SYSTEM__`
or unconditional, and all therefore compile. The client's sender
`CPythonNetworkStream::SendChangeLanguagePacket` is inside
`ENABLE_MULTI_LANGUAGE_SYSTEM` and also compiles.

**Where 245 came from.** The server declares
`HEADER_GC_REQUEST_CHANGE_LANGUAGE = 245` at `packet.h:229` — the
**game-to-client** direction. The client's CG enumerator uses that same 245 for
the **client-to-game** record. So the value was carried across from the GC
enumerator.

Three checks confirm the mismatch is total, not a near-miss:

- No server-side `HEADER_CG_*` is 245.
- No client-side `HEADER_CG_*` is 238.
- 245 is used exactly once on the server, by `HEADER_GC_REQUEST_CHANGE_LANGUAGE`.

**Consequence.** A stock client that calls `SendChangeLanguagePacket` puts byte
`0xf5` in the header. `CInputMain::Analyze` has no top-level `default:`
(Section 155.5), so the record is consumed and **silently ignored**: the account
language is never changed, no error is sent, and nothing is logged. The feature
is reachable from the client UI, is fully implemented on the server, and cannot
work. This is a live, user-visible legacy defect and it is recorded here as
found, not fixed: the rewrite must decide separately whether to reproduce the
mismatch or correct it, and either choice needs its own justification.

This is the second cross-tree enumerator divergence in the series. Section 156
found value 113 named `HEADER_CG_SYMBOL_CRC` on the server and
`HEADER_CG_GUILD_SYMBOL_CRC` on the client, where only the *name* differs and the
value agrees. Here the **value itself** differs, which is a stronger failure and
a different class of bug. **A name mismatch is a maintenance hazard; a value
mismatch is a broken wire protocol.** The two must not be filed under the same
heading.

### 157.3 A third "dead record" category: compiled-out dispatch

> **The second entry below is retracted in 157.10**; only the first is real.

The ledger previously held two categories of registered-but-unusable record:

- `HEADER_CG_TEXT` (64) — registered, never dispatched, client never sends it.
- `HEADER_CG_STATE_CHECKER` (206) — registered, client sends it, dispatch
  **commented out**.
  > **CORRECTED in 157.10 — this is wrong.** The `input_udp.cpp` case is
  > commented out, but `input.cpp:227` dispatches it live via an `else if`.

`HEADER_CG_WORLD_BOSS` (148) is a third and structurally different case. Its
registration at `packet_info.cpp` is **unconditional**, and so is nothing else:
the `case` at `input_main.cpp:3749` is wrapped in
`#if defined(__WORLD_BOSS_EVENT__)` at `:3748`-`:3752`, and
`__WORLD_BOSS_EVENT__` **has no `#define` anywhere in the tree**. Every one of its
twenty-odd occurrences is a `#if defined(...)` test.

So the record is registered, its struct is declared unconditionally, the client
has three senders for it (`PhaseGame.cpp:7445`, `:7458`, `:7470`), and the
server's `case` is **compiled out of the active build**. The comment text is the
giveaway — the case at `:3750-3751` says `break;` with a tab, and the
`#endif` at `:3752` carries no `// __WORLD_BOSS_EVENT__` trailing comment the way
`worldboss.cpp:908` does, which is a small stylistic tell that the block was
edited rather than maintained.

This is distinct from the commented-out case in an important way: a commented
`case` is dead source that a reader can see, while a `#if` with no `#define` is
dead source that **looks live** in every grep. A reviewer searching for
`HEADER_CG_WORLD_BOSS` finds a registration, a case, a handler, and three client
senders, and has no reason to suspect the case is not compiled. **A
`#if defined(X)` with no `#define X` is a stronger trap than a commented-out
line, and the census in Section 155 must treat "reachable by grep" and "compiled
in the active build" as separate claims.**

### 157.4 `HEADER_CG_PREMIUM_PLAYERS`: gated, but the gate is open

The mirror image, and the reason the two deserve to be recorded together. Its
struct `SPacketCGPremiumPlayers` is inside `#ifdef __ENABLE_PREMIUM_PLAYERS__` at
`packet.h:3204`, and its handler `CInputMain::RecvPremiumPlayersPacket` is inside
the same macro at `input_main.cpp:5369`. A naive conditional map would classify
it as a feature-gated record to be deferred.

But `__ENABLE_PREMIUM_PLAYERS__` **is** defined, unconditionally, at
`common/prodomodefines.h:130`, and its `case` at `input_main.cpp:3948` is
unconditional. So in the active build the declaration, the registration, the
dispatch, and the handler are all present, and the record is live.

The practical rule this establishes: **"gated" and "absent" are different
answers to different questions.** The question that matters is *is the gate
open in the active build*, and answering it requires finding the `#define`, not
the `#ifdef`. Three of the seven records in this family give three different
answers to that question — open (`PremiumPlayers`), open (`ChangeLanguage`, under
a differently-spelled macro), and **closed** (`WorldBoss`) — which is a good
argument for auditing feature macros explicitly rather than assuming.

### 157.5 `ENABLE_HEADER_100_FIX` is defined, so Section 156's record is inert

`input_login.cpp:1205-1209` groups two cases into a bare `break;`:

```cpp
case HEADER_CG_MOVE:
#ifdef ENABLE_HEADER_100_FIX
case HEADER_CG_MARK_LOGIN:
#endif
    break;
```

`ENABLE_HEADER_100_FIX` **is** defined, unconditionally, at
`common/prodomodefines.h:74`, with the comment `// __Fix__`. So the inner case
**is** compiled in.

Two consequences, and the second corrects an impression Section 156 could not
have settled on its own:

- `HEADER_CG_MOVE` is accepted and **silently dropped** in the login phase.
- `HEADER_CG_MARK_LOGIN` — the record Section 156 implemented as a 9-byte
  codec — is also accepted and **silently dropped** at login, because the `case`
  it falls into is a `break;` with no handler call.

So the client really does send a 9-byte `CgMarkLogin` at login
(`PythonNetworkStream.cpp:666` and the `GuildMark` senders), the server really
does register and dispatch it, and the login-phase path really does discard it.
The `GuildMarkLogin` handler is reached through a different phase.

**A record can be correctly framed and still be inert at a particular phase,
and the phase dispatcher — not the codec — is what decides.** This is the
concrete reason the Section 156 `CgMarkLogin` codec must not be described as
"wired up": it is a correct transport boundary for a record the active login
phase throws away. The alternative reading — that the client is sending header
100 at login and the server is deliberately ignoring it — is the one the source
actually supports, and it is worth writing down because "the client sends it" and
"the server acts on it" are different claims and only the second justifies
calling a path live.

All **43 of 43** mutations were caught. **Survivors: none.**

| group | mutations | what it covers |
|---|---|---|
| header constants | M01-M04 | each `header()` body pointed at another record's constant |
| size constants | M05-M12 | all four `WIRE_SIZE` and all four `PAYLOAD_SIZE` values |
| endianness helpers | M13-M15 | `read_u32_le` big-endian, `write_u32_le` big-endian, `read_u32_le` truncating to one byte |
| shared guards | M16-M18 | `check_exact` losing its `<` arm, its `>` arm, and `check_header` accepting everything |
| shared dispatch helpers | M19-M22 | `decode_parts` dropping the header check, dropping the length check; `decode_frame_parts` dropping the payload width, dropping the frame header |
| constructors | M23-M27 | `QuestConfirm` swapping its two fields, ignoring its PID; all three single-word constructors zeroing their argument |
| `encode_into` | M28-M31 | all three single-word records dropping their word; `QuestConfirm` emitting the word **before** the byte |
| `to_frame` | M32-M35 | `Target` and `ScriptSelectItem` dropping their word, `ScriptButton` **gaining** a second one, `QuestConfirm` dropping its byte |
| decode offsets | M36-M40 | every field read shifted by one byte |
| decode_frame offsets | M41-M42 | the frame-path reads shifted by one byte |
| error surface | M43 | the `Display` message swapping `{expected}` and `{actual}` |

Three of these are worth calling out because they test a property rather than a
line:

- **M31** reverses `QuestConfirm`'s two fields on the encode side only. The
  decoder is untouched, so a correct golden test catches it. This is the
  encode/decode pair agreeing while the *wire* is wrong — the exact risk the
  reversed field order in `packet.h:766-768` creates.
- **M15** truncates `read_u32_le` to a single byte. Because every word in the
  module goes through that one helper, a single mutation breaks all five word
  reads at once.
- **M33** makes `ScriptButton::to_frame` emit the word **twice**, producing an
  8-byte payload against a declared 4. It is caught by the payload-width
  assertion, which is a length check and not an equality check on content.

Every mutation was caught by **both** `-p protocol --lib` and
`-p protocol --test cg_wiring`, so the module tests and the public-surface tests
each contributed.

### 157.7 A plan that crashed before mutating anything

The first launch of this sweep died instantly with `KeyError: 'file'`. I had
written the plan with the keys `name`, `old`, `new`, and `anchor_count`, but the
harness also requires a `file` field per mutation.

The failure was harmless, and the reason it was harmless is worth stating: the
crash happened while **reading** the plan, before any mutation was applied, so
`cg_pick.rs` was untouched. I confirmed that rather than assuming it — the file
was still 47,280 bytes with an unchanged SHA-256 and no residue. Then I added
the `file` key, re-derived the `name` fields with their `M01`-style identifiers,
re-verified all 43 anchors, and relaunched.

**A mutation harness that crashes is not itself dangerous; a harness that
crashes halfway through is.** The difference is only visible if the pre-sweep
hash was captured *before* launching, which is why that capture is not optional.

### 157.10 CORRECTION: `HEADER_CG_STATE_CHECKER` is live, and three earlier claims were wrong

Sections 155.2, 155.5, 157.3 and 157.8 all record `HEADER_CG_STATE_CHECKER`
(206) as having **no live dispatch** and as "never implement". **That is wrong.**
The record has a live handler:

```cpp
// input.cpp:227, in CInputHandshake::Analyze (defined at input.cpp:209)
else if (bHeader == HEADER_CG_STATE_CHECKER)
{
    if (d->isChannelStatusRequested()) {
        return 0;
    }
    d->SetChannelStatusRequested(true);
    db_clientdesc->DBPacket(HEADER_GD_REQUEST_CHANNELSTATUS, d->GetHandle(), NULL, 0);
}
```

`CInputHandshake::Analyze` is live: it is called from
`CInputProcessor::Process` at `input.cpp:100`. The client sends the record from
`ServerStateChecker.cpp:59`. So the handshake phase accepts it, guards it with a
one-shot `isChannelStatusRequested()` flag, and asks the DB for channel status.
All of that is real behaviour.

**How the error happened.** Section 155.2 correctly found that
`case HEADER_CG_STATE_CHECKER` at `input_udp.cpp:111` is inside a
`/* ... */` block spanning `:106`-`:114`, and correctly concluded that line is
dead. It then generalised from *that one occurrence* to *the record's only
dispatch*. The generalisation was not checked.

**The real cause is a shape mismatch between phases.** The game and login
phases dispatch with `switch`/`case`:

- `CInputMain::Analyze` — `switch (bHeader)` with `case` arms
- `CInputLogin::Analyze` — `switch (bHeader)` with `case` arms

The **handshake phase dispatches with an `else if` chain over the same header**,
in `CInputHandshake::Analyze`. A census that searches for
`case HEADER_CG_X` therefore sees the game and login phases and is **blind to
the handshake phase**. A record handled there has zero `case` matches and is
still completely live.

**This is the exact complement of the Section 155.2 lesson.** 155.2 taught that
a `case` inside a comment is not a dispatch, and grep cannot tell. This teaches
that **a dispatch without a `case` is not a non-dispatch**, and grep cannot tell
that either. Both are failures of assuming one dispatch shape. The census must
match **all three** of `case HEADER_CG_X`, `HEADER_CG_X ==` (the `else if`
shape), and `Set(HEADER_CG_X,` (the registration), and must evaluate them
separately rather than counting `case` hits as the liveness measure.

**Correction to 155.5.** That section lists `HEADER_CG_STATE_CHECKER` as one of
the two registered headers with no `case` in `CInputMain::Analyze` that fall
through the missing `default:`. That statement is *literally true about
`CInputMain`* and *misleading about the protocol*. The record never reaches
`CInputMain` at all, because the handshake phase consumes it first. A record
that is handled earlier in the session must not be counted as a "silently
ignored game-phase record" — that is a different failure with a different
remedy, and the distinction decides whether a codec needs a phase-aware
dispatch entry.

**Correction to 157.3 and 157.8.** Both list the record as one of the four
"permanently unimplementable" backlog entries. The remaining three are correct;
this one is not, and it moves into the implementable set.

**The corrected liveness table, measured with a comment-stripped scan of all four
input files and both dispatch shapes:**

| record | `case` matches | `==` matches | live? |
|---|---|---|---|
| `HEADER_CG_PONG` (254) | 4 | 1 | **live** — handshake, login, game, dead-character |
| `HEADER_CG_STATE_CHECKER` (206) | 0 | 1 | **live** — handshake, via the `else if` shape |
| `HEADER_CG_CHANGE_LANGUAGE` (238) | 1 | 0 | live dispatch, but the client sends 245 |
| `HEADER_CG_WORLD_BOSS` (148) | 1 | 0 | registered and dispatched, `case` **compiled out** |
| `HEADER_CG_TEXT` (64) | 0 | 0 | **confirmed dead** — no live mention in any input file |

`HEADER_CG_TEXT` is the only record in the table with **zero** mentions of
either shape, so it is the one genuinely never-dispatched record. Its
classification from 155.1 stands. Everything else in the previous table needed
qualification or reversal.

**Two live header-only records now exist that the workspace does not yet
implement.** Together with `CgWarp` (Section 153) and `CgMarkIdxList`
(Section 156), the workspace will hold four header-only CG records, of which
**two are live and two are registered-but-inert at the login phase** — see
157.11.
### 157.11 Section 157 implementation: `protocol/src/cg_login.rs`

The retraction in 157.10 required a code change, so the three login-boundary
records are now implemented. `protocol/src/cg_login.rs` — 790 lines,
**46 module tests**, registered as `pub mod cg_login;` immediately before
`cg_micro`. Plus **3 wiring tests** in `protocol/tests/cg_wiring.rs`.

| record | header | wire | payload | field |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `CgStateChecker` | 206 `0xce` | 1 | 0 | *(header-only)* |
| `CgEmpire` | 90 `0x5a` | 2 | 1 | `empire: u8` @1 |
| `CgPong` | 254 `0xfe` | 1 | 0 | *(header-only)* |

The module is grouped by **phase boundary**, and the doc says so explicitly
rather than implying a domain family that does not exist. The reason
`CgPong` earns its place in a *login* module is that it is the only CG record in
the workspace dispatched in three phases, so it straddles the boundary; the
reason `CgStateChecker` earns its place is 157.10.

**Legacy policy deliberately kept out of the codecs**, all documented in the
module rather than encoded:

- `CInputLogin::Empire` closes the descriptor when `EMPIRE_MAX_NUM <=
  p->bEmpire`, and refuses re-selection for an account that already has
  characters. [`CgEmpire::empire`] stays opaque across all 256 values, and a test
  pins that `0xFF` round-trips unchanged.
- `CInputHandshake::Analyze`'s state-checker arm is a **one-shot**, guarded by
  `isChannelStatusRequested()` at `desc.h:178-179`: only the first such record
  per descriptor reaches `HEADER_GD_REQUEST_CHANNELSTATUS`. Session policy, not
  framing.
- `CInputProcessor::Pong` is `d->SetPong(true);` with **no `c_pData` parameter
  at all**, which is the positive proof that the record has no payload rather
  than merely that the handler ignores one.

#### A plausible out-of-bounds read that is not one

`input.cpp:107-110` looks like it reads past the end of a one-byte record:

```cpp
if (bHeader == HEADER_CG_PONG)
{
    sys_log(0, "PONG! %u", *(BYTE*)(c_pData + iPacketLen - sizeof(BYTE)));
}
```

It does not, and the reason is worth recording because the idiom *is* unsafe
elsewhere. `c_pData` points at the **header** byte — `input.cpp:78` reads the
header from it — and `iPacketLen` at that point is the **total record length**
returned by `CPacketInfo::Get`, which is 1 for a `sizeof(BYTE)` record. So the
address is `c_pData + 1 - 1`: the header byte, in bounds, and the line logs 254.

If `iPacketLen` were a *payload* length the same expression would read one byte
past the record. It is not, and that is not a general safety property — the
`else if` handlers in `CInputHandshake::Analyze` receive `c_pData` pointing at
the header, whereas the login and game analyzers pass a pointer to the
**payload**. **The same variable name means different things in adjacent
functions**, and `- sizeof(BYTE)` is a "last byte" idiom that is safe in one and
unsafe in the other. The module doc says exactly this, so a future reader does
not generalise from the one safe site.

#### Tests that were wrong before they were run

Three of the 46 module tests failed to compile or to pass on the first run, and
each was a real error rather than a test-harness quirk:

- `ClientFrame::payload` and `ClientFrame::header` are **public fields, not
  methods** (`cg_wire.rs:350`), so `.payload()` does not exist. Fixed in both
  the module and the wiring tests.
- `assert_eq!(x.is_err(), true)` is `clippy::bool_assert_comparison`, caught by
  strict Clippy in `cg_wiring.rs` and refactored to `assert!`. No suppression.
- `empire_reads_its_byte_at_offset_one` was written with the wrong header byte
  (`[0x00, 0xFF]`), so it asserted `Ok` where the decoder correctly returned
  `InvalidHeader`. The test was wrong, not the codec.

That last one is the useful case: a failing offset test usually means the codec
is wrong, and the correct response is still to determine *which* is wrong rather
than to relax the assertion.

### 157.13 Section 157 mutation receipt and post-sweep gate

All **27 of 27** mutations were caught. **Survivors: none.** Both the module
target and the wiring target contributed to detection.

| group | mutations | what it covers |
|---|---|---|
| header constants | M01-M03 | each `header()` body pointed at another record's constant |
| size constants | M04-M07 | all three `WIRE_SIZE` values and `CG_EMPIRE_PAYLOAD_SIZE` |
| shared guards | M08-M12 | `check_exact` losing its `<` arm, losing its `>` arm; `check_header` accepting every byte; `decode_parts` and `decode_frame_parts` each dropping the header check |
| constructors and encoders | M13-M17 | both header-only `encode_into` bodies emitting a corrupted header; `Empire` dropping the payload, dropping the header, and emitting the two bytes in the wrong order |
| frame projection | M18-M20 | both header-only `to_frame` bodies inventing a payload byte; `Empire::to_frame` dropping its payload |
| decode offsets | M21-M22 | `Empire` reading the header byte instead of the payload, on both the slice and the frame path |
| constructor | M23 | `CgEmpire::new` ignoring its argument |
| error surface | M24-M25 | both `Display` messages swapping `{expected}` and `{actual}` |
| guard wiring | M26-M27 | each decoder passing the wrong size constant to its shared helper |

Four of these test a property rather than a line:

- **M17** reverses the two bytes of `Empire::encode_into`. The decoder is
  untouched, so a correct golden test catches an encoder/decoder pair that
  agrees with itself while the wire is wrong.
- **M18** and **M19** each make one header-only record invent a one-byte payload.
  Both are caught by a *length* assertion rather than a content equality, which
  is what distinguishes a framing check from a value check.
- **M26** passes `CG_PONG_PAYLOAD_SIZE` to `decode_parts` and **M27** passes
  `CG_EMPIRE_WIRE_SIZE` to `decode_frame_parts` — the two records that differ
  between the slice and frame widths, so these two mutations together prove the
  codec does not treat wire width and payload width as interchangeable.
