#### An anchor plan that had to be rebuilt after `cargo fmt`

The first 27-entry plan was built **before** the final `cargo fmt --all`, and
`fmt` collapsed two multi-line struct literals into single lines:

```rust
// before
        return Err(CgLoginError::LengthMismatch {
            expected,
            actual,
        });
// after
        return Err(CgLoginError::LengthMismatch { expected, actual });
```

Six of the 27 anchors then resolved **zero** times, and two of the
`to_frame` mutations resolved **twice** because their anchors no longer
contained enough context to be unique. The plan was discarded and rebuilt from
the formatted text, using each `Vec::with_capacity(CONSTANT)` line and each
record's distinct `# Errors` doc paragraph as the disambiguating context.

This is the second time in this series that a plan had to be re-derived after
formatting, and the rule is now unconditional: **derive anchors from the
formatted source, and treat any zero-count or multi-count anchor as a plan
defect to fix before launching — never as a harmless no-op.** A zero-count
anchor means the mutation never ran, which is indistinguishable from "caught" in
a log that only prints the name.
#### Post-sweep gate receipt, and one compiler ICE that was not a code defect

| gate | result |
|---|---|
| `cargo fmt --all -- --check` | `FMT_OK` |
| `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets --locked --offline -- -D warnings` | `CLIPPY_OK` |
| `RUSTDOCFLAGS="-D warnings" cargo doc --workspace --no-deps --locked --offline` | `DOC_OK` |
| `cargo test --workspace --all-targets --no-fail-fast --locked --offline` | `TEST_OK` — **1,347 passed, 0 failed, 28 binaries** |
| `cargo test --workspace --doc --no-fail-fast --locked --offline` | `DOCTEST_OK` — **6 passed, 0 failed** |
| completion | `ALLDONE` |

The post-sweep figures are **identical** to the pre-sweep gate —
1,347 / 6 / 28 / 0 failed — which is the receipt that the sweep neither changed
the source nor leaked behaviour. The first post-sweep attempt is not a valid
receipt, because it never got that far.

**One attempt failed with a compiler crash, not a test failure.** It reported:

```
error: the compiler unexpectedly panicked. this is a bug.
error: cached cgu 8kolijjoenfr0deg7rw0vyinm should have an object file, but doesn't
error: could not compile `game-server` (test "game_loop_thread") due to 1 previous error
```

Two things about that are worth writing down.

First, the failure is in a crate this section never touched —
`game-server`'s `game_loop_thread` integration test — which is the first hint
that it is environmental rather than a defect. Second, the log **still shows
`DOCTEST_OK` and `ALLDONE`**, because the gate script is a chain of `&&`
followed by unconditional `echo` calls: a failed middle stage does not stop the
last one, and a reader scanning for markers sees four of six and has to notice
the absence. **A gate that ends in `ALLDONE` is not a passing gate.** The count
is what matters, and here the all-targets count was 0 against an expected
1,347, which is what exposed it.

`cargo clean -p game-server` (1,405 files, 559 MiB) and a re-run produced a
clean result. The lesson is narrow and mechanical: **when a gate's expected test
count drops to zero, suspect a corrupted incremental cache before suspecting
the code, and clear the affected package rather than the whole target tree.**
## Section 158 — completing the guild-mark family, and a client defect in `HACK`

### 158.1 The two remaining guild-mark records

Section 156 implemented headers 100, 104, and 113. The guild mark block at
`packet.h:2228-2253` has two more, and both are live:

```cpp
// packet.h:2248-2253
typedef struct command_mark_crclist
{
	BYTE	header;
	BYTE	imgIdx;
	DWORD	crclist[80];
} TPacketCGMarkCRCList;

// packet.h:2236-2241
typedef struct command_mark_upload
{
	BYTE	header;
	DWORD	gid;
	BYTE	image[16*12*4];
} TPacketCGMarkUpload;
```

| record | header | wire | payload | fields |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `TPacketCGMarkCRCList` | 101 `0x65` | **322** | 321 | `img_idx: u8` @1, `crc_list: [u32 LE; 80]` @2 |
| `TPacketCGMarkUpload` | 102 `0x66` | **773** | 772 | `gid: u32 LE` @1, `image: [u8; 768]` @5 |

Both are registered unconditionally (`packet_info.cpp`, `sizeof(TPacketCGMarkCRCList)`
and `sizeof(TPacketCGMarkUpload)`) and both dispatch from the **login** phase at
`input_login.cpp:1214` and `:1222`. All three header values — 101, 102, 105 —
agree between the server's `packet.h` and the client's `Packet.h:67-71`, and
all three client senders exist: `GuildMarkDownloader.cpp:344`,
`GuildMarkUploader.cpp:307`, and `PythonNetworkStreamPhaseGame.cpp:1201`.
**This is the first family in the series where server and client agree on every
value, every width, and every send site.** It is worth saying so plainly, because
157.2 found a family where the client sends a byte the server cannot dispatch.

#### The 768-byte image is read as 192 little-endian pixels, not as bytes

`CInputLogin::GuildMarkUpload` at `input_login.cpp:1059` does the emptiness test
word-wise:

```cpp
for (DWORD iPixel = 0; iPixel < SGuildMark::SIZE; ++iPixel)
    if (*((DWORD *) p->image + iPixel) != 0x00000000)
        isEmpty = false;
```

`SGuildMark::SIZE` is `WIDTH * HEIGHT` = `16 * 12` = **192** (`MarkImage.h`), and
each `DWORD` is 4 bytes, so the loop reads exactly 192 words = the full 768-byte
`image` field. An all-zero image deletes the guild mark; anything else saves it.

So the record has **two** legitimate interpretations, and the legacy code uses
both: the emptiness test reinterprets the 768 bytes as **192 little-endian
`u32` pixels**, while `SaveMark(DWORD guildID, BYTE * pbMarkImage)` at
`MarkManager.h:49` takes the very same storage as `BYTE *`. The **codec keeps
the 768 bytes opaque** — it is a raw byte field, and "is every word zero" is
mark-manager policy. But the little-endian pixel grouping is a wire fact that a
future pixel-level implementation needs, so it is documented rather than
discarded.

#### `TPacketCGHack` is not a guild mark record

`SPacketCGHack` sits at `packet.h:2328`, well outside the `// Guild Mark` block,
and is dispatched in three phases rather than one. It is grouped separately and
not added to `cg_mark.rs`.

| record | header | wire | payload | field |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `SPacketCGHack` | 105 `0x69` | **257** | 256 | `buf: [u8; 256]` @1 |

```cpp
// packet.h:2328-2332
typedef struct SPacketCGHack
{
	BYTE	bHeader;
	char	szBuf[255 + 1];
} SPacketCGHack;
```

It is a **client-originated diagnostic report**: `CPythonNetworkStream::NotifyHack`
at `PythonNetworkStreamPhaseGame.cpp:1187` queues a message the client believes
indicates tampering, `__SendHack` transmits it, and `CInputMain::Hack` at
`input_main.cpp:3219` logs it and closes the descriptor:

```cpp
sys_err("HACK_DETECT: %s %s", ch->GetName(), buf);
ch->GetDesc()->SetPhase(PHASE_CLOSE);
```

**The login phase accepts the record and throws it away.** `input_login.cpp:1239`
is a bare `break;` with no handler call, while the two game-phase sites at
`input_main.cpp:3844` and `:4122` both call `Hack`. So a `HEADER_CG_HACK` sent
before entering the game is consumed silently and never logged. That is the
third instance of the pattern in 157.5 and 157.11: **a correctly framed record
can still be inert at a particular phase, and the phase dispatcher decides.**

#### A client defect: the 257th byte is uninitialised stack memory

`__SendHack` at `PythonNetworkStreamPhaseGame.cpp:1196-1208`:

```cpp
TPacketCGHack kPacketHack;
kPacketHack.bHeader=HEADER_CG_HACK;
strncpy(kPacketHack.szBuf, c_szMsg, sizeof(kPacketHack.szBuf)-1);
if (!Send(sizeof(kPacketHack), &kPacketHack))
```

`kPacketHack` is a **stack local with no initialiser**. `strncpy` with `n = 255`
zero-fills from `strlen(c_szMsg)` up to index 254, so it does **not** write
index 255 — the last byte of `szBuf`. The client therefore transmits **one byte
of uninitialised stack memory** on every hack report.

The server's `strlcpy(buf, p->szBuf, sizeof(buf))` stops at the first NUL, and
for any message shorter than 255 characters byte 254 is already NUL, so the
garbage byte is not normally read. The leak is real but its blast radius is one
byte, and it is a **client** defect rather than a server one, so it is recorded
here for the parity record and not treated as a server finding.

The same function also means the message is **not guaranteed NUL-terminated** at
the byte the server can see if a 255-character message is sent: `strncpy` fills
indices 0-254 with the message and leaves 255 untouched, so a 255-character
message reaches the server with **no NUL in the 256-byte field**. The server's
`strlcpy` then copies 255 bytes and terminates its own 256-byte `buf`, so it is
still memory-safe — the *record* is unterminated while the *read* is bounded.
That distinction between "the field has a NUL" and "the read is bounded" is the
same trap as 157.11's `input.cpp` log line, and the codec keeps all 256 bytes
opaque for exactly this reason.
### 158.2 `protocol/src/cg_mark.rs` — the two large guild-mark records

`CgMarkCRCList` (101) and `CgMarkUpload` (102) are **added to the existing
`cg_mark.rs`** rather than given a new module, because they are the same
legacy comment block, the same registration table, and the same login-phase
dispatcher as the three records Section 156 put there. `CgHack` is **not**
added — see 158.3.

Four new size constants carry the layouts explicitly, so no magic number
appears at a use site:

| constant | value | why it exists |
|---|---|---|
| `CG_MARK_CRCLIST_WIRE_SIZE` | 322 | `1 + 1 + 4 * 80` |
| `CG_MARK_CRCLIST_PAYLOAD_SIZE` | 321 | wire size minus the header |
| `CG_MARK_CRCLIST_WORDS` | 80 | `DWORD crclist[80]` |
| `CG_MARK_UPLOAD_WIRE_SIZE` | 773 | `1 + 4 + 768` |
| `CG_MARK_UPLOAD_PAYLOAD_SIZE` | 772 | wire size minus the header |
| `CG_MARK_UPLOAD_IMAGE_SIZE` | 768 | `BYTE image[16*12*4]` |
| `CG_MARK_UPLOAD_PIXELS` | 192 | `SGuildMark::SIZE` = `WIDTH * HEIGHT` |

`CG_MARK_UPLOAD_PIXELS` exists **only for documentation and a test**. It is not
used by the codec, because the codec does not interpret the image. Its one test
asserts `CG_MARK_UPLOAD_PIXELS * 4 == CG_MARK_UPLOAD_IMAGE_SIZE`, which is what
keeps the little-endian pixel grouping in 158.1 from drifting away from the
field width without anyone noticing.

`CgMarkUpload` stores `[u8; 768]` and nothing else. The two legacy
interpretations from 158.1 — 192 LE `u32` pixels for the emptiness test, `BYTE *`
for `SaveMark` — are both documented on the type, and **neither is encoded**.
A 768-byte all-zero image and a 768-byte image with one set bit both round-trip
unchanged, and a test asserts they decode to *different* records, because the
legacy delete-versus-save decision must not leak into the codec.

#### A structural mistake worth recording

Appending the two new structs to `cg_mark.rs` put them **after**
`#[cfg(test)] mod tests { ... }`, so they became items of the test module and
every reference failed with "not found in this scope" — 42 errors at once, with
no obvious cause. The follow-on error was worse: the repair stripped the wrong
`}`, leaving `mod tests` unclosed and producing *"module is not supported in
`trait`s or `impl`s"*, which points at a completely different part of the file.

The general rule: **in a file that ends in a `#[cfg(test)] mod tests`, new
implementation code must be inserted before the `#[cfg(test)]` attribute, not
appended.** A brace-balance check (`{` count against `}` count) is the cheapest
way to catch this class of mistake, and it is what finally located the real
problem here.

Three further compile errors were ordinary API mismatches, all found by strict
Clippy or the compiler rather than by inspection:

- `read_u32_le` in this module takes `(bytes, at)` — two arguments — not the
  slice-only form used in `cg_login.rs`. **Helper signatures are per-module, and
  a sibling module's helper is not a drop-in.**
- `sorted.dedup()` on a fixed-size array needs `.to_vec()` first.
- `clippy::cast_possible_truncation` rejects `index as u32` and
  `(index % 251) as u8` in test helpers. Both were rewritten as
  `u32::try_from(index).expect(...)` and `u8::try_from(index % 251).expect(...)`.
  **No lint suppression was added**, in keeping with the standing rule.
### 158.3 Section 158 pre-sweep gate receipt

| gate | result |
|---|---|
| `cargo fmt --all -- --check` | `FMT_OK` |
| `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets --locked --offline -- -D warnings` | `CLIPPY_OK` |
| `RUSTDOCFLAGS="-D warnings" cargo doc --workspace --no-deps --locked --offline` | `DOC_OK` |
| `cargo test --workspace --all-targets --no-fail-fast --locked --offline` | `TEST_OK` — **1,380 passed, 0 failed, 28 binaries** |
| `cargo test --workspace --doc --no-fail-fast --locked --offline` | `DOCTEST_OK` — **6 passed, 0 failed** |

1,380 is 1,347 plus exactly 33, and 33 is 31 new `cg_mark` tests plus 2 new
wiring tests. The workspace now holds **148 Rust files** and **105,084 scanned
lines**. The file grew from 1,040 to 1,533 lines.

**The first attempt at this gate failed on strict Clippy and is not a receipt.**
`clippy::cast_possible_truncation` rejected two `as` casts inside test helpers —
`index as u32` and `(index % 251) as u8`. Both were rewritten as
`u32::try_from(index).expect(...)` and `u8::try_from(index % 251).expect(...)`.
The standing rule applies: **a quality failure is fixed by refactoring the code,
never by adding a suppression.**

Note that the failed run still printed `DOC_OK`. This is the same gate-script
weakness recorded in 157.13: a failed stage does not stop the later `echo`
calls, so the marker list alone is not evidence. The all-targets count of 0
against an expected 1,380 is what exposed it.

#### The mutation plan survived formatting, but only because it was re-checked

The 29-entry plan was derived from the source **before** the gate's
`cargo fmt --all`, when `cg_mark.rs` hashed to `a4731206`. After formatting the
same file hashed to `e7e390fa`. Rather than assume the anchors still held, all 29
were re-counted against the formatted text: all 29 still resolved exactly once,
so the plan was launched unchanged against the formatted source.

This is the third section in a row where formatting has been a hazard, and the
contrast with 157.13 is the point. There, six anchors resolved zero times and two
resolved twice, and the plan had to be rebuilt. Here, none changed. **The
difference is not luck — it is that the count is re-verified after `fmt` and the
plan is only launched once every entry still reports exactly 1.** Verifying is
the procedure; whether it happens to matter this time does not change that it
has to happen every time.
## Section 159 — the last four records over 16 bytes, and a wrong memory note about `TItemPos`

### 159.1 The four remaining wide records

After Section 158 implements `MARK_CRCLIST` and `MARK_UPLOAD`, four records
above 16 bytes remain unimplemented. All four are live, and all four header
values — 106, 239, 230, 144 — **agree between the server's `packet.h` and the
client's `Packet.h`**, as do the widths.

| record | header | wire | declaration |
|---|---|---|---|
| `SPacketCGInventoryProtected` | 144 `0x90` | **17** | `packet.h:3300-3309` |
| `TPacketSash` | 230 `0xe6` | **23** | `packet.h:2807-2821` |
| `SPacketCGWhisperDetails` | 239 `0xef` | **26** | `packet.h:3259-3263` |
| `SPacketCGChangeName` | 106 `0x6a` | **27** | `packet.h:2454-2458` |

Every width was checked by arithmetic against its registration, using the two
length constants that determine the fixed buffers:

- `CHARACTER_NAME_MAX_LEN = 24` at `common/length.h:15`, so every name field is
  `char[25]`. `SPacketCGWhisperDetails` is `1 + 25 = 26` and
  `SPacketCGChangeName` is `1 + 1 + 25 = 27`. Both match.
- `INVENTORY_PROTECTED_PASSWORD_MAX_LEN = 6` at `common/length.h:36`, so each
  password field is `char[7]`. `SPacketCGInventoryProtected` is
  `1 + 1 + 7 + 7 + 1 = 17`. Matches.

```cpp
// packet.h:2454-2458          // packet.h:3259-3263
typedef struct SPacketCGChangeName  typedef struct SPacketCGWhisperDetails
{                                   {
	BYTE header;                     	BYTE header;
	BYTE index;                      	char name[CHARACTER_NAME_MAX_LEN + 1];
	char name[CHARACTER_NAME_MAX_LEN+1];
}                                   } 
```

Two of the four share the 25-byte name field, and a third carries two 7-byte
password buffers, so **three of the four are "a fixed C-string buffer" records**.
`TPacketSash` is the outlier: it has no string at all.

#### A wrong memory note about `TItemPos`, corrected here

An earlier note in this project recorded `TItemPos` as four bytes with fields
`bWindow`, `bPosition`, and `wApplyIndex`. **That is wrong for this codebase.**
There is exactly **one** definition, at `common/length.h:1040-1057`:

```cpp
typedef struct SItemPos
{
	BYTE window_type;
	WORD cell;
    // ... constructors and operator overloads, no data members ...
} TItemPos;
```

Two data members, `BYTE` then `WORD`, under the workspace `#pragma pack(1)`, so
`TItemPos` is **3 bytes**. `TPacketSash` confirms it by arithmetic:

```
header 1 + subheader 1 + bWindow 1 + dwPrice 4 + bPos 1 + TItemPos 3 + dwItemVnum 4 + dwMinAbs 4 + dwMaxAbs 4 = 23
```

which is exactly the registered `sizeof(TPacketSash)`. With a 4-byte `TItemPos`
the record would be 24 bytes and **the registration would not match the struct**,
which is the kind of mismatch that is obvious in hindsight and easy to get wrong
a priori.

The memory note is corrected as part of this section. The lesson is narrow: the
field names `bWindow`/`wApplyIndex` belong to a *different* item-position type
elsewhere in this family of headers, and a remembered name is not evidence of a
remembered width. **When a width is load-bearing, re-derive it from the single
defining struct and check it arithmetically against a registration** — a
`sizeof` in `packet_info.cpp` is an independent witness, and two independent
numbers agreeing is worth more than either alone.

Note also that `TPacketSash` has both a `bWindow: bool` **and** a `TItemPos` whose
own first member is `window_type`. These are two different window concepts in one
record, and a reader skimming the field list will conflate them. They are kept
as separate fields in the codec for exactly that reason.
### 159.2 Liveness of the four, using the corrected three-shape census

| record | `case` | `==` | phase | client sender |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `SPacketCGChangeName` (106) | 1 | 0 | **login** — `input_login.cpp:1242` | `PythonNetworkStreamPhaseSelect.cpp` |
| `SPacketCGWhisperDetails` (239) | 1 | 0 | game — `input_main.cpp:3938` | `PythonNetworkStreamPhaseGame.cpp` |
| `TPacketSash` (230) | 1 | 0 | game — `input_main.cpp:3862` | `PythonNetworkStreamPhaseGame.cpp` |
| `SPacketCGInventoryProtected` (144) | 3 | 0 | game — `input_main.cpp:3869` | `PythonNetworkStreamPhaseGame.cpp` |

All four are live on **both** trees: a `case` arm on the server and a real
sender in the client. Unlike Section 157's `HEADER_CG_CHANGE_LANGUAGE`, there is
no value divergence anywhere in this group, and unlike `HEADER_CG_WORLD_BOSS`
there is no compiled-out arm.

`SPacketCGInventoryProtected` is the only one of the four with a **sub-header**,
and it is the only one in the whole backlog with a two-level dispatch:

```cpp
// input_main.cpp:3869
case HEADER_CG_INVENTORY_PROTECTED:
    Sash(ch, c_pData);          // no: InventoryProtected(ch, c_pData)
    break;
// input_main.cpp:5397 and :5400 are the sub-arms of the handler
case SUBHEADER_CG_INVENTORY_PROTECTED_ACTIVATE:        // 0
case SUBHEADER_CG_INVENTORY_PROTECTED_PASSWORD_CHANGE: // 1
```

The two sub-header values are named at `packet.h:3294-3295` and again in the
client at `Packet.h:3393-3394`, and both trees agree on them. So the record's
`bySubHeader` byte is **not** an opaque payload byte: it selects between two
documented behaviours, and the codec must preserve it exactly so the handler
above can dispatch on it — which is the same rule Section 156 applied to
`WorldBoss` and `PremiumPlayers` and the opposite of what applies to
`CgEmpire::empire`, where the byte really is opaque.

**That contrast is the point worth keeping.** A second byte is opaque when the
handler passes it to something that validates it later, and sub-typed when the
handler switches on it immediately. The difference is visible only in the
handler body, never in the struct, so it cannot be derived from the wire layout
and must be read from the code each time.
### 159.3 `SPacketCGChangeName` — the login-phase record, and why its name field must stay raw

`HEADER_CG_CHANGE_NAME` (106) is the only record in this group that is dispatched
during the **login** phase, at `input_login.cpp:1242`. Its handler is
`CInputLogin::ChangeName` at `input_login.cpp:221`:

```cpp
void CInputLogin::ChangeName(LPDESC d, const char * data)
{
	TPacketCGChangeName * p = (TPacketCGChangeName *) data;
	const TAccountTable & c_r = d->GetAccountTable();
	if (!c_r.id) { sys_err("no account table"); return; }
	if (p->index >= PLAYER_PER_ACCOUNT) { ...; d->DelayedDisconnect(5); return; }
	if (!c_r.players[p->index].dwID) { ...; d->SetPhase(PHASE_CLOSE); return; }
	if (!c_r.players[p->index].bChangeName) return;
	if (!check_name(p->name)) { ...send HEADER_GC_CHARACTER_CREATE_FAILURE...; return; }
	...
	strlcpy(pdb.name, p->name, sizeof(pdb.name));
	db_clientdesc->DBPacket(HEADER_GD_CHANGE_NAME, d->GetHandle(), &pdb, sizeof(TPacketGDChangeName));
}
```

Three things here are codec-relevant.

**The `index` byte is range-checked above the codec.** `p->index >= PLAYER_PER_ACCOUNT`
rejects it, so the codec must still preserve all 256 `u8` values and must not
pre-truncate to the four-slot range. The bound check belongs to the reducer, not
to the record. This is the same split already recorded for `CgEmpire::empire`
and `PLAYER_PER_ACCOUNT` in the `AGENTS.md` note about
`input_login.cpp:265-304` — and note that this handler **does** perform the check
before indexing, unlike the select path there.

**The name is `char[25]` raw storage and must stay that way.** `check_name` is a
function pointer, `extern int (*check_name)(const char * str)` at
`game/config.h:85`, assigned per locale in `locale_service.cpp`. The active
implementations — `check_name_alphabet` at `locale_service.cpp:317` is the
simplest — begin with:

```cpp
if (!str || !*str) return 0;
if (strlen(str) < 2) return 0;
for (tmp = str; *tmp; ++tmp) { if (isdigit(*tmp) || isalpha(*tmp)) continue; else return 0; }
```

So the handler reads the 25-byte field as a **NUL-terminated C string** with no
length bound of its own. Two consequences for the rewrite:

1. The codec must **not** require a NUL, reject a non-NUL-terminated buffer, or
   reinterpret the bytes as text. The field is 25 opaque bytes with fixed
   storage, exactly like every other `char[N]` on the wire. Requiring a NUL would
   be new validation that the legacy server does not perform, and it would change
   which records decode.
2. A client that fills all 25 bytes with non-NUL data makes `strlen` and the
   `*tmp` loop read past the end of the record. That is a **legacy robustness
   follow-up in the C++ server**, not a Rust codec bug and not something the
   rewrite should silently "fix" at the framing layer. It is recorded here
   alongside the other two C++ findings, and it stays separate from the codec
   exactly like the unchecked-create-index finding in `AGENTS.md`.

The mirror image is worth stating too: `strlcpy` truncates to `sizeof(pdb.name)`,
so an over-long name is silently cut on the DB path even though `check_name`
rejected anything non-alphanumeric. Neither the truncation nor the length policy
is framing, and neither belongs in the codec.

#### The `char[25]` element is shared, and it is a wire element

`SPacketCGChangeName` and `SPacketCGWhisperDetails` both carry
`char name[CHARACTER_NAME_MAX_LEN + 1]` — the same 25 bytes, from the same
constant, in the same packed record. That makes a single named constant for the
25-byte field a genuine shared wire element rather than a coincidental repeat,
and it is worth one constant rather than a literal `25` at each use site. What
the constant must **not** do is grow a helper that returns a `&str`: the field is
not guaranteed to be NUL-terminated (see above), so the only safe accessor is a
fixed-size byte array.
### 159.4 `TPacketSash` is bidirectional, and one of its sub-header names is wrong

`TPacketSash` looked like an ordinary one-direction record. It is not, and getting
this wrong would have produced a plausible-looking but incorrect codec.

**The struct and its enum are shared by both directions.** The declaration sits
inside one enum that serves client-to-server *and* server-to-client:

```cpp
// packet.h:2804-2818
#ifdef __SASH_SYSTEM__
enum
{
	HEADER_CG_SASH = 230,
	HEADER_GC_SASH = 231,
	SASH_SUBHEADER_GC_OPEN   = 0,   // 0
	SASH_SUBHEADER_GC_CLOSE,        // 1
	SASH_SUBHEADER_GC_ADDED,        // 2
	SASH_SUBHEADER_GC_REMOVED,      // 3
	SASH_SUBHEADER_CG_REFINED,      // 4  <-- continues the GC numbering
	SASH_SUBHEADER_CG_CLOSE  = 0,   // 0  <-- explicit reset restarts numbering
	SASH_SUBHEADER_CG_ADD,          // 1
	SASH_SUBHEADER_CG_REMOVE,       // 2
	SASH_SUBHEADER_CG_REFINE,       // 3
};
```

The explicit `= 0` on `SASH_SUBHEADER_CG_CLOSE` is not decoration — it is what
restarts the numbering after the GC half. Remove it and the whole CG half shifts
to 4..7.

**`SASH_SUBHEADER_CG_REFINED` is a GC value with a `CG_` name.** Its value is 4
because it continues from `SASH_SUBHEADER_GC_REMOVED`, and both trees use it
only in the server-to-client direction:

- `server/server/game/char.cpp:10420-10421` builds the record with
  `sPacket.header = HEADER_GC_SASH;` and
  `sPacket.subheader = SASH_SUBHEADER_CG_REFINED;` — an **outbound GC** packet.
- `client/Client/UserInterface/PythonNetworkStreamPhaseGame.cpp:5166` handles
  `case SASH_SUBHEADER_CG_REFINED:` on an **inbound GC** packet.

So the CG sub-header domain is **0 through 3 only** — `CLOSE`, `ADD`, `REMOVE`,
`REFINE`. A reader who trusts the name concludes there are five CG sub-headers,
writes a `SashSubHeader` enum with five values, and then cannot explain why the
server's `switch` has no arm for 4.

**The server silently drops 4 and everything above.** `CInputMain::Sash` switches
on 0..3 and its `default: break;` discards all other values with no log and no
error. This is the same "unknown value consumed silently" behaviour already
recorded for unknown *headers* in the client analyzers, here appearing on a
*sub-header*. It is legacy framing behaviour, so the codec preserves all 256
`u8` values and does not reject 4; the drop stays in the handler.

**Most of the 23 bytes are unread for most sub-headers.** One fixed record
serves four sub-commands, and each reads a different subset:

| sub-header | reads | ignores |
|---|---|---|
| `CLOSE` (0) | nothing | every field |
| `ADD` (1) | `tPos`, `bPos` | `bWindow`, `dwPrice`, `dwItemVnum`, `dwMinAbs`, `dwMaxAbs` |
| `REMOVE` (2) | `bPos` | everything else |
| `REFINE` (3) | nothing | every field |

The codec still carries all 23 bytes, because the frame is fixed-width and the
ignored fields are still on the wire. But a consumer must not assume a field is
meaningful because the record type declares it — `dwPrice` in a `REMOVE` request
is a stale value from the client, not a request.

**The two window fields are unrelated, and the wire shows it.** `TPacketSash` has
a top-level `bWindow: bool` at offset 2 *and* a `TItemPos` at offset 7 whose first
member is `window_type`. `char.cpp:10422` sets `bWindow` from
`m_bSashCombination` while `char.cpp:10415-10417` sets `tPos.window_type =
INVENTORY` — two independent decisions, written side by side. The client reads
`bWindow` directly (`PythonNetworkStreamPhaseGame.cpp:5163` passes it to
`ActSash`). A codec that merged them, or that modelled `tPos.window_type` as
`bool`, would be wrong.

**Feature gate is open.** `__SASH_SYSTEM__` is defined at
`common/prodomodefines.h:15`, so the record, its enum, and the live
`input_main.cpp:3862` dispatch are all in the active build. The client's
`Packet.h:2869-2880` carries the identical enum, values included.
### 159.5 `SPacketCGInventoryProtected` — two sub-arms, two password buffers, and a 6-byte limit

`HEADER_CG_INVENTORY_PROTECTED` (144) is dispatched at `input_main.cpp:3869` to
`CInputMain::RecvActivateProtectedSystem`, whose whole body is a two-arm switch:

```cpp
void CInputMain::RecvActivateProtectedSystem(LPCHARACTER ch, const char * c_pData)
{
	const SPacketCGInventoryProtected* kRecv = reinterpret_cast<const SPacketCGInventoryProtected*>(c_pData);
	switch (kRecv->bySubHeader)
	{
		case SUBHEADER_CG_INVENTORY_PROTECTED_ACTIVATE:          // 0
			ch->ActivateProtectedSystem(kRecv->szPasswordNow, kRecv->bActivated);
			break;
		case SUBHEADER_CG_INVENTORY_PROTECTED_PASSWORD_CHANGE:   // 1
			ch->ChangeProtectedSystemPassword(kRecv->szPasswordNow, kRecv->szPasswordNew);
			break;
		default:
			break;
	}
}
```

Layout: `byHeader 1 + bySubHeader 1 + szPasswordNow[7] + szPasswordNew[7] +
bActivated 1 = 17`, matching the registration exactly. The `char[7]` width comes
from `INVENTORY_PROTECTED_PASSWORD_MAX_LEN = 6` at `common/length.h:36`.

Three observations that affect the codec.

**The two sub-arms use different field sets.** The `ACTIVATE` arm reads
`szPasswordNow` and `bActivated`; the `PASSWORD_CHANGE` arm reads both password
buffers and **ignores `bActivated`**. So the trailing `bool` is meaningful for
one sub-header and stale for the other. It is still on the wire for both — the
frame is fixed-width — so the codec carries it unconditionally. The default arm
silently discards all 254 other `bySubHeader` values, with no log, exactly as
`TPacketSash` does.

**This is the second sub-typed second byte in the backlog, and it is a different
case from `CgEmpire`.** Both `CgInventoryProtected::by_sub_header` and
`CgSash::subheader` are named enumerations in `packet.h` and switch on
immediately. `CgEmpire::empire` is also a `u8` at offset 1, but its handler does
not switch on it — it is compared against `EMPIRE_MAX_NUM` later and can be out of
range. **The struct cannot tell you which kind of byte you have; only the
handler can.** That is the recurring lesson of this batch, and it is why every
one of these records was read at its dispatch site rather than derived from its
layout.

**Both password fields are read as C strings, and the legacy server does not bound
them.** `ActivateProtectedSystem` and `ChangeProtectedSystemPassword` receive
`char *` pointers into the record. A client that fills all 7 bytes of
`szPasswordNow` with non-NUL data causes the downstream length handling to read
past the end of the 17-byte frame — the same class of legacy robustness gap as
the 25-byte character name in 159.3. It is a C++ follow-up, deliberately **not**
a Rust codec change: the codec preserves 7 opaque bytes per field and adds no
NUL requirement, because adding one would reject records the legacy server
accepts.
### 159.6 `SPacketCGWhisperDetails` and the shared 25-byte name element

`HEADER_CG_WHISPER_DETAILS` (239) is the simplest of the four: `header 1 +
char name[25] = 26`, dispatched at `input_main.cpp:3938`. Its handler is
`CInputMain::WhisperDetails`:

```cpp
if (!*CGWhisperDetails->name) return;
...
strncpy(GCWhisperDetails.name, CGWhisperDetails->name, sizeof(GCWhisperDetails.name) - 1);
LPCHARACTER pkChr = CHARACTER_MANAGER::instance().FindPC(CGWhisperDetails->name);
LPDESC pkDesc = P2P_MANAGER::instance().Find(CGWhisperDetails->name);
```

Same pattern as 159.3: the 25-byte field is dereferenced as a NUL-terminated C
string with no bound, and the first byte is tested for emptiness before anything
else. Two `Find` calls walk the string as a C string, so a non-NUL-terminated
buffer reads past the 26-byte frame. Recorded as a C++ robustness follow-up; the
codec keeps 25 opaque bytes and imposes nothing.

One asymmetry worth preserving: this handler does **not** call `check_name`, so the
whisper target is never validated for alphabet or length on the way in. It is
passed straight to two lookups. The rewrite must not "helpfully" add a
`check_name` equivalent at the codec.

#### The 25-byte name element, stated once

`CHARACTER_NAME_MAX_LEN = 24` (`common/length.h:15`) means every name field in
this family is `char[25]`. Two of the four records in this section carry it and
both are `char[CHARACTER_NAME_MAX_LEN + 1]`, not a literal 25, in both trees. So
Section 159 implements **one** named constant for that field and uses it in both
records, rather than repeating the literal.

What the shared element must not gain is a text accessor. All three consumers
here — `check_name`, `FindPC`, `P2P_MANAGER::Find` — expect a NUL, and none of
them bounds the read, so the buffer is genuinely not a Rust `&str`. The only safe
surface is a fixed-size byte array plus the raw bytes, and any NUL-aware
behaviour belongs to the handler layer above the codec.

### 159.7 Section 159 implementation plan

Two new modules, split by wire shape rather than by header value:

- **`protocol/src/cg_name.rs`** — `CgChangeName` (106, 27), `CgWhisperDetails`
  (239, 26), `CgInventoryProtected` (144, 17). All three carry fixed
  `char[N+1]` storage. `cg_name.rs` owns `CG_CHARACTER_NAME_FIELD_SIZE = 25` and
  `CG_INVENTORY_PROTECTED_PASSWORD_FIELD_SIZE = 7`. Both sub-header bytes are
  documented as sub-typed and **all 256 `u8` values are preserved**, because the
  legacy `default:` arms drop them silently.
- **`protocol/src/cg_sash.rs`** — `CgSash` (230, 23). The only backlog record
  containing a `TItemPos`, so it gets a local `ItemPos { window_type: u8,
  cell: u16 }` with `ITEM_POS_WIRE_SIZE = 3`, pinned by the arithmetic in 159.1.
  The `bWindow` and `window_type` fields stay separate and separately named.

A dedicated `ItemPos` type in `cg_sash.rs` is a transitional choice. `TItemPos`
appears in many non-CG records across the whole wire, so once the item records
are reached it should move to a shared item module. Putting it in `cg_sash.rs`
now keeps the Section 159 diff small and gives the later move a single call site
to relocate; the alternative, extracting a shared item module now, would mean
touching item records whose audit has not been done.

The `TPacketSash` GC direction is **out of scope for this section**. The CG
codec is the incoming record; `HEADER_GC_SASH` is a server-to-client record and
belongs in the GC set, not here. What this section records is the shared layout,
so the GC codec can be built from the same table later.
### 158.4 Section 158 mutation sweep receipt

Plan: `/tmp/mut158.json`, 29 entries, every one a one-occurrence replacement in
`protocol/src/cg_mark.rs`. Result: `/tmp/mut158_res.json`. Log: `/tmp/mut158.log`.

**29 of 29 caught. Zero survivors.**

| evidence | value |
|---|---|
| pre-sweep size | 55,589 B |
| pre-sweep SHA-256 | `e7e390fa74a2468379dda0f75fa0a57194b107d5cee19c88eb7e280e940b6bde` |
| post-sweep size | 55,589 B |
| post-sweep SHA-256 | `e7e390fa74a2468379dda0f75fa0a57194b107d5cee19c88eb7e280e940b6bde` |
| anchors re-resolving exactly once after restore | 29 / 29 |
| `.mutbak` / `.orig` debris | none |
| test count | 58 |
| brace balance | 255 / 255 |

**Restoration is proven by the hash, not by string absence.** A check for "no
mutation replacement string appears in the file" reports a false negative here,
and it always will: several `new` values in this plan are ordinary values that
legitimately occur elsewhere in a 1,533-line file — `0` as a dropped field
default, `HEADER_CG_MARK_UPLOAD` in an import list, a one-digit size change in a
different constant. That check is unsound by construction. Byte-identical SHA-256
plus identical size plus all 29 anchors resolving exactly once is the proof, and
it is the same four-part evidence used in every prior section.

#### Distribution of the catches, and why it matters

Every mutation produced `exit 101` — a genuine test failure or compile error, not
a hang or a crash. But the **reporting targets** split three ways:

| group | mutations | detected by | test failures reported |
|---|---|---|---|
| size constants that participate in framing | M01, M03, M07 | both lib and `cg_wiring` | 8, 8, 3 |
| size constants used only internally | M02, M04 | lib only | 3, 3 |
| everything else | the other 24 | lib only | **0** |

Twenty-four mutations reported `failed: 0` and an empty `failing_targets` list,
and were still caught. That means the harness caught them through the **compile
step**, not through a failing assertion — a const-size change ripples into array
lengths and `copy_from_slice` bounds, so the code stops compiling before any test
runs. A mutation is genuinely caught either way, but the two mechanisms are worth
distinguishing: the compile-time ones prove the constants are load-bearing, and
the `failed: 3` / `failed: 8` ones prove the **wiring** tests see the sizes
independently of the library.

That is the reason this project keeps public `cg_wiring` integration tests at
all. Without them, M01, M03 and M07 would still be caught — but only by a
compiler error, and a codec whose size constants nothing else references would
then look fully tested while no external caller had checked a single byte.
### 159.8 `protocol/src/cg_name.rs` and `protocol/src/cg_sash.rs` — implementation

Two new modules, as planned in 159.7, plus `pub mod` lines in `protocol/src/lib.rs`
and two new public wiring tests in `protocol/tests/cg_wiring.rs`.

**`cg_name.rs`** — 33,398 B, **41 tests**. `CgChangeName` (106, 27 bytes),
`CgWhisperDetails` (239, 26 bytes), and `CgInventoryProtected` (144, 17 bytes),
sharing one `CgNameError` with the same three variants the sibling modules use.
Two constants carry the shared widths:

```
CG_CHARACTER_NAME_FIELD_SIZE              = 25   // CHARACTER_NAME_MAX_LEN + 1
CG_INVENTORY_PROTECTED_PASSWORD_FIELD_SIZE =  7   // INVENTORY_PROTECTED_PASSWORD_MAX_LEN + 1
```

Both records' name fields are `[u8; 25]` with **no NUL-aware accessor at all** —
not a `&str`, not a `cstr`, not a `truncate_at_nul` helper. That omission is
deliberate and documented in the module header, because every legacy consumer
reads the field as a C string (`check_name`'s `strlen`, `FindPC`, `P2P_MANAGER::
Find`) while none of them bounds the read. A helper that returned `&str` would
either panic on a non-NUL-terminated buffer or silently paper over a real legacy
over-read.

`CgInventoryProtected::activated` is decoded as `bytes[16] != 0`, matching the
C++ `bool` — every nonzero byte is `true`. A test pins `1`, `2`, `0x80` and
`0xFF` as true and `0` as false, because narrowing to `== 1` would be a real
compatibility bug and an untested one.

**`cg_sash.rs`** — 24,260 B, **27 tests**. `CgSash` (230, 23 bytes) plus the
transitional `ItemPos` type. `ItemPos::WIRE_SIZE` is `1 + 2 = 3` and the record
width is written as arithmetic rather than as a bare `23`:

```rust
pub const CG_SASH_WIRE_SIZE: usize = 1 + 1 + 1 + 4 + 1 + ItemPos::WIRE_SIZE + 4 + 4 + 4;
```

so if `TItemPos`'s width is ever revised the record width follows automatically
instead of silently disagreeing with the registration. A test asserts the
constant equals 23 and equals the expanded sum, and the wiring test asserts
`resolve_cg_base_size(HEADER_CG_SASH) == Some(CG_SASH_WIRE_SIZE)`, so the
inventory table and the codec must agree.

`CgSash::subheader` accepts all 256 values. The module header explains why the
CG domain stops at 3 even though the enum declares a fifth name, and that
`SASH_SUBHEADER_CG_REFINED` is a server-to-client value with a misleading
`CG_` prefix.

#### Four test bugs, all of them my fault, none of them code bugs

The first Section 159 run was 3 failures, and all three were wrong expectations
rather than wrong code. They are worth listing because each one is a mistake that
is easy to repeat when writing assertions about sibling records.

1. **A shared "all three records reject the empty slice identically" test was
   wrong by construction.** The three records are 27, 26 and 17 bytes, so an empty
   input produces three *different* `Truncated { needed }` values. The test
   asserted all three were `needed: 0`. Rewritten as
   `an_empty_input_reports_each_records_own_width`, which asserts each record
   reports **its own** size. The general rule: a test that compares several
   records' errors to one value is only valid when those records are the same
   width, and this batch deliberately groups records of *different* widths.
2. **Popping a byte from a frame is a truncation, not a length mismatch.** I
   expected `LengthMismatch { expected: 25, actual: 24 }` and got
   `Truncated { needed: 25, available: 24 }`. The decoder checks `actual < expected`
   first, which is correct. Both directions are now asserted.
3. **Then the fix for (2) introduced a third bug**: `pop()` followed by one
   `push()` restores the original 25 bytes, so the "too long" case silently
   decoded. It needed two pushes. This is the same class as an anchor that
   resolves zero times — a test that stops testing anything while still reading
   like a test. A short comment now says why there are two.
4. **A round-trip sweep over "distinct bytes at every offset" failed on the
   `window` field**, because the generator produced `14` and a C++ `bool`
   re-encodes as `1`. The sweep was pinning the wrong invariant: it wanted
   every *offset* verified, not every *value*. The generator now pins that one
   byte to `0` or `1` and sweeps the other 21.

The general lesson is the one from 157.13 in a new place: **an assertion that
cannot fail is worse than no assertion, because it raises the test count without
raising confidence.** The fix is always to ask what the assertion is actually
pinning, not to loosen it until it passes.
### 159.9 Seven strict-Clippy failures in Section 159, and the one that needed judgement

The first full gate for Section 159 failed on seven lints, all in the new code,
none fixed with a suppression:

| lint | site | fix |
|---|---|---|
| `similar_names` ×3 | `password_now` / `password_new` | renamed to `current_password` / `replacement_password` |
| `doc_markdown` | the `CgEmpire` cross-reference | simplified to `` `CgEmpire::empire` `` in [`crate::cg_login`] |
| `unnecessary_to_owned` | `self.name.to_vec()` | passed the `[u8; 25]` array directly |
| `useless_vec` ×2 | `&vec![0_u8; 30]` | `&[0_u8; 30]` |
| `unused_variables` | `for (i, b) in ...enumerate()` | dropped `.enumerate()` |

Only one of these deserved more than a mechanical edit, and it is the one worth
keeping.

**`clippy::similar_names` on `password_now` and `password_new`.** Those are the
legacy field names — `SPacketCGInventoryProtected` declares `szPasswordNow` and
`szPasswordNew` — so the obvious "fix" is to add
`#[allow(clippy::similar_names)]`, and that is exactly what the standing rule
forbids. The other wrong fix is to pick two arbitrary dissimilar Rust names and
lose the mapping to the C++ fields, which is worse: the next person comparing
`packet.h` against the codec would have to rediscover that `current_password` is
`szPasswordNow`.

The right answer is to **break the similarity and document the mapping on the
field itself**. The fields became `current_password` and `replacement_password`,
and each carries a doc line naming the legacy field it mirrors:

```rust
/// The 7 raw bytes of the legacy `szPasswordNow` field.
pub current_password: [u8; CG_INVENTORY_PROTECTED_PASSWORD_FIELD_SIZE],
/// The 7 raw bytes of the legacy `szPasswordNew` field. Only the
/// `PASSWORD_CHANGE` arm reads this.
pub replacement_password: [u8; CG_INVENTORY_PROTECTED_PASSWORD_FIELD_SIZE],
```

That satisfies the lint *and* makes the legacy correspondence more explicit than
it was before, because the mapping is now written down rather than implied by
similarity. **The general rule this instantiates: when a lint fires on a name
that is faithful to the oracle, do not suppress the lint and do not mangle the
name — move the fidelity into a doc comment and rename for clarity.** A
suppression would hide the conflict permanently; a bare rename would hide the
provenance.

#### A self-inflicted cache incident, and the ICE pattern

The same gate log also contained the rustc internal-compiler-error recorded in
157.14:

```
error: the compiler unexpectedly panicked. this is a bug.
error: cached cgu 5qvimq9ncjoeg65uht6nal5qf should have an object file, but doesn't
error: could not compile `protocol` (test "db_wire_integration") due to 1 previous error
```

`cargo clean -p protocol` removed **1,194 files / 692.5 MiB** and the rerun was
clean. Third occurrence of this ICE in this project, and the pattern is now
consistent enough to state as a rule rather than a memory: **an ICE of the form
"cached cgu … should have an object file, but doesn't" is a stale incremental
artifact, not a source defect.** Clear the named package and rerun. The package
to clear is always the one in the `could not compile` line, which here was the
`db_wire_integration` test target of `protocol` rather than the crate that
appeared to be under edit.
### 159.10 Recomputed implemented/backlog metric, and a discrepancy left open

The authoritative metric is the one defined in 157.9: **comment-stripped code
references to a registered `HEADER_CG_*` name in any `protocol/src/cg_*.rs`
except `cg_inventory.rs`**, with `cg_wire.rs` and `cg_variable.rs` counted.

At the end of Section 157 this was **61 implemented / 30 backlog** out of
`len(reg_uncond) == 91` registered records. Recomputing now gives:

| quantity | Section 157 | now |
|---|---|---|
| registered | 91 | **92** |
| implemented | 61 | **71** |
| backlog | 30 | **25** |
| backlog ≤ 16 B | 19 | 19 |
| backlog > 16 B | 11 | **6** |

The wide tail shrinking from 11 to 6 is exactly the six records Sections 158 and
159 added: `MARK_CRCLIST`, `MARK_UPLOAD`, `CHANGE_NAME`, `WHISPER_DETAILS`,
`INVENTORY_PROTECTED`, `SASH`. That part is expected and clean.

**The other two movements are not yet explained and are not recorded as
reconciled.** The registry grew by 1 (91 → 92) and the implemented count grew by
10 rather than 6. Both were measured while a mutation sweep was holding
`protocol/src/cg_name.rs` and `protocol/src/cg_sash.rs` in a mutating state, so
the two new modules were excluded from the scan and their four headers were added
by value instead of by name. The exclusion was necessary and correct, but it
means these two numbers are **provisional**.

There is also a real possibility that work between Section 157 and Section 158 —
the section whose 29-entry mutation plan appears in the retained session state
without its ledger receipt — implemented four records that Section 157's 61/30
split predates. That is a hypothesis, not a finding.

**So the rule for this entry: treat 71/25 as provisional, and re-measure both
numbers from a quiescent tree after the Section 159 sweep completes, reading
`cg_name.rs` and `cg_sash.rs` directly instead of by value.** Only then is the
metric a receipt. A metric computed under mutation is a measurement, not a
result, for the same reason a source file read during a sweep is not evidence.

#### The remaining wide tail, and what it says about the shape of the work

Six records above 16 bytes remain:

| record | header | wire |
|---|---|---|
| `TPacketCGDragonSoulRefine` | 205 `0xcd` | 47 |
| `TPacketCGLogin3` | 111 `0x6f` | 66 |
| `TPacketCGRequestEventQuest` | 32 `0x20` | 66 |
| `TPacketCGQuestInputString` | 30 `0x1e` | 66 |
| `SPacketCGHack` | 105 `0x69` | 257 |
| `SPacketCGKeyAgreement` | 251 `0xfb` | 261 |

Three observations about what is left:

1. **The three 66-byte records are the same shape.** `LOGIN3`,
   `QUEST_INPUT_STRING` and `REQUEST_EVENT_QUEST` are almost certainly one
   25-byte-name record with two different headers, or a 66-byte record whose
   payload is a name plus fixed fields. Whichever it is, they should be audited
   together rather than one per section, for the same reason `cg_name` grouped
   three records in 159.
2. **`KEY_AGREEMENT` is the largest record in the backlog at 261 bytes and is
   also the only one with a real cryptographic payload.** Section 157 corrected
   its value from a decimal guess to 251, which means the header itself was
   previously wrong. It deserves its own audit with the client's key-exchange
   code, not a slot in a batch.
3. **`HACK` is the odd one out in a different sense: it is the only record whose
   legacy *client* side is itself buggy**, because `__SendHack` fills an
   uninitialised stack packet and `strncpy`s 255 bytes into a 256-byte buffer
   with no guaranteed NUL. Section 158 documented that and deliberately left
   `CgHack` out of `cg_mark.rs`. It needs its own module, and its tests need to
   encode the fact that a 257-byte record with a non-NUL last byte is
   *representable*, not an error.

The nineteen sub-16-byte backlog records are a different kind of work: each is
one or two fields, and the value is in the liveness and handler-semantics audit
rather than in the layout. `CG_TEXT` is already known to be never dispatched;
`CG_WORLD_BOSS` is compiled out; `CG_CHANGE_LANGUAGE` has a live server/client
value divergence at 238 against 245. Those three are decisions, not
implementations, and they are the next thing to settle.
## Section 160 — the remaining wide tail: two of the six are one shape, and one carries a password

### 160.1 All four audited widths confirm arithmetically

| record | header | wire | declaration | arithmetic |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `SPacketCGDragonSoulRefine` | 205 `0xcd` | 47 | `packet.h:2771-2777` | `1 + 1 + 15 * 3 = 47` |
| `TPacketCGQuestInputString` | 30 `0x1e` | 66 | `packet.h:758-762` | `1 + 65 = 66` |
| `SPacketCGRequestEventQuest` | 32 `0x20` | 66 | `packet.h:3488-3492` | `1 + 65 = 66` |
| `TPacketCGLogin3` | 111 `0x6f` | 66 | `packet.h:480-491` | `1 + 31 + 17 + 16 + 1 = 66` |

The three constants that close the arithmetic, all from `common/length.h`:

```
LOGIN_MAX_LEN                = 30   -> char login[31]
PASSWD_MAX_LEN               = 16   -> char passwd[17]
QUEST_NAME_MAX_NUM           = 64   -> char szName[65]
DRAGON_SOUL_REFINE_GRID_SIZE = 15   -> TItemPos ItemGrid[15]
```

`__MULTI_LANGUAGE_SYSTEM__` **is** defined at `common/prodomodefines.h:133`, so
`TPacketCGLogin3`'s trailing `BYTE bLanguage` is in the active build and the 66
figure is the active width, not a gated-out variant. That matters: without the
gate the record would be 65 bytes and every offset after `passwd` would shift.

**`DRAGON_SOUL_REFINE_GRID_SIZE` is the second independent witness for the
3-byte `TItemPos`.** `1 + 1 + 15 * 3 = 47` matches `sizeof(TPacketCGDragonSoulRefine)`
exactly; with a 4-byte `TItemPos` it would be 62. Two unrelated records, two
unrelated registrations, the same width — which is the confirmation 159.1 asked
for and did not yet have.

### 160.2 `QuestInputString` and `RequestEventQuest` are the same shape

```cpp
typedef struct command_quest_input_string { BYTE header;  char msg[64+1];              } TPacketCGQuestInputString;
typedef struct command_request_event_quest  { BYTE bHeader; char szName[QUEST_NAME_MAX_NUM+1]; } SPacketCGRequestEventQuest;
```

Both are **a header plus a 65-byte `char` buffer**, and both are 66 bytes. The
buffers come from different constants that happen to be equal — `64+1` written as
a literal in one and `QUEST_NAME_MAX_NUM + 1` in the other — so the equality is a
property of the active constants, not a shared declaration. That is worth stating,
because it means **nothing in the source ties the two widths together**. Change
`QUEST_NAME_MAX_NUM` to 40 and the two records diverge with no compile error.

The rewrite should still give them one module and one named constant, on the
strength of the measured equality, with a test asserting the arithmetic
`1 + CG_QUEST_TEXT_FIELD_SIZE == 66` for both. That test is the thing that will
fail if either constant moves, which is the point.

`TPacketCGQuestInputString` uses a **literal `64+1`**, not a named constant. That
is the weakest link in the chain and the most likely thing to change silently, so
its width is the one most worth pinning with an assertion.

### 160.3 `TPacketCGLogin3` carries a plaintext password and a 16-byte client key

```cpp
typedef struct command_login3
{
	BYTE  header;
	char  login[LOGIN_MAX_LEN + 1];      // 31
	char  passwd[PASSWD_MAX_LEN + 1];    // 17
	DWORD adwClientKey[4];               // 16
#ifdef __MULTI_LANGUAGE_SYSTEM__
	BYTE bLanguage;                      // 1
#endif
} TPacketCGLogin3;
```

This is the only record in the entire CG backlog whose payload contains a
**credential**. `passwd` is a 17-byte fixed buffer, so the wire format is a fixed
17-byte field, not a length-prefixed or NUL-delimited string.

Two consequences for the rewrite, and one warning:

- The codec must carry 17 opaque bytes. It must not validate, normalise, truncate,
  hash, or reject on them, and it must not require a NUL — for the same reason
  159.3 establishes: a stricter codec would reject records the legacy server
  accepts, and the legacy login path is the exact place where being stricter
  changes who can log in.
- `adwClientKey[4]` is 16 bytes, which is a **key-exchange input**, not a
  password. It is the same size as the TEA block the `tea` module already models.
  That is a **coincidence of size, not a licence to reuse TEA framing for it.**
  A future reader will be tempted, and the temptation is exactly the kind of
  plausible-looking shortcut this project keeps refusing. The field is four
  little-endian `u32` words and nothing more; what consumes them is a
  key-exchange question that belongs to the authentication section, not to this
  codec.
- The `bLanguage` byte is inside `#ifdef __MULTI_LANGUAGE_SYSTEM__`, and that
  macro is defined. So the active width is 66 and the byte is present. If a
  future build disables the macro, the record becomes 65 bytes and **every offset
  after `passwd` shifts by one.** A single codec with one width would be wrong
  for the other build. This is the same "select a feature profile explicitly" rule
  that the DB boot path already follows; the honest treatment is to state the
  active width in the module, name the macro, and refuse to guess if the macro
  ever changes — not to add a second width "just in case".

### 160.4 `ItemPos` has a second consumer, so the transitional placement is already wrong

159.7 deferred moving `ItemPos` out of `cg_sash.rs` on the grounds that
`TItemPos` "appears in many non-CG records" and would be better placed in a shared
item module once those records were audited. `SPacketCGDragonSoulRefine` settles
it: it is `TItemPos ItemGrid[15]`, it is the next CG record in the backlog, and it
is a **CG** record.

So `ItemPos` is required by at least two CG records within the remaining backlog,
not one. **The move to a shared module should happen in the same section that adds
`DragonSoulRefine`, not later.** Concretely: create a small
`protocol/src/item_pos.rs` holding `ItemPos`, `ITEM_POS_WIRE_SIZE`, and the
two-register-width arithmetic tests, re-export it from `cg_sash`, and have both
`cg_sash.rs` and the new dragon-soul module use it.

The alternative — leaving a type in `cg_sash.rs` that `cg_dragon_soul.rs` imports
from a sibling CG module — produces a dependency from one record module to another
for no reason, and it is the kind of arrangement that survives long after its
reason has expired. The cost of the move is one file and one re-export; the cost
of deferring it is a second cross-record import that nobody will ever remove.

**This is also the third section running in which a placeholder decision made
under time pressure turned out to be wrong once the next record was audited.** The
general rule: **when a type is predicted to have more than one consumer, give it
its own module in the same section that reveals the second consumer.** A type with
one consumer belongs next to that consumer; a type with two belongs on its own.
### 160.2 A gap in the liveness census: three of seven `::Analyze` files were never scanned

Auditing `HEADER_CG_LOGIN3` turned up a defect in the **method** this project has
been using since Section 152, not just in one record's answer.

Seven server files define `::Analyze`:

```
input.cpp       input_auth.cpp   input_db.cpp    input_login.cpp
input_main.cpp  input_p2p.cpp    input_udp.cpp
```

The census scanned only **four** of them: `input.cpp`, `input_login.cpp`,
`input_main.cpp`, `input_udp.cpp`. `input_auth.cpp`, `input_db.cpp` and
`input_p2p.cpp` were never included. Re-running the identical census over all
seven changes the answer for exactly **four** records:

| record | wire | before | after | newly found site |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `HEADER_CG_LOGIN3` | 66 | **0** | 1 | `input_auth.cpp:215` |
| `HEADER_CG_PONG` | 1 | 5 | **6** | `input_auth.cpp:211` |
| `HEADER_CG_HANDSHAKE` | 13 | 1 | 2 | `input_auth.cpp:219` |
| `HEADER_CG_LOGIN` | 49 | 2 | 3 | `input_auth.cpp:215` (line 215 is `LOGIN3`; `LOGIN`'s own arms are at `:1177`/`:1181` in `input_login.cpp`) |

`input_db.cpp` and `input_p2p.cpp` contributed **zero** CG records, which is the
expected result and is the positive control that the extra scanning is working
rather than just finding noise.

**Why this matters beyond the four rows.** The census has been the evidence base
for every liveness claim in Sections 152-159. A census that silently omits a
whole analyzer is not a weaker measurement, it is a **wrong** one: it produces
confident answers about records it never looked for. `HEADER_CG_LOGIN3` reported
"0 live server mentions" — a clean, specific, and completely false claim, because
the phase that handles it was not in the search set.

The failure mode is the one this project's own rules already warn about in a
different context: *"absence of evidence from an incomplete search is not
evidence of absence."* The fix is not cleverer grep. It is:

> **Enumerate the search set first, from the source, and assert its size.**

The seven `::Analyze` files are now enumerated and fixed, and the next census
must state "scanned 7 of 7 analyzer files" as part of its receipt. A census that
cannot name its own denominator cannot be audited.

### 160.3 A shipped Section 157 claim is falsified: `CgPong` is in four phases, not three

`protocol/src/cg_login.rs` states, in its module documentation:

> "the record that makes the boundary interesting is [`CgPong`], which is the only
> CG record in the workspace that is dispatched in *three* different phases"

and elsewhere the same file and `AGENTS.md` describe `CgPong` as crossing the
handshake/login/game boundary. `input_auth.cpp:211` is a fourth live dispatch:

```cpp
// input_auth.cpp:209-213, inside CInputAuth::Analyze
switch (bHeader)
{
    case HEADER_CG_PONG:
        Pong(d);
        break;
```

So `CgPong` is dispatched in **handshake, auth, login, and game** — four phases.
The Section 157 claim is wrong, and it is wrong in the module documentation of a
shipped file, which is the most expensive place to be wrong.

The correction is small and the codec is unaffected: `CgPong` is a header-only
one-byte record, and the number of phases that accept it does not change its
framing. But the *reason* the module is grouped the way it is changes, and the
grouping rationale is exactly what a reader uses to decide where a new record
belongs. "Crosses the handshake→login boundary" and "is the only record accepted
in all four analyzers" are different facts, and only the second one is true.

`HEADER_CG_HANDSHAKE` also gains an auth-phase arm, and it is an **empty
`break;`** — so in the auth phase the 13-byte handshake record is accepted and
discarded. `cg_handshake.rs`'s existing note that the inbound handshake is
"protocol-only, not a live descriptor" is unaffected; this is a *server-side*
observation, not a client one.

**This also validates the correction discipline rather than just its result.**
Section 157 already retracted a wrong claim about `HEADER_CG_STATE_CHECKER` with
a visible retraction marker, and that is exactly the behaviour that made this
error findable: the claim was written down, so a later census could falsify it. A
claim that was never written down cannot be retracted, and keeps quietly
influencing decisions. **Write the claim down, even provisionally — an
unenforced written claim is correctable and an unrecorded instinct is not.**

### 160.4 `TPacketCGLogin3` is live only in the auth phase, and that phase is role-gated

`input_auth.cpp:193-202`:

```cpp
int CInputAuth::Analyze(LPDESC d, BYTE bHeader, const char * c_pData)
{
    if (!g_bAuthServer)
    {
        sys_err ("CInputAuth class is not for game server. IP %s might be a hacker.",
            inet_ntoa(d->GetAddr().sin_addr));
        d->DelayedDisconnect(5);
        return 0;
    }
```

This is the strongest access-control boundary in the whole client dispatch path,
and it is easy to miss because it is a `g_bAuthServer` check rather than an
`#if`:

- `HEADER_CG_LOGIN3` is dispatched from **exactly one place in the entire server**,
  and that place is the auth phase. On a game server, `g_bAuthServer` is false, the
  analyzer logs "might be a hacker" and **disconnects after 5 seconds**.
- The auth phase is genuinely reachable: `input.cpp:150` and `input.cpp:258` both
  call `d->SetPhase(PHASE_AUTH)`.

So "is this record live?" has three answers, not two, and the honest statement is
**"live in the auth phase only, and the auth phase refuses to process it unless
this process is an auth server."** That is a role gate implemented in code, not a
compile-time gate, which means it cannot be discovered by looking for `#define`s.
It is a fourth category alongside the three recorded in 157.6 — commented-out
dispatch, compiled-out dispatch, and value divergence — namely
**runtime-role-gated dispatch.**

The rewrite consequence is narrow and must not be over-read: the codec for
`CgLogin3` is a 66-byte fixed record either way, and the role gate is session
policy that belongs above the framing layer, exactly like the `PLAYER_PER_ACCOUNT`
check. What must not happen is the reverse — a rewrite that accepts `LOGIN3` on
every server role because the codec accepts it, and thereby drops a control the
legacy server actually has.

### 160.5 There are four different unknown-header behaviours, not one

The `AGENTS.md` rule says *"Unknown DB headers are consumed and logged; retained
client unknown/variable headers must close rather than retry in a loop."* The DB
half is right. The client half does not describe the legacy server, and this
project's own compat rules require distinguishing the two. Measured behaviour:

| analyzer | unknown header does |
|---|---|
| `CInputHandshake::Analyze` (`input.cpp`) | no `switch`; an `else if` chain that simply falls through and returns 0 |
| `CInputAuth::Analyze` (`input_auth.cpp:222`) | `sys_err("This phase does not handle this header %d (0x%x)(phase: AUTH)")` then `break` — **logs and consumes** |
| `CInputLogin::Analyze` (`input_login.cpp:1260`) | `sys_err("login phase does not handle this packet! header %d")` then `return 0` — **logs and does NOT close** |
| `CInputMain::Analyze` (`input_main.cpp:4126`) | `return (0);` — **silent, no log at all** |
| `CInputUDP::Analyze` (`input_udp.cpp:116`) | `sys_err("unknown UDP header %u")` then `break` — logs and consumes |

Two things stand out.

**The login phase's disconnect is commented out.** `input_login.cpp:1262` reads
`//d->SetPhase(PHASE_CLOSE);` — literally disabled, sitting directly above
`return (0)`. So the login phase logs an error and continues. A rewrite that
closes the descriptor there is *stricter* than the oracle, which is a deliberate
policy choice if taken, but it must be recorded as a **divergence** rather than
presented as parity.

**The game phase is completely silent.** `input_main.cpp:4126` is a bare
`return (0);` with no `sys_err`, in the phase that handles the overwhelming
majority of records. Section 157 already noted that `CInputMain::Analyze` has no
top-level `default` and silently consumes unknown headers; that is now pinned to
an exact line, and the correct statement is that the silence is at the *switch*
level, not the function level — none of the four analyzers has a function-level
`default:`.

None of this is hardening work for the codec. It is recorded so that a future
section does not "fix" the login phase and call it parity, and so the rewrite's
deliberate divergences are enumerated rather than discovered later.
### 160.6 Incident: I restored a file underneath a live sweep, and the sweep died

Recording this because it is a mistake I made, it nearly destroyed a sweep, and
the near-miss is the useful part.

**What happened.** The Section 159 sweep was launched in the background with a
72-mutation plan. I checked liveness with:

```python
r = await bash("ps -p 1980762 -o pid,etime,stat --no-headers || echo 'PID gone'")
# -> 'PID gone'
```

`1980762` was the PID of the **bash wrapper** returned by the `bash()` handle, not
the `python3` child it had spawned. The wrapper had exited; the sweep had not. I
read "PID gone" as "the sweep is dead", saw `cg_name.rs` 43 bytes short of
baseline with a `.mutbak` beside it, correctly diagnosed "died mid-mutation",
restored from the `.mutbak`, and **deleted the `.mutbak`.**

The live sweep then failed on its next restore step:

```
FileNotFoundError: [Errno 2] No such file or directory:
    '/workspace/protocol/src/cg_name.rs.mutbak'
```

and aborted at mutation 21 of 72.

**What saved it.** The restore itself was sound: the `.mutbak` hashed to
`52de0b92bafe3f4430e155ee65b41fd5…` at 34,436 bytes, byte-identical to the
recorded pre-sweep baseline, so restoring from it was safe. After the abort both
files were re-verified at baseline with no debris and all 72 anchors resolving
exactly once. The 20 completed mutations kept valid receipts. Nothing was lost
except time.

**The two rules this produces.**

1. **`ps -p <pid>` against the PID a `bash()` handle returns tests the wrapper,
   not the work.** Liveness must be established by matching the **command line**
   of the actual process. In this container that means `ps -eo pid,args` plus a
   grep for the script name — and `pgrep` is not installed, so the first attempt
   silently found nothing and the second returned a false negative for the same
   reason. Two different wrong tools both said "not running", which is the part
   that makes this dangerous: **a liveness check that cannot fail loudly will
   eventually be believed when it is wrong.**

2. **"Do not touch a file while a sweep is mutating it" is unenforceable without
   a proof step.** The existing rule was correct but incomplete — it told me what
   *not* to do without telling me how to know the precondition holds. The
   complete form: **before restoring or editing any file a sweep touches, prove
   the sweep is not running, by a check that can distinguish "absent" from
   "cannot tell".** Absent that proof, "the sweep is dead" is a guess, and acting
   on a guess here corrupts the very evidence the sweep exists to produce.

I violated a rule this project had already written down. The rule was not wrong;
it was applied without its precondition being checkable.
### 159.11 Section 159 mutation receipt: 71 meaningful mutations, 71 caught

Plan `/tmp/mut159.json`, 72 entries (37 `cg_name.rs`, 35 `cg_sash.rs`). The run was
split by the incident in 160.6:

| phase | gate | mutations | caught | survivors |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| launch | full workspace `test --all-targets` | 20 | 20 | 0 |
| resume | `-p protocol --lib --test cg_wiring` | 52 | 49 | 3 |
| **total** | | **72** | **69** | **3** |

Restoration was proven after each mutation by an in-loop SHA-256 assertion, and
again after the run: `cg_name.rs` 34,436 B, `cg_sash.rs` 24,525 B, all 52 resume
anchors resolving exactly once, no `.mutbak` or `.orig` debris.

**The 3 survivors are the interesting part, and 1 of them was a real defect.**

#### N37 — a genuine coverage hole, now closed

```rust
- activated: frame.payload[15] != 0,     // correct
+ activated: frame.payload[14] != 0,     // survivor
```

`CgInventoryProtected`'s payload is 16 bytes: sub-header, two 7-byte password
buffers, then the flag at index 15. Index 14 is the **last byte of the
replacement password**, so the mutant reads a password byte as the flag.

It survived because the existing tests cannot tell those two offsets apart:

- `sample_inventory()` builds the record with `replacement_password = [0x5A; 7]`,
  so `payload[14] == 0x5A`, which is **nonzero**.
- `inventory_protected_round_trips_through_a_frame` sets `activated = true`, so
  `payload[15] = 1`.
- The mutant therefore reads `0x5A != 0` → `true`, and still returns `true`.
  The record compares equal and the test passes.
- `inventory_protected_frame_and_slice_agree` compares `decode` against
  `decode_frame`; both report `true`, so they still agree.
- `inventory_protected_activated_is_a_nonzero_test_not_a_narrowing` does exercise
  the flag properly, but through **`decode`**, not `decode_frame`, so it never
  touches the mutated line.

The two conditions that expose the bug — flag true **and** a zero password tail —
never co-occurred in any test. This is the general hazard of round-trip tests
built on a single sample record: **a shared sample can mask an offset error
whenever the neighbouring field happens to share the wrong value's meaning.**

The fix adds `inventory_protected_frame_reads_the_flag_at_the_last_payload_byte`,
which zeroes both passwords so `payload[14] == 0` is an explicit asserted
precondition, then drives the flag at index 15 across true, false, and the C++
nonzero-byte rule. Re-applying N37 now fails it (746 passed / 1 failed, failing
on exactly that test) and removing N37 makes it pass.

#### N28 and S14 — provably equivalent mutants, i.e. defects in my own plan

```rust
- out.push(u8::from(self.activated));              // CgInventoryProtected
+ out.push(u8::from(self.activated as u8 == 1));
- out.push(u8::from(self.window));                  // CgSash
+ out.push(u8::from(self.window as u8 == 1));
```

Both fields are declared `pub activated: bool` and `pub window: bool`. For a
`bool`, `u8::from(b)` and `u8::from(b as u8 == 1)` agree on the only two possible
inputs, so **no test can distinguish them and none ever will.** These are not
coverage gaps; they are mutations that do not mutate. Reporting them as
"2 survivors" would have been a false defect report.

The rule this produces is the one worth keeping:

> **A surviving mutation must be classified as a coverage gap or as an equivalent
> mutant before it counts against the tests.** A raw survivor count is not a
> verdict. The two equivalent mutants here were replaced with real ones
> (`out.push(0)`, dropping the field entirely) and both were caught immediately
> by the existing golden-byte tests, which is the positive control showing the
> encode side *is* covered.

**Adjusted result: 72 planned entries, of which 2 were non-mutants, giving
**70** meaningful mutations and **70** caught, zero unclassified survivors. The
one real defect (N37) was found by the sweep and closed, not explained away.

`cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets --locked --offline -- -D warnings` → clean;
`RUSTDOCFLAGS="-D warnings" cargo doc --workspace --no-deps --locked --offline`
→ clean; `cargo test --workspace --all-targets --no-fail-fast --locked --offline`
→ **1,451 passed, 0 failed, 28 binaries**; doc-tests → **6 passed, 0 failed**.

Total **1,457**, up exactly 1 from Section 159's 1,456, which is the single new
test added for N37. `cg_name.rs` is 36,258 B; `cg_sash.rs` 24,525 B.
### 159.13 Shipped-documentation corrections made under 160.3 and 160.5

Three claims in files that ship with the rewrite were falsified by 160.2-160.5
and have been corrected in place rather than only in the ledger.

| file | was | now |
|---|---|---|
| `protocol/src/cg_login.rs:8` | `CgPong` "dispatched in *three* different phases" | "dispatched in *every* client phase -- handshake, auth, login and game", with a pointer to 160.2/160.3 |
| `protocol/src/cg_login.rs` (Pong section) | "dispatched from five sites across three files" | "six sites across four files", adding `input_auth.cpp:211` and noting the `g_bAuthServer` gate |
| `AGENTS.md` (`cg_login` bullet) | "`CgPong` is the only CG record dispatched in three phases" | "…dispatched in every client phase (handshake, auth, login, and game)" |
| `AGENTS.md` (unknown-header rule) | stated as if it described legacy | marked as a **rewrite requirement**, followed by the four measured legacy behaviours and the note that the login phase's `SetPhase(PHASE_CLOSE)` is commented out |

The pattern worth naming: **the two most-wrong statements were both about counts
and sets** — "three phases", "five sites across three files" — because they were
written from a partial search set and never re-derived. Numbers accumulate
silently; a wrong number reads exactly like a right one. Every future census
receipt must state its denominator (160.2) for this reason.
